Abstract

We develop polynomial-time algorithms for near-optimal minimax mean estimation under ℓ2\ell_{2}-squared loss in a Gaussian sequence model under convex constraints. The parameter space is an origin-symmetric, type-2 convex body K⊂ℝnK\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, and we assume additional regularity conditions: specifically, we assume KK is well-balanced, i.e., there exist known radii r,R>0r,R>0 such that r​B2⊆K⊆R​B2rB_{2}\subseteq K\subseteq RB_{2}, as well as oracle access to the Minkowski gauge of KK. Under additional conditions guaranteeing an efficient approximate quadratic-form-maximization oracle on KK, our procedures achieve the minimax rate up to factors that depend polylogarithmically on the dimension, while remaining computationally efficient.

We further extend our methodology to the linear regression and robust heavy-tailed settings, establishing polynomial-time near-optimal estimators when the constraint set satisfies the regularity conditions above. To the best of our knowledge, these results provide the first general framework for attaining statistically near-optimal performance under such broad geometric constraints while preserving computational tractability.

1 Introduction

Many statistical estimation problems are naturally formulated as constrained mean estimation or constrained regression problems. Given observations corrupted by stochastic noise, one seeks to estimate a signal known to belong to a prescribed constraint set K⊂ℝnK\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}. Of particular interest in this work are origin-symmetric convex constraints possessing favorable geometric structure, such as ellipsoids, hyperrectangles, ℓp\ell_{p}-balls for p≥2p\geq 2, and, more generally, quadratically convex orthosymmetric sets. Such constraint classes arise naturally in nonparametric smoothing, signal recovery, and regression. For example, classical Sobolev smoothness classes become ellipsoidal constraints after expansion in an appropriate orthonormal basis, leading to the well-known Gaussian sequence formulation of nonparametric estimation Pinsker (1980); Tsybakov (2009). More general quadratically convex orthosymmetric constraints, including hyperrectangles and ℓp\ell_{p}-balls for p>2p>2, were studied in the seminal work of Donoho et al. (1990). Ellipsoidal constraints have also played an important role in regression and prediction problems Goldenshluger and Tsybakov (2001); Goldenshluger and Tsybakov (2003); Pathak et al. (2024).

From a decision-theoretic perspective, a fundamental goal is to characterize the minimax risk over the constraint class KK. There is a long history of such results for structured type-2 classes. Pinsker’s classical theorem characterizes the asymptotically minimax risk over ellipsoids in the Gaussian sequence model Pinsker (1980), while Donoho et al. (1990) showed that, for quadratically convex orthosymmetric sets, the minimax risk is closely related to geometric quantities such as Kolmogorov widths. More recently, a substantially more general theory has emerged. In particular, Neykov (2022) derived sharp minimax rates for constrained mean estimation in the Gaussian sequence model for essentially any bounded convex constraint, expressing the optimal rate in terms of the local geometry of KK. Subsequently, Prasadan and Neykov (2026) relaxed convexity to the substantially weaker assumption of star-shapedness, thereby covering an even broader range of constraint sets. In the regression setting, Prasadan and Neykov (2025a) obtained analogous minimax characterizations.

Despite this information-theoretic progress, a major obstacle remains. The general minimax-optimal procedures developed in these works are not computationally efficient. Their constructions rely on carefully designed local packing sets adapted to the geometry of KK. Such packings can contain exponentially many points and are typically difficult to construct or even approximate. Consequently, although these estimators attain the optimal statistical rate for very general constraint sets, they need not admit polynomial-time implementations.

The goal of the present work is therefore different: rather than treating arbitrary convex or star-shaped constraints, we focus on the important subclass of origin-symmetric type-2 convex bodies and ask whether their additional geometric structure can be exploited to obtain computationally efficient, near-minimax estimators.

Our contribution

In this paper, we develop a new framework that yields polynomial-time, near-minimax estimators for constrained mean estimation, robust mean estimation with heavy-tailed noise, and constrained linear regression. Our approach bypasses the packing-set bottleneck entirely. Instead, we build on a classical inequality of B. Carl, which relates the entropy numbers of a convex body to its Kolmogorov nn-widths. This geometric connection allows us to translate statistical rate calculations into width-approximation problems, avoiding the need to construct packing sets.

The central technical ingredient of our work is a new algorithm for efficiently approximating optimal projections of the Kolmogorov widths of the constraint set. These approximations are sufficiently accurate to be used within an iterative estimation procedure whose risk matches the minimax rate up to factors that are polylogarithmic in the dimension (see Remark 2.15).

There is, however, a price to pay: our methods require nontrivial geometric regularity of the constraint set. First, Carl’s inequality yields meaningful constants only for type-2 (see (1.3) and the discussion surrounding it for the definition of a type-2 set), origin-symmetric convex bodies.11 1 In fact, Carl’s inequality holds for all origin-symmetric convex bodies, but the resulting constants are too coarse unless the body is type-2. Second, the efficient approximation of the optimal projections of the Kolmogorov widths requires the constraint set to be type-222 2 Here and throughout the paper, when we say type-2 convex bodies we mean convex bodies in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with sufficiently small type-2 constants (see (1.3))., well-balanced, and to satisfy several additional structural conditions. While these assumptions cover a wide range of constraint classes used in modern statistics, they do exclude convex classes that are meaningful and are statistically minimax-tractable (at least in theory and some in practice). Examples of sets over which our algorithm cannot work well include rigid bodies such as the ℓp\ell_{p} balls for 1≤p<21\leq p<2.

On the other hand, we note that the “dream” of obtaining a polynomial-time minimax algorithm (even with a polylogarthmic slack) whenever one has polynomial-time access to the Minkowski gauge of the origin-symmetric convex set KK, without imposing any additional structural assumptions on KK, is likely unattainable — at least assuming the standard low-degree conjecture for planted submatrix recovery. We demonstrate this in appendix G.5.

1.1 Related Work

We now review several related works. In the Gaussian sequence model setting, when the constraint set is an ellipsoid, a classical result due to Pinsker Pinsker (1980) shows that linear estimators are optimal. One can implement Pinsker’s estimator in polynomial time. A similar result holds for linear regression over ellipsoidal constraints Goldenshluger and Tsybakov (2001); Goldenshluger and Tsybakov (2003). Since ellipsoids are type-2 sets, our framework provides alternative polynomial-time, near-minimax-rate-optimal estimators. Notably, there exist ellipsoids over which the least squares estimator is grossly suboptimal (see, e.g., Zhang (2013)). We emphasize that the least squares estimator is perhaps the most natural estimator in this problem: it simply projects the data YY onto the set KK. This fact highlights the need to develop computationally efficient algorithms beyond least squares. Another computationally natural procedure is the Bayes estimator corresponding to the uniform prior on KK, namely the posterior mean. For a convex set KK, the posterior density is proportional to

exp⁡(−‖Y−θ‖222​σ2)​𝟏​(θ∈K),\displaystyle\exp\left(-\frac{\|Y-\theta\|_{2}^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)\mathbf{1}(\theta\in K),

and is therefore log-concave; consequently, its mean can be approximated in polynomial time using algorithms for sampling truncated Gaussian distributions over convex bodies Cousins and Vempala (2018). Nevertheless, on suitably stretched ellipsoids this estimator can exhibit the same unfavorable behavior as the least squares estimator and can therefore also be grossly suboptimal relative to the minimax risk. We demonstrate this in appendix F.

A related geometric perspective appears in Mourtada (2025), who studies Gaussian location models from the viewpoint of universal coding and sequential prediction. He shows that minimax redundancy is characterized by global covering numbers, and contrasts this with non-sequential Gaussian mean estimation, whose minimax risk is governed by local covering numbers; our work takes the latter local-entropy characterization as its statistical starting point and exploits type-2 geometry and Carl’s inequality to obtain computationally efficient estimators via Kolmogorov-width approximations.

Chandrasekaran and Jordan Chandrasekaran and Jordan (2013) study computational–statistical tradeoffs in the Gaussian sequence model by projecting onto tractable convex outer relaxations of the parameter space, with weaker relaxations reducing computation at the cost of increased statistical error or sample size. In contrast, our goal is to obtain polynomial-time, near-minimax estimation over the original constraint set for a broad class of type-2 convex bodies, using Carl’s inequality and efficiently approximated Kolmogorov-width projections rather than replacing the constraint by an outer relaxation.

Zhang (2013) proposes a near minimax optimal estimator for a linear regression problem with an ℓq\ell_{q} constraints on the signal for q≤1q\leq 1. The author’s algorithm is implementable only when q=1q=1. Our work is significantly different, as we require the constraint set to be of type-2 (which the ℓ1\ell_{1} ball is not). Despite this major difference, there are also some similarities: both our work and Zhang (2013) use approximations of the Kolmogorov widths of the constraint set, as well as Euclidean projections. Javanmard and Zhang (2012) argue that for bounded symmetric convex polytopes, K={x∈ℝn:‖A​x‖∞≤1}K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\|Ax\|_{\infty}\leq 1\}, defined by some matrix A∈ℝm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, the truncated series estimator33 3 A truncated series estimator uses the optimal Euclidean projection from a carefully selected Kolmogorov width, to project the data on a lower dimensional subspace. is nearly optimal for the Gaussian sequence model problem, provided that mm is not too large. However, the authors mention that they do not know how to efficiently implement their estimator. They also formulate a class of constraints of the type {x∈ℝn:‖A​x‖p≤1}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\|Ax\|_{p}\leq 1\} for p>0p>0, although they only show the near optimality result for the truncated series when p=∞p=\infty. Javanmard and Zhang (2012) do conjecture however (see Conjecture 7.1 therein), that the truncated series estimator remains near optimal (within log⁡m\log m of optimal) for sets of the type {x∈ℝn:‖A​x‖p≤1}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\|Ax\|_{p}\leq 1\} for p≥2p\geq 2. While we cannot verify their conjecture, we do show that our estimator provably works near optimally for any well-balanced constraint of the type K={x∈ℝn:‖A​x‖p≤1}K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\|Ax\|_{p}\leq 1\} for any p≥2p\geq 2 (we lose logarithmic factors in mm).

Finally, we note a recent related work by Kur and Putterman (2022), which develops computationally efficient estimators for multidimensional convex and Lipschitz nonparametric regression. The estimators proposed there are fundamentally different from those studied in this paper, as they are specifically tailored to the structure of convex and Lipschitz constraints, whereas our approach is designed to address constrained estimation problems in a considerably more general setting.

1.2 Definitions and Notation

We now outline some definitions and commonly used notation.

We use a lot of absolute constants which we denote with c,C,L,Tc,C,L,T and variations, whose values can change from line to line. We use ρK\rho_{K} to denote the Minkowski gauge (also called Minkowski functional) of a convex body KK. The gauge ρK\rho_{K} is a norm, whenever KK is bounded, origin-symmetric (which we will assume throughout the paper) and absorbing. We use ∥⋅∥p\|\cdot\|_{p} to denote the standard ℓp\ell_{p} norm for p≥1p\geq 1. We use ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| to denote an arbitrary norm on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. We use ∥⋅∥op\|\cdot\|_{\operatorname{op}}, ∥⋅∥F\|\cdot\|_{F} and ∥⋅∥∗\|\cdot\|_{*} to denote the operator, Frobenius and nuclear norms of a matrix respectively, and we use λmin​(A)\lambda_{\min}(A) and λmax​(A)\lambda_{\max}(A) to denote the minimum and maximum eigenvalues for symmetric positive semi-definite (psd) matrix AA. The trace of a matrix is denoted with tr\operatorname{tr}. For two matrices A,B∈ℝm×nA,B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, we put ⟨A,B⟩=tr⁡(A⊤​B)\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\top}B) for the standard Frobenius (Hilbert-Schmidt) dot product. We write ≤\leq and ≥\geq for symmetric psd matrices to mean inequalities in the psd sense. We typically use the letter Π\Pi to denote projections – often when indexed by a closed convex body ΠK\Pi_{K} means (weak) Euclidean projection on KK. We write diag⁡(A)\operatorname{diag}(A) for a square matrix AA to extract its diagonal values, while diag⁡(v)\operatorname{diag}(v) for a vector vv means a matrix with diagonal entries equal to vv and 00 entries otherwise. We denote the nn-dimensional identity matrix with InI_{n}, occasionally omitting the index when the dimension is clear from the context. We use Sn−1S^{n-1} for the unit Euclidean sphere in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, while B2​(x,r)B_{2}(x,r) means the closed Euclidean ball {y∈ℝn:‖x−y‖2≤r}\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\|x-y\|_{2}\leq r\} centered at xx, with the shorthand B2=B2​(0,1)B_{2}=B_{2}(0,1) for the unit Euclidean ball. We will write a∧ba\wedge b and a∨ba\vee b to denote the minimum and maximum of two real numbers a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R}. Occasionally we will use O⁡(1)O(1) and Ω⁡(1)\Omega(1) to denote that a quantity is upper or lower bounded by an absolute constant, respectively. The inequalities ≲\lesssim and ≳\gtrsim suppress absolute constant factors. We write ≍\asymp if both ≲\lesssim and ≳\gtrsim hold.

We continue with the definition of Kolmogorov width which is central to this work.

Definition 1.1 (Kolmogorov width).

Let K⊂ℝnK\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a compact set. The kk-th Kolmogorov width of KK with respect to the Euclidean norm is defined as

dk​(K)=infP∈𝒫ksupθ∈K‖θ−P​θ‖2,d_{k}(K)=\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}_{k}}\sup_{\theta\in K}\left\lVert\theta-P\theta\right\rVert_{2}, (1.1)

where 𝒫k\mathcal{P}_{k} is the set of all projection operators that project a vector onto a kk dimensional subspace of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Next we give a definition of the entropy numbers of a convex body.

Definition 1.2 (Entropy numbers).

Let K⊂ℝnK\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a compact set. The kk-th entropy number of KK with respect to the Euclidean norm is defined as

ek(K)=inf{ϵ>0:∃x1,…,xk∈ℝn such that K⊂⋃i=1k(xi+ϵB2)}.e_{k}(K)=\inf\bigl\{\epsilon>0:\exists x_{1},\dots,x_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\text{ such that }K\subset\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}\bigl(x_{i}+\epsilon B_{2}\bigr)\bigr\}. (1.2)

The local entropy of a body is defined as follows.

Definition 1.3 (Local Metric Entropy).

Given a set KK, define the η\eta-packing number of KK as the maximum cardinality M=M⁡(η,K)M=M(\eta,K) of a set {ν1,…,νM}⊂K\{\nu_{1},\dots,\nu_{M}\}\subset K such that ‖νi−νj‖>η\|\nu_{i}-\nu_{j}\|>\eta for all i≠ji\neq j. Given a fixed sufficiently large constant c>0c>0, define the local metric entropy of KK as log⁡MKloc​(η)\log M_{K}^{\operatorname{loc}}(\eta) where MKloc​(η)=supν∈KM⁡(η/c,B⁡(ν,η)∩K)M_{K}^{\operatorname{loc}}(\eta)=\sup_{\nu\in K}M(\eta/c,B(\nu,\eta)\cap K). When clear from the context we drop the index KK from MKloc​(η)M_{K}^{\operatorname{loc}}(\eta).

The local entropy plays a fundamental role in what follows as Neykov (2022); Prasadan and Neykov (2026) show it determines the minimax rate for the constraint mean estimation problem.

1.3 Geometric background: type-2 constants and Carl’s inequality

We briefly recall the Banach-space geometry underlying the main argument. If K⊂ℝnK\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is an origin-symmetric convex body, its Minkowski gauge ρK\rho_{K} is a norm, and it is useful to regard KK as the unit ball of the normed space

EK:=(ℝn,ρK).\displaystyle E_{K}:=(\mathbb{R}^{n},\rho_{K}).

The relevant geometric parameter is the Rademacher type-2 constant. We use the following second-moment convention: T2​(K)T_{2}(K) is the smallest T≥1T\geq 1 such that, for every finite collection x1,…,xm∈ℝnx_{1},\ldots,x_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

𝔼ϵ​ρK2​(∑i=1mϵi​xi)≤T2​∑i=1mρK2​(xi),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}\rho_{K}^{2}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\epsilon_{i}x_{i}\right)\leq T^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\rho_{K}^{2}(x_{i}), (1.3)

where ϵ1,…,ϵm\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{m} are independent Rademacher random variables. Thus a small type-2 constant means that random signed sums behave, in the norm ρK\rho_{K}, approximately as they do in a Hilbert space. Carl Carl (1985) uses the equivalent first-moment definition of Rademacher type; by the Kahane–Khintchine inequality the two conventions agree up to an absolute constant, which is immaterial for our purposes.

A few examples help calibrate this assumption. Type is invariant under invertible linear changes of coordinates, and hence every ellipsoid has T2​(K)=1T_{2}(K)=1. For 2≤p<∞2\leq p<\infty, let BpnB_{p}^{n} be the unit ball of the ℓp\ell_{p} norm. Then T2​(Bpn)≲p∧log⁡(1+n)T_{2}(B_{p}^{n})\lesssim\sqrt{p}\wedge\sqrt{\log(1+n)} (Bhattiprolu et al., 2021, see equation (8) e.g.), which implies T2​(B∞n)≲log⁡(1+n)T_{2}(B_{\infty}^{n})\lesssim\sqrt{\log(1+n)}; the same latter bound therefore holds for hyperrectangles. In the opposite direction, for 1≤p<21\leq p<2, taking xi=eix_{i}=e_{i} in (1.3) gives

T2​(Bpn)≥n1/p−1/2.\displaystyle T_{2}(B_{p}^{n})\geq n^{1/p-1/2}.

This illustrates why ℓp\ell_{p} balls with p<2p<2 fall outside the regime of this paper. More generally, every nn-dimensional normed space has a finite type-2 constant (indeed T2≲nT_{2}\lesssim\sqrt{n} by John’s theorem), so in finite dimensions our phrase “type-2 body” should be understood as a body whose type-2 constant is sufficiently small, typically constant or polylogarithmic in nn. In Section 6 we show, in particular, that the QCO bodies considered there satisfy T2​(K)≲log⁡nT_{2}(K)\lesssim\sqrt{\log n}.

We next recall the form of Carl’s inequality that is used in the paper. For a bounded linear operator S:E→FS:E\to F, let εk​(S)\varepsilon_{k}(S) denote the smallest radius such that S⁡(BE)S(B_{E}) can be covered by kk translates of that radius multiple of BFB_{F}, and define Carl’s entropy modulus

gm​(S):=infk≥1k1/m​εk​(S).\displaystyle g_{m}(S):=\inf_{k\geq 1}k^{1/m}\varepsilon_{k}(S). (1.4)

Theorem 5 of Carl (1985) (see also Appendix A.4 where we state the result in our notation), in the real case, states the following. If EE has Rademacher type pp, F∗F^{*} (the dual space of FF) has Rademacher type qq, and sj​(S)s_{j}(S) denotes either the jj-th Kolmogorov number or the jj-th Gelfand number of SS, then

(∏j=1msj​(S))1/m≲τp​(E)​τq​(F∗)​m−1+1/p+1/q​gm​(S).\displaystyle\left(\prod_{j=1}^{m}s_{j}(S)\right)^{1/m}\lesssim\tau_{p}(E)\tau_{q}(F^{*})\,m^{-1+1/p+1/q}\,g_{m}(S). (1.5)

Here τp\tau_{p} denotes Carl’s first-moment Rademacher type-pp constant; when p=2p=2 it is equivalent, up to an absolute factor, to the second-moment constant T2T_{2} in (1.3). The case relevant here is p=q=2p=q=2, for which the power of mm disappears. By contrast, without any type assumption Carl’s universal bound has an additional factor mm:

(∏j=1msj​(S))1/m≲m​gm​(S).\displaystyle\left(\prod_{j=1}^{m}s_{j}(S)\right)^{1/m}\lesssim m\,g_{m}(S). (1.6)

This is the precise sense in which the type-2 hypothesis makes Carl’s inequality quantitatively useful for us.

To specialize (1.5) to a convex body, take E=EKE=E_{K}, F=(ℝn,∥⋅∥2)F=(\mathbb{R}^{n},\|\cdot\|_{2}) (thus F∗=FF^{*}=F), and let SS be the identity map. Then S⁡(BE)=KS(B_{E})=K, the dual space F∗F^{*} is again Euclidean and has type-2 constant one, and εk​(S)=ek​(K)\varepsilon_{k}(S)=e_{k}(K) with the convention of Definition 1.2. Carl’s operator-theoretic Kolmogorov numbers are indexed so that dj​(S)d_{j}(S) corresponds to approximation by a subspace of dimension strictly smaller than jj; this differs by one from Definition 1.1. Using monotonicity to absorb this harmless index shift gives

(∏j=1mdj​(K))1/m≲T2​(K)​infk≥1k1/m​ek​(K).\displaystyle\left(\prod_{j=1}^{m}d_{j}(K)\right)^{1/m}\lesssim T_{2}(K)\inf_{k\geq 1}k^{1/m}e_{k}(K). (1.7)

We emphasize that our ek​(K)e_{k}(K) is the non-dyadic covering convention: it uses kk balls. Many modern texts instead reserve “entropy number” for the dyadic quantity obtained using 2k−12^{k-1} balls; Carl’s entropy modulus (1.4), and all entropy numbers in this paper, use the former convention.

1.4 Organization

The paper is structured as follows. In Section 2 we give background results and we state and prove our main result conditionally on the existence of a quadratic form maximization (QFM) oracle for the convex body KK. In Section 3 we argue that indeed such QFM oracles exist for a variety of type-2 convex bodies. In Section 4 we extend the results of Section 2 to the problem of robust heavy-tailed mean estimation. In Section 5 we discuss the extension of our main result to a linear regression setting. In Section 6 we make some remarks about sets on which our algorithm can be implemented. We close out the paper with a brief discussion of selected open problems in Section 7.

2 Conditional Algorithm

Let us observe a single data point Y=μ+ξY=\mu+\xi where μ∈K⊂ℝn\mu\in K\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} for some known compact convex set KK, and ξ=(ξ1,…,ξn)\xi=(\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{n}) is a mean-zero sub-Gaussian random vector with i.i.d. components. We assume that the sub-Gaussian parameter of ξi\xi_{i}, σ2\sigma^{2} (or an accurate upper bound) is known to the statistician. Here by sub-Gaussian parameter we understand the smallest constant σ2∈ℝ+\sigma^{2}\in\mathbb{R}_{+} such that for all λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R} we have 𝔼​exp⁡(λ⋅ξi)≤exp⁡(λ2⋅σ2/2)\mathbb{E}\exp(\lambda\cdot\xi_{i})\leq\exp(\lambda^{2}\cdot\sigma^{2}/2). We remark that this assumption implies that Var⁡(ξi)≤σ2\operatorname{Var}(\xi_{i})\leq\sigma^{2}. Denote the variance Var⁡(ξi)=σ¯2\operatorname{Var}(\xi_{i})=\underline{\sigma}^{2}, noting that σ¯2≤σ2\underline{\sigma}^{2}\leq\sigma^{2}.

When ξ∼N⁡(0,σ2​In)\xi\sim N(0,\sigma^{2}I_{n}), which is part of our model class, Neykov (2022) and later Prasadan and Neykov (2026) showed that when KK is a star-shaped set the minimax rate is given by (η⋆2∧d2)(\eta^{\star 2}\wedge d^{2})44 4 In fact, it is easy to see that η⋆≲d\eta^{\star}\lesssim d and hence the minimax rate can be written as simply η⋆2\eta^{\star 2}., where d=diam⁡(K)d=\mathrm{diam}(K) and η⋆:=η⋆​(K)=sup{η≥0:η2/σ2≤log⁡MKloc​(η)}\eta^{\star}:=\eta^{\star}(K)=\sup\{\eta\geq 0:\eta^{2}/\sigma^{2}\leq\log M^{\operatorname{loc}}_{K}(\eta)\} with MKloc​(η)M^{\operatorname{loc}}_{K}(\eta) being the local entropy of the set KK. The goal of the present paper is to construct a polynomial-time algorithm which nearly achieves the minimax rate over a range of convex bodies KK. Observe that we define the minimax rate with σ\sigma rather than σ¯\underline{\sigma} (in the Gaussian case which gives the lower bound, we have σ¯≡σ\underline{\sigma}\equiv\sigma). We will later see (see Section 4) that this can be relaxed to using σ¯\underline{\sigma} in the definition of η⋆\eta^{\star}, but it requires having more than a single sample.

Throughout the paper, we impose several requirements on the set KK. First, KK is symmetric about 00, so that its Minkowski gauge ρK\rho_{K} defines a norm on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Second, its type-2 constant T2​(K)T_{2}(K), defined in (1.3), is “small” in the sense discussed in Section 1.3; for example, a log⁡n\sqrt{\log n} factor is small for our purposes, whereas a n\sqrt{n} factor is not. Third, we assume an oracle for computing ρK\rho_{K} (which implies a weak membership oracle for KK; see Grötschel et al. (2012)). Finally, there are known constants r,R∈ℝ+r,R\in\mathbb{R}_{+} such that r​B2⊆K⊆R​B2rB_{2}\subseteq K\subseteq RB_{2}. The geometric dependence of the running time on these radii is polynomial in log⁡(R/r)\log(R/r); see Remark A.1 so rr and RR may in principle be exponentially small or large in nn. We refer to such a set as well-balanced. Also, R=d/2R=d/2 always works when the diameter d=diam⁡(K)d=\mathrm{diam}(K) is known, since KK is origin symmetric; otherwise necessarily R≥d/2R\geq d/2.

The bridge between entropy and widths is the specialization of Carl’s inequality recorded in (1.7). We now use it to establish a result guaranteeing the existence of a sufficiently small Kolmogorov width.

Lemma 2.1.

Let KK be a type-2 convex body with type-2 constant T2​(K)T_{2}(K), such that r​B2⊆K⊆R​B2rB_{2}\subseteq K\subseteq RB_{2} for some known r,Rr,R. Let κ:=κ⁡(K)≥1\kappa:=\kappa(K)\geq 1 be a given scalar which can depend on KK. Let η⋆:=η⋆​(K)\eta^{\star}:=\eta^{\star}(K) be the minimax rate defined through the equation η⋆=supη{η≥0:η2/σ2≤log⁡MKloc​(η)}\eta^{\star}=\sup_{\eta}\{\eta\geq 0:\eta^{2}/\sigma^{2}\leq\log M_{K}^{\operatorname{loc}}(\eta)\}. Assume that κ−1/2d~/T2(K)≥2η⋆\kappa^{-1/2}\tilde{d}/T_{2}(K)\geq 2\eta^{\star} and ⌈⌈logc⁡(κ1/2⋅T2​(K))⌉⋅4​η⋆2/σ2⌉≤d~2/(C2​σ2)\lceil\lceil\log_{c}(\kappa^{1/2}\cdot T_{2}(K))\rceil\cdot 4\eta^{\star 2}/\sigma^{2}\rceil\leq\tilde{d}^{2}/(C^{2}\sigma^{2}) for d~=2​R≥d=diam⁡(K)\tilde{d}=2R\geq d=\mathrm{diam}(K) and where C>0C>0 is some absolute constant. Then for m=⌈d~2/(C2​σ2)⌉∧nm=\lceil\tilde{d}^{2}/(C^{2}\sigma^{2})\rceil\wedge n, we have

dm(K)≲κ−1/2⋅d~/c,\displaystyle d_{m}(K)\lesssim\kappa^{-1/2}\cdot\tilde{d}/c, (2.1)

with cc being the constant from the definition of local entropy, which is sufficiently large.

Remark 2.2.

Let us remark here that the constant cc can be taken to be sufficiently large. Since κ≥1\kappa\geq 1 the statement (2.1) is not vacuous and does not follow from the trivial bound dm​(K)≤d~d_{m}(K)\leq\tilde{d}.

Proof of Lemma 2.1.

First consider the case when KK is a singleton, i.e., K={0}K=\{0\} since we are assuming it is origin-symmetric. Then the statement is clearly true since all dm​(K)≡0d_{m}(K)\equiv 0 for all m∈[n]m\in[n]. Furthermore if σ=0\sigma=0, m=nm=n and thus (2.1) continues to hold. Next, consider the non-trivial case when KK contains at least two points and σ>0\sigma>0. It is easy to see that the former implies that for small δ\delta, log⁡Mloc​(δ)≥log⁡2​c>1\log M^{\operatorname{loc}}(\delta)\geq\log 2c>1. This in turn implies, η⋆>0\eta^{\star}>0.

Observe now that for any δ≥2​η∗\delta\geq 2\eta^{*} we have log⁡Mloc​(δ)≤log⁡Mloc​(2​η⋆)≤4​η⋆2/σ2\log M^{\operatorname{loc}}(\delta)\leq\log M^{\operatorname{loc}}(2\eta^{\star})\leq 4\eta^{\star 2}/\sigma^{2} (see Neykov (2022) Lemma II.8 where it is shown that for convex sets the map δ↦log⁡Mloc​(δ)\delta\mapsto\log M^{\operatorname{loc}}(\delta) is non-increasing). Set κ−1/2⋅d~/T2(K)=Υ\kappa^{-1/2}\cdot\tilde{d}/T_{2}(K)=\Upsilon. Under our assumptions we have that Υ≥2​η∗\Upsilon\geq 2\eta^{*}. Next, by Lemma 3 of Yang and Barron (1999) (see also Appendix A.5 where we restate this lemma in our notation) we know that

log⁡M⁡(Υ​cj−1)−log⁡M⁡(Υ​cj)≤log⁡Mloc​(Υ​cj)≤4​η⋆2/σ2,\displaystyle\log M(\Upsilon c^{j-1})-\log M(\Upsilon c^{j})\leq\log M^{\operatorname{loc}}(\Upsilon c^{j})\leq 4\eta^{\star 2}/\sigma^{2}, (2.2)

for j=0,1,…j=0,1,\ldots. Here recall from the definition of local entropy that we use M⁡(δ)M(\delta) to denote the δ\delta packing of KK. Note that for j≥⌈logc⁡(κ1/2⋅T2​(K))⌉j\geq\lceil\log_{c}(\kappa^{1/2}\cdot T_{2}(K))\rceil we have log⁡M⁡(Υ​cj)=0\log M(\Upsilon c^{j})=0. Thus upon summing all the inequalities for j=0,…,⌈logc⁡(κ1/2⋅T2​(K))⌉j=0,\ldots,\lceil\log_{c}(\kappa^{1/2}\cdot T_{2}(K))\rceil we have

log⁡M⁡(Υ​c−1)≤⌈logc⁡(κ1/2⋅T2​(K))⌉​4​η⋆2/σ2,\displaystyle\log M(\Upsilon c^{-1})\leq\lceil\log_{c}(\kappa^{1/2}\cdot T_{2}(K))\rceil 4\eta^{\star 2}/\sigma^{2},

This implies that for k=M⁡(Υ​c−1)≤exp⁡(⌈logc⁡(κ1/2⋅T2​(K))⌉​4​η⋆2/σ2)k=M(\Upsilon c^{-1})\leq\exp(\lceil\log_{c}(\kappa^{1/2}\cdot T_{2}(K))\rceil 4\eta^{\star 2}/\sigma^{2}), we have ek(K)≤κ−1/2⋅d~/(T2(K)c)e_{k}(K)\leq\kappa^{-1/2}\cdot\tilde{d}/(T_{2}(K)c). Hence by (1.7) and since the Kolmogorov widths are decreasing in mm, we have

dm(K)≤(∏k=1mdk(K))1/m≲T2(K)exp(⌈logc(κ1/2⋅T2(K))⌉4η⋆2/σ2/m)κ−1/2⋅d~/(T2(K)c).\displaystyle d_{m}(K)\leq(\prod_{k=1}^{m}d_{k}(K))^{1/m}\lesssim T_{2}(K)\exp(\lceil\log_{c}(\kappa^{1/2}\cdot T_{2}(K))\rceil 4\eta^{\star 2}/\sigma^{2}/m)\kappa^{-1/2}\cdot\tilde{d}/(T_{2}(K)c). (2.3)

Next select m=⌈d~2/(C2​σ2)⌉∧nm=\lceil\tilde{d}^{2}/(C^{2}\sigma^{2})\rceil\wedge n, where d~=2​R\tilde{d}=2R is an upper bound on dd. Since both RR and σ\sigma are assumed to be known, this is a legitimate choice of mm. By assumption ⌈⌈logc⁡(κ1/2⋅T2​(K))⌉⋅4​η⋆2/σ2⌉≤d~2/(C2​σ2)\lceil\lceil\log_{c}(\kappa^{1/2}\cdot T_{2}(K))\rceil\cdot 4\eta^{\star 2}/\sigma^{2}\rceil\leq\tilde{d}^{2}/(C^{2}\sigma^{2}), it is clear by (2.3) that:

dm(K)≲κ−1/2⋅d~/c,\displaystyle d_{m}(K)\lesssim\kappa^{-1/2}\cdot\tilde{d}/c,

where we note that in case m=nm=n the above inequality is trivial as dn​(K)=0d_{n}(K)=0. ∎

Remark 2.3 (Near-optimality of linear projection estimators).

We now digress to provide a useful observation. Lemma 2.1, together with Carl’s inequality, also suggests a connection between type-22 geometry and the performance of linear projection estimators in the Gaussian sequence model. Indeed, if PmP_{m} is an orthogonal projection onto an mm-dimensional subspace, then the estimator μ^=Pm​Y\widehat{\mu}=P_{m}Y satisfies

supμ∈K𝔼μ​‖μ^−μ‖22=σ2​m+supμ∈K‖(I−Pm)​μ‖22.\displaystyle\sup_{\mu\in K}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\|\widehat{\mu}-\mu\|_{2}^{2}=\sigma^{2}m+\sup_{\mu\in K}\|(I-P_{m})\mu\|_{2}^{2}.

Consequently, optimizing over all rank-mm projections gives

infPmsupμ∈K𝔼μ​‖Pm​Y−μ‖22=σ2​m+dm​(K)2.\displaystyle\inf_{P_{m}}\sup_{\mu\in K}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\|P_{m}Y-\mu\|_{2}^{2}=\sigma^{2}m+d_{m}(K)^{2}.

Thus, if one can find

m≲η⋆2σ2such thatdm​(K)≲η⋆,\displaystyle m\lesssim\frac{\eta^{\star 2}}{\sigma^{2}}\qquad\text{such that}\qquad d_{m}(K)\lesssim\eta^{\star},

then a linear projection estimator is minimax optimal up to an absolute constant.

Carl’s inequality and the argument of Lemma 2.1 almost yield such a conclusion. In particular, by telescoping the local entropy bounds across scales, one obtains, up to absolute constants,

log⁡M⁡(K,C​η⋆)≲η⋆2σ2​(1+log⁡diam⁡(K)η⋆).\displaystyle\log M(K,C\eta^{\star})\lesssim\frac{\eta^{\star 2}}{\sigma^{2}}\left(1+\log\frac{\mathrm{diam}(K)}{\eta^{\star}}\right).

Combining this global covering bound with Carl’s inequality therefore suggests the existence of an mm satisfying

m≲η⋆2σ2​(1+log⁡diam⁡(K)η⋆),dm​(K)≲T2​(K)​η⋆.\displaystyle m\lesssim\frac{\eta^{\star 2}}{\sigma^{2}}\left(1+\log\frac{\mathrm{diam}(K)}{\eta^{\star}}\right),\qquad d_{m}(K)\lesssim T_{2}(K)\eta^{\star}.

Hence the best linear projection estimator should satisfy a risk bound of the form

infm{σ2​m+dm​(K)2}≲(T2​(K)2+1+log⁡diam⁡(K)η⋆)​η⋆2.\displaystyle\inf_{m}\left\{\sigma^{2}m+d_{m}(K)^{2}\right\}\lesssim\left(T_{2}(K)^{2}+1+\log\frac{\mathrm{diam}(K)}{\eta^{\star}}\right)\eta^{\star 2}.

We note that the factor log⁡(diam⁡(K)/η⋆)\log(\mathrm{diam}(K)/\eta^{\star}) need not, in general, be logarithmic in the ambient dimension, since the diameter d=diam⁡(K)d=\operatorname{diam}(K) may be arbitrarily large relative to the noise level. In the Gaussian sequence model, however, this dependence on the global diameter can be removed by a sample-splitting localization argument: using one independent Gaussian copy to construct a pilot estimator (namely the Euclidean projection of the copy onto KK), the remaining estimation problem can be localized to the symmetric body 2​K∩C​n​σ​B22K\cap C\sqrt{n}\sigma B_{2}, so that the corresponding logarithmic factor is replaced by log⁡(C​n​ση⋆)≲log⁡n.\log\left(\frac{C\sqrt{n}\sigma}{\eta^{\star}}\right)\lesssim\log n. We emphasize that this produces a sample-split, adaptive estimator rather than a single fixed linear estimator. Details of this construction are given in Appendix B.1. It is natural to ask whether the logarithmic loss above is necessary. More specifically, we conjecture that for type-22 bodies one may have

infm{σ2​m+dm​(K)2}≲poly⁡(T2​(K))​η⋆2.\displaystyle\inf_{m}\left\{\sigma^{2}m+d_{m}(K)^{2}\right\}\lesssim\operatorname{poly}(T_{2}(K))\,\eta^{\star 2}.

Such a result would imply that a suitably chosen linear projection estimator is minimax optimal, up to a factor depending only on the type-22 constant. The main difficulty is that the minimax rate is governed by local metric entropy, whereas Carl’s inequality relates Kolmogorov widths to global metric entropy; it is presently unclear whether the type-22 assumption alone is sufficient to bridge this gap without an additional multiscale logarithmic loss. In addition, it is worth emphasizing that this observation does not by itself yield a polynomial-time algorithm for computing the best linear projection estimator, since one must still determine the appropriate dimension mm and compute an optimal Kolmogorov-width projection PmP_{m}, neither of which is obviously computationally tractable.

Unfortunately, we do not know the optimal projection that yields a small Kolmogorov width. In addition, even calculating the Kolmogorov width dm​(K)d_{m}(K) precisely in general is likely NP hard – see, for instance, Brieden (2002) where the author shows that calculating d0​(K)d_{0}(K) for (even symmetric) convex polytopes cannot be computed in polynomial-time within a factor of 1.0901.090, unless P=NP. Thus, the fact (2.1) appears useless at first glance. However, since we are interested in having a minimax optimal estimator up to “small” factors, we do not need to find the precise optimal Kolmogorov projection. Taking inspiration from Varadarajan et al. (2007), we propose to solve the following semi-definite program (SDP) relaxation of the Kolmogorov width problem

argminXmaxp∈K⁡p⊤​X​p,\displaystyle\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}_{X}\max_{p\in K}p^{\top}Xp, (2.4)
subject to ​tr⁡(X)=n−m,\displaystyle\mbox{subject to }\operatorname{tr}(X)=n-m,
0≤X≤I,X⊤=X\displaystyle~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~0\leq X\leq I,X^{\top}=X

As observed in Varadarajan et al. (2007), the optimal value X⋆X^{\star} that this SDP returns, satisfies p⊤​X⋆​p≤dm2​(K)p^{\top}X^{\star}p\leq d^{2}_{m}(K) for all p∈Kp\in K. The proof of this fact is elementary, and we include a proof below for convenience of the reader. The proof also helps motivate program (2.4).

Lemma 2.4.

The solution to the above SDP problem, X⋆X^{\star}, satisfies: p⊤​X⋆​p≤dm2​(K)p^{\top}X^{\star}p\leq d^{2}_{m}(K) for all p∈Kp\in K.

Proof of Lemma 2.4.

Let Pn−m=I−PmP_{n-m}=I-P_{m}, where PmP_{m} is the optimal Kolmogorov width projection, i.e.,

supp∈K‖(I−Pm)​p‖22=dm2​(K).\displaystyle\sup_{p\in K}\|(I-P_{m})p\|_{2}^{2}=d^{2}_{m}(K).

This is equivalent to supp∈Kp⊤​Pn−m​p≤dm2​(K)\sup_{p\in K}p^{\top}P_{n-m}p\leq d^{2}_{m}(K). Note that Pn−mP_{n-m} is a feasible point to the SDP hence the result follows. ∎

Notably, solving the SDP requires maximizing a quadratic form over a convex body (cf. (2.4)), a formidable task on its own. The authors of Varadarajan et al. (2007) do not encounter this issue, since their body KK is a convex polytope with finitely many vertices, making the quadratic maximization tractable (the maximum is attained at a vertex and can be found by enumerating all vertices). In our setting, no such guarantee holds. We will now assume that there exists an oracle 𝒪K\mathcal{O}_{K} which takes a symmetric psd matrix XX and outputs a vector 𝒪K​(X)∈K\mathcal{O}_{K}(X)\in K such that

𝒪K​(X)⊤​X​𝒪K​(X)≥κ−1​maxp∈K​p⊤​X​p,\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{K}(X)^{\top}X\mathcal{O}_{K}(X)\geq\kappa^{-1}\max_{p\in K}p^{\top}Xp, (2.5)

for some ‘‘small’’55 5 Here by small we mean that κ⁡(K)\kappa(K) is a constant slowly growing with nn. constant κ=κ⁡(K)≥1\kappa=\kappa(K)\geq 1 with probability at least 1−q1-q for some q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1) with log⁡q−1\log q^{-1} being a parameter involved in the number of iterations needed to compute the oracle, whose value will be specified later (see Section 3). In other words, we suppose there exists an approximate solution to the quadratic maximization problem. Later we will see that there is a rich class of type-2 bodies for which such an oracle indeed exists. In order to state our algorithm for approximately solving the SDP, we consider the projection of a vector v∈ℝnv\in\mathbb{R}^{n} onto the convex set

Sk={w∈ℝn:0≤wi≤1,∑i=1nwi=k},\displaystyle S_{k}=\{\,w\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:0\leq w_{i}\leq 1,\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}=k\,\},

where k∈{0,…,n}k\in\{0,\ldots,n\} is given. The projection is defined as

ΠSk​(v)=arg⁡minw∈Sk​12​‖w−v‖22.\displaystyle\Pi_{S_{k}}(v)=\arg\min_{w\in S_{k}}\frac{1}{2}\|w-v\|_{2}^{2}.

ΠSk​(v)\Pi_{S_{k}}(v) can be implemented efficiently (see Algorithm 2). Given the oracle 𝒪K\mathcal{O}_{K} and the projection ΠSk​(⋅)\Pi_{S_{k}}(\cdot), we may approximately solve the SDP with projected sub-gradient descent. We formalize the algorithm below:

 

Algorithm 1 SDP with projected sub-gradient descent

 
0:  Convex body KK, value m∈{0,…,n}m\in\{0,\ldots,n\}, oracle 𝒪K\mathcal{O}_{K} for solving quadratic maximization over KK, a tuning parameter C∈ℝ+C\in\mathbb{R}_{+}, M=1∨⌈4​(n−m)​C4​κ2⌉M=1\vee\lceil 4(n-m)C^{4}\kappa^{2}\rceil maximal number of iterations, γ=1/(κ​C2)∈ℝ\gamma=1/(\kappa C^{2})\in\mathbb{R} is the learning rate.
0:  A symmetric psd matrix X⋆⁣⋆X^{\star\star}
1:  Set X(1)=diag⁡(((n−m)/n,(n−m)/n,…,(n−m)/n))X^{(1)}=\operatorname{diag}(((n-m)/n,(n-m)/n,\ldots,(n-m)/n))
2:  if m==nm==n then
3:   return X(1)X^{(1)}
4:  end if
5:  for k= 1, …, M do
6:   Evaluate pk=𝒪K​(X(k))p_{k}=\mathcal{O}_{K}(X^{(k)})
7:   Set γk=γ/‖pk‖22\gamma_{k}=\gamma/\|p_{k}\|_{2}^{2}
8:   X(k+1)=X(k)−γk​pk​pk⊤X^{(k+1)}=X^{(k)}-\gamma_{k}p_{k}p_{k}^{\top}
9:   Eigendecompose X(k+1)=U​Λ​U⊤X^{(k+1)}=U\Lambda U^{\top}
10:   v=ΠSn−m​(diag⁡(Λ))v=\Pi_{S_{n-m}}(\operatorname{diag}(\Lambda))
11:   X(k+1)=U​diag⁡(v)​U⊤X^{(k+1)}=U\operatorname{diag}(v)U^{\top}
12:  end for
13:  return X⋆⁣⋆:=∑k=1Mγk​X(k)∑k=1MγkX^{\star\star}:=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{M}\gamma_{k}X^{(k)}}{\sum_{k=1}^{M}\gamma_{k}}
 

Next we write down the sub-routine for ΠSn−m\Pi_{S_{n-m}} used in Algorithm 2 as Algorithm 2. We give the justification of Algorithms 2 and 2 below.

 

Algorithm 2 Projection onto the capped simplex Sk={w:0≤wi≤1,∑iwi=k}S_{k}=\{w:0\leq w_{i}\leq 1,\sum_{i}w_{i}=k\}

 
0:  Vector v∈ℝnv\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, integer k∈{0,…,n}k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}
0:  Projected vector w⋆=arg⁡minw∈Sk⁡‖w−v‖22w^{\star}=\arg\min_{w\in S_{k}}\|w-v\|_{2}^{2}

2:  Sort the breakpoints in increasing order
3:  for each interval [bj,bj+1)[b_{j},b_{j+1}) between consecutive breakpoints do
4:   Let I0={i:vi−bj≥1}I_{0}=\{i:v_{i}-b_{j}\geq 1\}, I1={i:0<vi−bj<1}I_{1}=\{i:0<v_{i}-b_{j}<1\}
5:   if |I1|==0|I_{1}|==0 then
6:    if |I0|==k|I_{0}|==k then
7:     Set θ=bj\theta=b_{j}
8:     break
9:    end if
10:    next
11:   end if
12:   Compute
θ=∑i∈I1vi+|I0|−k|I1|\displaystyle\theta=\frac{\sum_{i\in I_{1}}v_{i}+|I_{0}|-k}{|I_{1}|}
13:   if θ∈[bj,bj+1)\theta\in[b_{j},b_{j+1}) then
14:    break
15:   end if
16:  end for
17:  Return wi⋆=min⁡{1,max⁡{0,vi−θ}}w_{i}^{\star}=\min\{1,\max\{0,v_{i}-\theta\}\} for all ii
 

We start by justifying Algorithm 2 which finds ΠSk​v\Pi_{S_{k}}v. Specifically, we have:

Lemma 2.5 (Projection onto the capped simplex).

Let v∈ℝnv\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and k∈{0,…,n}k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}. Then the unique minimizer of

minw∈Sk⁡12​‖w−v‖22\displaystyle\min_{w\in S_{k}}\frac{1}{2}\|w-v\|_{2}^{2}

is given componentwise by

wi⋆=min⁡{1,max⁡{0,vi−θ⋆}},\displaystyle w_{i}^{\star}=\min\{1,\max\{0,v_{i}-\theta^{\star}\}\},

where the scalar θ⋆\theta^{\star} is a solution of

∑i=1nmin⁡{1,max⁡{0,vi−θ⋆}}=k.\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\min\{1,\max\{0,v_{i}-\theta^{\star}\}\}=k.

In addition, observe that wiw_{i} are ordered in the same way, in other words (vi−vj)​(wi−wj)≥0(v_{i}-v_{j})(w_{i}-w_{j})\geq 0 for any i,ji,j.

The proof of Lemma 2.5 is deferred to the appendix. It is clear that this justifies Algorithm 2. We now argue that the projection of a matrix, on the set of symmetric psd matrices which are smaller than the identity matrix in the psd sense and have fixed trace, is given by a simple spectral decomposition plus a projection on the capped simplex.

Lemma 2.6.

Let XX be a symmetric matrix. Then the projection of XX onto the set {W symmetric psd:0≤W≤I,tr(W)=k}\{W\text{ symmetric psd}:0\leq W\leq I,\operatorname{tr}(W)=k\} in the Frobenius norm (i.e., W⋆=argminW‖X−W‖F2W^{\star}=\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}_{W}\|X-W\|_{F}^{2}) is given by

W⋆=U​diag⁡(ΠSk​(diag⁡(Λ)))​U⊤, where ​X=U​Λ​U⊤,\displaystyle W^{\star}=U\operatorname{diag}(\Pi_{S_{k}}(\operatorname{diag}(\Lambda)))U^{\top},\text{ where }X=U\Lambda U^{\top},

is the spectral decomposition of XX.

Proof.

Let W⋆W^{\star} be the minimizer of ‖X−W⋆‖F2\|X-W^{\star}\|_{F}^{2} for W⋆∈{W symmetric psd:0≤W≤I,tr(W)=k}W^{\star}\in\{W\text{ symmetric psd}:0\leq W\leq I,\operatorname{tr}(W)=k\}. Suppose W⋆=U⋆​Λ⋆​U⋆⁣⊤W^{\star}=U^{\star}\Lambda^{\star}U^{\star\top}, where Λ⋆\Lambda^{\star} is a diagonal matrix sorted in descending way (same as sorting as the diagonal entries of Λ\Lambda). Let λ=diag⁡(Λ)\lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\Lambda) and λ⋆=diag⁡(Λ⋆)\lambda^{\star}=\operatorname{diag}(\Lambda^{\star}). We have

‖X−W⋆‖F2=‖X‖F2−2​tr⁡(X⊤​W)+‖W‖F2=‖λ‖22−2​tr⁡(X⊤​W)+‖λ⋆‖22.\displaystyle\|X-W^{\star}\|_{F}^{2}=\|X\|_{F}^{2}-2\operatorname{tr}(X^{\top}W)+\|W\|_{F}^{2}=\|\lambda\|_{2}^{2}-2\operatorname{tr}(X^{\top}W)+\|\lambda^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}.

Note that

tr⁡(X⊤​W)=∑i∑j(ui⊤​uj⋆)2​λi​λj⋆=λ⊤​A​λ⋆,\displaystyle\operatorname{tr}(X^{\top}W)=\sum_{i}\sum_{j}(u_{i}^{\top}u_{j}^{\star})^{2}\lambda_{i}\lambda^{\star}_{j}=\lambda^{\top}A\lambda^{\star},

where A={Ai​j}i,j∈[n]=(ui⊤​uj⋆)2A=\{A_{ij}\}_{i,j\in[n]}=(u_{i}^{\top}u_{j}^{\star})^{2} is a doubly stochastic matrix (by the orthonormality of UU and U⋆U^{\star}). By Birkhoff–von Neumann’s theorem A=∑i∈[L]αi​PiA=\sum_{i\in[L]}\alpha_{i}P_{i} for some permutation matrices PiP_{i}, L∈ℕL\in\mathbb{N} and ∑i∈[L]αi=1\sum_{i\in[L]}\alpha_{i}=1. Thus

tr⁡(X⊤​W)=∑i∈[L]αi​λ⊤​Pi​λ⋆≤λ⊤​λ⋆,\displaystyle\operatorname{tr}(X^{\top}W)=\sum_{i\in[L]}\alpha_{i}\lambda^{\top}P_{i}\lambda^{\star}\leq\lambda^{\top}\lambda^{\star},

where the last inequality comes from the rearrangement inequality since both λ\lambda and λ⋆\lambda^{\star} are vectors sorted in descending order.

We conclude that

‖X−W⋆‖F2≥‖λ‖22−2​λ⊤​λ⋆+‖λ⋆‖22=‖λ−λ⋆‖22.\displaystyle\|X-W^{\star}\|_{F}^{2}\geq\|\lambda\|_{2}^{2}-2\lambda^{\top}\lambda^{\star}+\|\lambda^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}=\|\lambda-\lambda^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}.

The above inequality is also clearly an equality whenever U⋆=UU^{\star}=U. Since the projection of λ\lambda onto the set SkS_{k} is ΠSk​(λ)\Pi_{S_{k}}(\lambda) as we showed in Lemma 2.5 the result follows.

∎

The following theorem establishes the validity of Algorithm 2.

Theorem 2.7.

Given as input a convex body KK, a value mm for which dm(K)≤Lκ−1/2d~/cd_{m}(K)\leq L\kappa^{-1/2}\tilde{d}/c for a constant L>0L>0, and an oracle 𝒪K\mathcal{O}_{K} satisfying (2.5) with probability at least 1−q1-q with q=M−11+d~3/σ3q=\frac{M^{-1}}{1+\tilde{d}^{3}/\sigma^{3}}, Algorithm 2 outputs a matrix X⋆⁣⋆X^{\star\star} which, up to an absolute constant factor, satisfies

supp∈Kp⊤​X⋆⁣⋆​p≲d~2/c2,\displaystyle\sup_{p\in K}p^{\top}X^{\star\star}p\lesssim\tilde{d}^{2}/c^{2},

with probability at least 1−(1+d~3/σ3)−11-(1+\tilde{d}^{3}/\sigma^{3})^{-1}.

Remark 2.8.

Let us remark that similarly to Lemma 2.1 the above statement is not vacuous, and contracts the diameter d~\tilde{d}, provided that the constant cc is taken to be sufficiently large and CC from the definition of γ\gamma in Algorithm 2 is also sufficiently large.

Remark 2.9.

Observe that since M=1+⌈4​(n−m)​C4​κ2⌉M=1+\lceil 4(n-m)C^{4}\kappa^{2}\rceil and the oracle works with polynomially many iterations in log⁡q−1\log q^{-1} (see Section 3), if κ\kappa is a “small” constant (i.e., κ≪n\kappa\ll n), and in addition log⁡d~/σ\log\tilde{d}/\sigma is polynomial in nn, we are guaranteed to have log⁡[M⁡(1+d~3/σ3)]\log[M(1+\tilde{d}^{3}/\sigma^{3})] is polynomial in nn, so that our oracle algorithm will run in polynomial time.

Proof of Theorem 2.7.

We first establish the high probability bound. Since we have MM iterations, and the oracle succeeds with probability 1−M−1/(1+d~3/σ3)1-M^{-1}/(1+\tilde{d}^{3}/\sigma^{3}) every time, by the union bound it will fail with probability smaller than 1/(1+d~3/σ3)1/(1+\tilde{d}^{3}/\sigma^{3}), which establishes the claim. Let us now show the guarantee assuming that the oracle never fails.

Let us begin by observing that the function f⁡(X):=supp∈Kp⊤​X​p=supp∈K⟨X,p​p⊤⟩f(X):=\sup_{p\in K}p^{\top}Xp=\sup_{p\in K}\langle X,pp^{\top}\rangle is convex as a maximum of linear functions. It is also well known that p⋆​p⋆⁣⊤p^{\star}p^{\star\top} is a sub-gradient of this function, where p⋆=argmaxp∈K⟨X,p​p⊤⟩p^{\star}=\mathop{\mathrm{argmax}}_{p\in K}\langle X,pp^{\top}\rangle. Next, note that by our definition of the oracle, the vector 𝒪K​(X)\mathcal{O}_{K}(X) is near sub-gradient of the map in the following sense:

f⁡(X)=supp∈K⟨X,p​p⊤⟩≤⟨X,𝒪K​(X)​𝒪K​(X)⊤⟩+(1−κ−1)⋅f⁡(X)\displaystyle f(X)=\sup_{p\in K}\langle X,pp^{\top}\rangle\leq\langle X,\mathcal{O}_{K}(X)\mathcal{O}_{K}(X)^{\top}\rangle+(1-\kappa^{-1})\cdot f(X) (2.6)

Put g(k)=pk​pk⊤g^{(k)}=p_{k}p_{k}^{\top}. Recall that X⋆X^{\star} is the true optimum, which satisfies by Lemma 2.4 that supp∈Kp⊤​X⋆​p≤dm2​(K)\sup_{p\in K}p^{\top}X^{\star}p\leq d^{2}_{m}(K) for all p∈Kp\in K. Observe that we have

f⁡(X(k))−f⁡(X⋆)≤⟨g(k),X(k)−X⋆⟩+(1−κ−1)⋅f⁡(X(k)),\displaystyle f(X^{(k)})-f(X^{\star})\leq\langle g^{(k)},X^{(k)}-X^{\star}\rangle+(1-\kappa^{-1})\cdot f(X^{(k)}),

where we used (2.6) and the fact that ⟨g(k),X⋆⟩≤f⁡(X⋆)\langle g^{(k)},X^{\star}\rangle\leq f(X^{\star}). Since Euclidean projection on a convex set shrinks the distance to any point in the set, we have

‖X(k+1)−X⋆‖F2\displaystyle\|X^{(k+1)}-X^{\star}\|_{F}^{2} ≤‖X(k)−X⋆‖F2+2​γk​⟨g(k),X⋆−X(k)⟩+γk2​‖g(k)‖F2\displaystyle\leq\|X^{(k)}-X^{\star}\|_{F}^{2}+2\gamma_{k}\langle g^{(k)},X^{\star}-X^{(k)}\rangle+\gamma_{k}^{2}\|g^{(k)}\|_{F}^{2}

∎

Once we have obtained the matrix X⋆⁣⋆=V​Λ​V⊤=∑i∈[n]λi​vi​vi⊤X^{\star\star}=V\Lambda V^{\top}=\sum_{i\in[n]}\lambda_{i}v_{i}v_{i}^{\top}, our algorithm proceeds with constructing the matrix A⋆⁣⋆=(I−X⋆⁣⋆)1/2=∑i∈[n]1−λi​vi​vi⊤A^{\star\star}=(I-X^{\star\star})^{1/2}=\sum_{i\in[n]}\sqrt{1-\lambda_{i}}v_{i}v_{i}^{\top}. Consider now the vector A⋆⁣⋆​YA^{\star\star}Y. It is equal to

A⋆⁣⋆​Y=A⋆⁣⋆​μ+A⋆⁣⋆​ξ.\displaystyle A^{\star\star}Y=A^{\star\star}\mu+A^{\star\star}\xi.

In order to estimate A⋆⁣⋆​μA^{\star\star}\mu, we will use A⋆⁣⋆​YA^{\star\star}Y. We have the following lemma justifying that this is not a bad choice.

Lemma 2.10.

Suppose d~≳σ\tilde{d}\gtrsim\sigma. Then, the estimator A⋆⁣⋆​YA^{\star\star}Y of A⋆⁣⋆​μA^{\star\star}\mu satisfies

‖A⋆⁣⋆​Y−A⋆⁣⋆​μ‖22≤d~2/T2,\displaystyle\|A^{\star\star}Y-A^{\star\star}\mu\|_{2}^{2}\leq\tilde{d}^{2}/T^{2},

with probability at least 1−exp(−d~2/(σ2C2′))1-\exp(-\tilde{d}^{2}/(\sigma^{2}C^{{}^{\prime}2})).

Proof.

Applying the Hanson-Wright inequality Rudelson and Vershynin (2013), we obtain:

ℙ(∥A⋆⁣⋆ξ∥22−σ¯2tr(A⋆⋆2)≥t)≤exp(−ct2/(σ4∥A⋆⋆2∥F2)∧t/(σ2∥A⋆⋆2∥op))\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\|A^{\star\star}\xi\|_{2}^{2}-\underline{\sigma}^{2}\operatorname{tr}(A^{\star\star 2})\geq t)\leq\exp(-ct^{2}/(\sigma^{4}\|A^{\star\star 2}\|^{2}_{F})\wedge t/(\sigma^{2}\|A^{\star\star 2}\|_{\operatorname{op}})) (2.10)

Note that ∥A⋆⋆2∥op≤1\|A^{\star\star 2}\|_{\operatorname{op}}\leq 1. In addition ∥A⋆⋆2∥F2=tr((I−X⋆⁣⋆)2)≤tr(I−X⋆⁣⋆)=m\|A^{\star\star 2}\|^{2}_{F}=\operatorname{tr}((I-X^{\star\star})^{2})\leq\operatorname{tr}(I-X^{\star\star})=m.

Hence we can select t=d~2/c2≳m​σ2t=\tilde{d}^{2}/c^{2}\gtrsim m\sigma^{2} to claim that (2.10) holds with high probability, i.e., probability at least 1−exp(−c′d~4/(σ4m)∧d~2/(c2σ2))1-\exp(-c^{\prime}\tilde{d}^{4}/(\sigma^{4}m)\wedge\tilde{d}^{2}/(c^{2}\sigma^{2})). This implies c′​d~4/(σ4​m)∧d~2/(c2​σ2)≍d~2/(C2′​σ2)c^{\prime}\tilde{d}^{4}/(\sigma^{4}m)\wedge\tilde{d}^{2}/(c^{2}\sigma^{2})\asymp\tilde{d}^{2}/(C^{{}^{\prime}2}\sigma^{2}) for some C′>0C^{\prime}>0. So that the bound is always 1−exp(−d~2/(C2′σ2))1-\exp(-\tilde{d}^{2}/(C^{{}^{\prime}2}\sigma^{2})). Since the mean of ‖A⋆⁣⋆​ξ‖22\|A^{\star\star}\xi\|_{2}^{2} is σ¯2tr(A⋆⋆2)=σ¯2m≲σ2d~2/(C2σ2)\underline{\sigma}^{2}\operatorname{tr}(A^{\star\star 2})=\underline{\sigma}^{2}m\lesssim\sigma^{2}\tilde{d}^{2}/(C^{2}\sigma^{2}) we complete the proof. ∎

Remark 2.11.

Lemma 2.10 is the reason why we assumed that the noise ξ\xi has independent components, so that we can apply the Hanson-Wright inequality. We note that the formula for the minimax rate remains unchanged even if the noise has dependent entries Prasadan and Neykov (2026). In Section 4 we will see that if we have more samples the noise can be arbitrary provided that its covariance matrix has a bounded operator norm.

Our main algorithm starts at 00 and works by iteratively refining the estimate arguing that at each step we have better and better approximation of μ\mu. These approximations will be shown to decay exponentially as the iteration proceeds, and in that sense the following lemma is very useful. Assuming that we have ”trapped” μ\mu in an Euclidean ball of certain radius we demonstrate how we can find an even better estimator of μ\mu provided that the conditions of Lemma 2.1 are satisfied.

Lemma 2.12.

Suppose we have an estimator μ^j∈K\hat{\mu}_{j}\in K of μ\mu such that ‖μ^j−μ‖2≤d~j\|\hat{\mu}_{j}-\mu\|_{2}\leq\tilde{d}_{j} happens with high probability, for some d~j∈ℝ+\tilde{d}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}_{+} such that d~j≥2​r∨C​σ\tilde{d}_{j}\geq 2r\vee C\sigma. Let K(j)=K∩B⁡(0,d~j/2)K_{(j)}=K\cap B(0,\tilde{d}_{j}/2). Obtain mm and the matrix Aj⋆⁣⋆A_{j}^{\star\star} from Lemma 2.1 and Algorithm 2 for the set K(j)K_{(j)}66 6 We explain later that the oracle 𝒪K(j)\mathcal{O}_{K_{(j)}} can also be run in polynomial-time, provided that the oracle 𝒪K\mathcal{O}_{K} can be run in polynomial-time., assuming that the conditions of Lemma 2.1 hold. Then the estimator μ~j+1=(Aj⋆⁣⋆​Y−Aj⋆⁣⋆​μ^j)/2\tilde{\mu}_{j+1}=(A^{\star\star}_{j}Y-A_{j}^{\star\star}\hat{\mu}_{j})/2 of (μ−μ^j)/2(\mu-\hat{\mu}_{j})/2 used in Lemma 2.10 satisfies:

ℙ(∥μ~j+1−(μ−μ^j)/2∥2≥d~j/L,∥μ^j−μ∥2≤d~j)≤exp(−d~j2/(C2′σ2))+11+d~j3/σ3.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\|\tilde{\mu}_{j+1}-(\mu-\hat{\mu}_{j})/2\|_{2}\geq\tilde{d}_{j}/L,\|\hat{\mu}_{j}-\mu\|_{2}\leq\tilde{d}_{j})\leq\exp(-\tilde{d}_{j}^{2}/(C^{{}^{\prime}2}\sigma^{2}))+\frac{1}{1+\tilde{d}_{j}^{3}/\sigma^{3}}.

for some absolute constant LL.

Proof.

Let us first condition on the event that our oracle did not fail (which happens with probability at least 1−(1+d~j3/σ3)−11-(1+\tilde{d}_{j}^{3}/\sigma^{3})^{-1}). On the event ‖μ^j−μ‖2≤d~j\|\hat{\mu}_{j}-\mu\|_{2}\leq\tilde{d}_{j} we have that, ν=(μ−μ^j)/2∈K(j)=K∩B⁡(0,d~j/2)\nu=(\mu-\hat{\mu}_{j})/2\in K_{(j)}=K\cap B(0,\tilde{d}_{j}/2). Recall that Aj⋆⁣⋆=(I−Xj⋆⁣⋆)1/2A_{j}^{\star\star}=(I-X_{j}^{\star\star})^{1/2}, and let Xj⋆⁣⋆=V​Λ​V⊤X_{j}^{\star\star}=V\Lambda V^{\top} be the eigendecomposition of Xj⋆⁣⋆X_{j}^{\star\star}.

‖ν−Aj⋆⁣⋆​ν‖22\displaystyle\|\nu-A_{j}^{\star\star}\nu\|_{2}^{2} =‖ν−∑i1−λi​vi​(vi⊤​ν)‖22=∑i(1−1−λi)2​(vi⊤​ν)2\displaystyle=\|\nu-\sum_{i}\sqrt{1-\lambda_{i}}v_{i}(v_{i}^{\top}\nu)\|^{2}_{2}=\sum_{i}(1-\sqrt{1-\lambda_{i}})^{2}(v_{i}^{\top}\nu)^{2}
=∑iλi2(1+1−λi)2​(vi⊤​ν)2≤∑iλi​(vi⊤​ν)2=ν⊤​Xj⋆⁣⋆​ν≲(d~j/c)2,\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\frac{\lambda_{i}^{2}}{(1+\sqrt{1-\lambda_{i}})^{2}}(v_{i}^{\top}\nu)^{2}\leq\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}(v_{i}^{\top}\nu)^{2}=\nu^{\top}X_{j}^{\star\star}\nu\lesssim(\tilde{d}_{j}/c)^{2},

where we used 0≤λi≤10\leq\lambda_{i}\leq 1. Next, ‖μ~j+1−(μ−μ^j)/2‖2≤‖Aj⋆⁣⋆​Y/2−Aj⋆⁣⋆​μ/2‖2+‖Aj⋆⁣⋆​(μ−μ^j)/2−(μ−μ^j)/2‖2≲d~j/(2​T)+(d~j/c)≤d~j/L\|\tilde{\mu}_{j+1}-(\mu-\hat{\mu}_{j})/2\|_{2}\leq\|A_{j}^{\star\star}Y/2-A_{j}^{\star\star}\mu/2\|_{2}+\|A_{j}^{\star\star}(\mu-\hat{\mu}_{j})/2-(\mu-\hat{\mu}_{j})/2\|_{2}\lesssim\tilde{d}_{j}/(2T)+(\tilde{d}_{j}/c)\leq\tilde{d}_{j}/L, with probability at least 1−exp(−d~j2/(C2′σ2))−(1+d~j3/σ3)−11-\exp(-\tilde{d}_{j}^{2}/(C^{{}^{\prime}2}\sigma^{2}))-(1+\tilde{d}_{j}^{3}/\sigma^{3})^{-1} by Lemma 2.10. This completes the proof. ∎

Finally we can describe the iteration of our algorithm.

 

Algorithm 3 Near-optimal Estimation Algorithm

 
0:  Convex body KK, r,R∈ℝ+r,R\in\mathbb{R}_{+} such that r​B2⊆K⊆R​B2rB_{2}\subseteq K\subseteq RB_{2}, observation Y=μ+ξY=\mu+\xi, constant L~=L/(3+1)\tilde{L}=L/(\sqrt{3}+1) where LL is from Lemma 2.12; We assume L~>2​(3+1)\tilde{L}>2(\sqrt{3}+1)77 7 This assumption can be met upon selecting CC from the definition of mm and cc from the definition of local entropy sufficiently large.
0:  Estimator μ^\hat{\mu} of μ\mu
1:  Set d~1=2​R\tilde{d}_{1}=2R, K(1):=KK_{(1)}:=K, number of iterations M=⌈logL~/(2​(3+1))⁡R/r⌉M=\lceil\log_{\tilde{L}/(2(\sqrt{3}+1))}R/r\rceil
2:  Set μ^1:=0\hat{\mu}_{1}:=0
3:  if σ≤r/n\sigma\leq r/\sqrt{n} then
4:   return YY;
5:  end if
6:  for j = 1, …, M do
7:   Find m=⌈d~j2/(C2​σ2)⌉∧nm=\lceil\tilde{d}_{j}^{2}/(C^{2}\sigma^{2})\rceil\wedge n, and calculate the matrix Aj⋆⁣⋆A_{j}^{\star\star} for the set K(j)K_{(j)}
8:   Find μ~j+1=(Aj⋆⁣⋆​Y−Aj⋆⁣⋆​μ^j)/2\tilde{\mu}_{j+1}=(A_{j}^{\star\star}Y-A_{j}^{\star\star}\hat{\mu}_{j})/2
9:   Set μ¯j+1=ΠK(j)​μ~j+1\bar{\mu}_{j+1}=\Pi_{K_{(j)}}\tilde{\mu}_{j+1}88 8 Here we set ϵ=d~j/L\epsilon=\tilde{d}_{j}/L in Lemma E.1 when evaluating the weak projection.
10:   Lift back to KK: μ^j+1=ΠK​(2​μ¯j+1+μ^j)\hat{\mu}_{j+1}=\Pi_{K}(2\bar{\mu}_{j+1}+\hat{\mu}_{j})99 9 Here we set ϵ=2​d~j/L~\epsilon=2\tilde{d}_{j}/\tilde{L} in Lemma E.1 when evaluating the weak projection.
11:   Set d~j+1=2​(3+1)​d~j/L~\tilde{d}_{j+1}=2(\sqrt{3}+1)\tilde{d}_{j}/\tilde{L}
12:   Set K(j+1):=K∩B2​(0,d~j+1/2)K_{(j+1)}:=K\cap B_{2}(0,\tilde{d}_{j+1}/2)
13:   if d~j+1≤(2​r)∨(C​σ)\tilde{d}_{j+1}\leq(2r)\vee(C\sigma) then
14:    return μ^:=μ^j+1\hat{\mu}:=\hat{\mu}_{j+1}
15:   end if
16:  end for
17:  return μ^:=μ^M+1\hat{\mu}:=\hat{\mu}_{M+1}
 

We make several comments about the algorithm. Our first observation is that Algorithm 2 does not require knowledge of η⋆\eta^{\star}, which may be difficult to evaluate precisely. Instead, the algorithm continues contracting for as long as further contraction is possible, thereby progressively reducing the distance between the current iterate and the signal μ\mu. The various reasons for which this contraction procedure may terminate are addressed by the preceding lemmas, which together guarantee that the resulting estimator is near-minimax optimal in expectation.

Note that, since we can evaluate the Minkowski gauge of KK, we have a (weak) separation oracle for KK Grötschel et al. (2012), which in turn enables (weak) projection in polynomial-time (see Theorem 2.5.9 in Dadush (2012), see also Lee et al. (2018)). The properties of this weak projection are summarized in Lemma E.1, where it is observed that it can output a vector that is in KK which is closer (up to an absolute constant factor) to any vector in the set KK than the original vector. When we write ΠK\Pi_{K} we mean using this weak projection. In addition, for any jj the set K(j)K_{(j)} also admits weak projection. This is because the Minkowski gauge of K(j)K_{(j)} satisfies

ρK(j)​(x)=ρK​(x)∨(2/d~j⋅‖x‖2),\displaystyle\rho_{K_{(j)}}(x)=\rho_{K}(x)\vee(2/\tilde{d}_{j}\cdot\|x\|_{2}), (2.11)

and can therefore be explicitly evaluated. In addition K(j)K_{(j)} is well balanced since r​B2⊆K(j)⊆d~j/2​B2rB_{2}\subseteq K_{(j)}\subseteq\tilde{d}_{j}/2B_{2}. Thus when we write ΠK(j)\Pi_{K_{(j)}} we mean the weak projection on K(j)K_{(j)}. Since the projections are “weak” they need not shrink distance to any point in KK. Hence the need for scaling factors: (3+1)(\sqrt{3}+1) and 2​(3+1)2(\sqrt{3}+1) in our algorithm.

We remark that our estimator is not proper, because when r>σ​nr>\sigma\sqrt{n} the estimator YY need not be in KK. This can be remedied by outputting ΠK​Y\Pi_{K}Y in the case when r>σ​nr>\sigma\sqrt{n}, with ϵ=σ​n\epsilon=\sigma\sqrt{n} in Lemma E.1 or setting r=r∧n​σr=r\wedge\sqrt{n}\sigma which circumvents this issue altogether.

Next, to ensure that the matrix Aj⋆⁣⋆A_{j}^{\star\star} is calculable, we need to show the existence of the oracle 𝒪K(j)\mathcal{O}_{K_{(j)}} for any j=1,…,Mj=1,\ldots,M. We will do so in the following section, Section 3, but for now we will show that if the original set KK is type-2, the sets K(j)K_{(j)} remain type-2. This is so since its Minkowski gauge satisfies (2.11), and is thus type-2 with constant at most

T2​(K(j))≤2​max⁡(T2​(K),T2​(B2​(0,d~j/2)))=2​max⁡(T2​(K),1)=2​T2​(K).\displaystyle T_{2}(K_{(j)})\leq\sqrt{2}\max(T_{2}(K),T_{2}(B_{2}(0,\tilde{d}_{j}/2)))=\sqrt{2}\max(T_{2}(K),1)=\sqrt{2}T_{2}(K).

Furthermore, as K(j)⊆KK_{(j)}\subseteq K, it is clear that the local entropy log⁡MK(j)loc​(δ)≤log⁡MKloc​(δ)\log M^{\operatorname{loc}}_{K_{(j)}}(\delta)\leq\log M^{\operatorname{loc}}_{K}(\delta) for any δ\delta. What is more, the latter implies that we have η⋆​(K(j))≤η⋆​(K)\eta^{\star}(K_{(j)})\leq\eta^{\star}(K).

Before we go on to show that our algorithm is nearly minimax optimal we first show the following lemma, justifying why one can output YY when σ\sigma is small.

Lemma 2.13.

Let σ≳r/n\sigma\gtrsim r/\sqrt{n}. Then the minimax rate η⋆≳r\eta^{\star}\gtrsim r. On the other hand if σ≲r/n\sigma\lesssim r/\sqrt{n} we have η⋆≍n​σ\eta^{\star}\asymp\sqrt{n}\sigma.

Proof.

Recall that the minimax rate η⋆\eta^{\star} satisfies η⋆=sup{η≥0:η2/σ2≤log⁡Mloc​(η)}\eta^{\star}=\sup\{\eta\geq 0:\eta^{2}/\sigma^{2}\leq\log M^{\operatorname{loc}}(\eta)\}. Observe that for η≲r\eta\lesssim r we have log⁡Mloc​(η)≍n\log M^{\operatorname{loc}}(\eta)\asymp n. On the other hand since σ≳r/n\sigma\gtrsim r/\sqrt{n}, the ratio (η/σ)2≲n(\eta/\sigma)^{2}\lesssim n. Thus η⋆≥η\eta^{\star}\geq\eta by definition. Since η\eta can be taken as η≍r\eta\asymp r the proof follows.

For the second part observe that since σ≲r/n\sigma\lesssim r/\sqrt{n} then n​σ≲r\sqrt{n}\sigma\lesssim r and therefore log⁡Mloc​(n​σ)≍n\log M^{\operatorname{loc}}(\sqrt{n}\sigma)\asymp n. Thus for η≍n​σ\eta\asymp\sqrt{n}\sigma it follows that η2/σ2≍log⁡Mloc​(η)\eta^{2}/\sigma^{2}\asymp\log M^{\operatorname{loc}}(\eta). On the other hand, η⋆\eta^{\star} cannot be larger than n​σ\sqrt{n}\sigma since otherwise η⋆2/σ2≳n≳log⁡Mloc​(η⋆)\eta^{\star 2}/\sigma^{2}\gtrsim n\gtrsim\log M^{\operatorname{loc}}(\eta^{\star}). ∎

We now state and prove the main result of the paper:

Theorem 2.14.

Set κ¯:=maxk∈[M]⁡κ⁡(K(k))\overline{\kappa}:=\max_{k\in[M]}\kappa(K_{(k)}) and suppose log⁡(R/r)\log(R/r) is polynomial in nn, while κ¯\overline{\kappa} and T2​(K)T_{2}(K) are polylogarithmic in nn. Define Υ⁡(K):=(1∨(2​2​T2​(K)​κ¯1/2)∨(2​C​ΛK))2\Upsilon(K):=(1\vee\left(2\sqrt{2}\,T_{2}(K)\overline{\kappa}^{1/2}\right)\vee\left(2C\sqrt{\Lambda_{K}}\right))^{2}, where ΛK:=1+⌈logc⁡(κ¯1/2​2​T2​(K))⌉\Lambda_{K}:=1+\left\lceil\log_{c}\!\left(\overline{\kappa}^{1/2}\sqrt{2}\,T_{2}(K)\right)\right\rceil. Then the output μ^\hat{\mu} of Algorithm 2 satisfies

𝔼​‖μ^−μ‖22≲Υ⁡(K)​η⋆2​(K),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\hat{\mu}-\mu\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim\Upsilon(K)\eta^{\star 2}(K),

and is thus nearly minimax optimal.

Remark 2.15 (Tracking the order of Υ⁡(K)\Upsilon(K)).

We briefly make explicit the dependence of Υ⁡(K)\Upsilon(K) on the dimension. In Section 3, under two alternative sets of additional assumptions on KK, we obtain respectively

κ¯≲T22​(K)​log⁡nA,\displaystyle\overline{\kappa}\lesssim T_{2}^{2}(K)\log n_{A},

and

κ¯≲T210​(K)​log4⁡(e​T2​(K)).\displaystyle\overline{\kappa}\lesssim T_{2}^{10}(K)\log^{4}\!\bigl(eT_{2}(K)\bigr).

Recalling that the definition of Υ⁡(K)\Upsilon(K) contributes an additional factor T22​(K)T_{2}^{2}(K), we obtain, respectively,

Υ⁡(K)\displaystyle\Upsilon(K) ≲T24​(K)​log⁡nA,\displaystyle\lesssim T_{2}^{4}(K)\log n_{A},
Υ⁡(K)\displaystyle\Upsilon(K) ≲T212​(K)​log4⁡(e​T2​(K)).\displaystyle\lesssim T_{2}^{12}(K)\log^{4}\!\bigl(eT_{2}(K)\bigr).

For example, in the QCO case considered in Section 6, where T2​(K)≲log⁡nT_{2}(K)\lesssim\sqrt{\log n}, these bounds become

Υ⁡(K)\displaystyle\Upsilon(K) ≲(log⁡n)2​log⁡nA,\displaystyle\lesssim(\log n)^{2}\log n_{A},
Υ⁡(K)\displaystyle\Upsilon(K) ≲(log⁡n)6​log4⁡(e​log⁡n),\displaystyle\lesssim(\log n)^{6}\log^{4}\!\bigl(e\sqrt{\log n}\bigr),

respectively. Thus, although Υ⁡(K)\Upsilon(K) grows only polylogarithmically with the dimension in these examples, the resulting logarithmic factors can be substantial and should not be regarded as negligible.

Proof of Theorem 2.14.

Let

ρ:=2​(3+1)L~<1.\displaystyle\rho:=\frac{2(\sqrt{3}+1)}{\widetilde{L}}<1.

d~j=2​R​ρj−1,d~j+1=ρ​d~j.\displaystyle\widetilde{d}_{j}=2R\rho^{j-1},\qquad\widetilde{d}_{j+1}=\rho\widetilde{d}_{j}.

𝔼​‖Y−μ‖22=n​σ¯2≤n​σ2≲η⋆2​(K)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|Y-\mu\|_{2}^{2}=n\underline{\sigma}^{2}\leq n\sigma^{2}\lesssim\eta^{\star 2}(K)

by Lemma 2.13. Hence, throughout the remainder of the proof, we may assume

σ>r/n.\displaystyle\sigma>r/\sqrt{n}.

In addition, if σ≳R\sigma\gtrsim R then the minimax rate η⋆≍R\eta^{\star}\asymp R and therefore since our estimator μ^∈K\hat{\mu}\in K, we have

𝔼​‖μ^−μ‖22≲R2≲η⋆2.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\hat{\mu}-\mu\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim R^{2}\lesssim\eta^{\star 2}.

Thus we assume throughout that σ≲R\sigma\lesssim R, and we observe that in that case η⋆≳σ\eta^{\star}\gtrsim\sigma.

We will repeatedly use that

T2​(K(j))≤2​T2​(K),η⋆​(K(j))≤η⋆​(K),\displaystyle T_{2}(K_{(j)})\leq\sqrt{2}\,T_{2}(K),\qquad\eta^{\star}(K_{(j)})\leq\eta^{\star}(K),

as established above. Put

κ¯:=maxj∈[M]⁡κ⁡(K(j))\displaystyle\overline{\kappa}:=\max_{j\in[M]}\kappa(K_{(j)})

and

ΛK:=1+⌈logc⁡(κ¯1/2​2​T2​(K))⌉.\displaystyle\Lambda_{K}:=1+\left\lceil\log_{c}\!\left(\overline{\kappa}^{1/2}\sqrt{2}\,T_{2}(K)\right)\right\rceil.

Finally, define

ΓK:=1∨(2​2​T2​(K)​κ¯1/2)∨(2​C​ΛK).\Gamma_{K}:=1\vee\left(2\sqrt{2}\,T_{2}(K)\overline{\kappa}^{1/2}\right)\vee\left(2C\sqrt{\Lambda_{K}}\right). (2.12)

Up to absolute constants and the harmless ceiling in ΛK\Lambda_{K}, this is the factor appearing in the statement preceding (2.20).

We now make the inductive probability argument explicit. Define

Hj:={∥μ^j−μ∥2≤d~j}.\displaystyle H_{j}:=\left\{\|\widehat{\mu}_{j}-\mu\|_{2}\leq\widetilde{d}_{j}\right\}.

Thus no loss is incurred in making this reduction.

We can now derive the accumulated probability bound explicitly. Let

t0:=C7​ΓK​η⋆​(K),\displaystyle t_{0}:=C_{7}\Gamma_{K}\eta^{\star}(K),

𝔼​‖μ^−μ‖22≲t02+∫t0∞t​exp⁡(−t2C~2​σ2)​𝑑t+σ3​∫t0∞d​tt2≲ΓK2​η⋆2​(K)+σ2​exp⁡(−c​ΓK2​η⋆2​(K)σ2)+σ3ΓK​η⋆​(K)≲ΓK2​η⋆2​(K),\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathbb{E}\|\widehat{\mu}-\mu\|_{2}^{2}&\lesssim t_{0}^{2}+\int_{t_{0}}^{\infty}t\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{\widetilde{C}^{2}\sigma^{2}}\right)dt+\sigma^{3}\int_{t_{0}}^{\infty}\frac{dt}{t^{2}}\\ &\lesssim\Gamma_{K}^{2}\eta^{\star 2}(K)+\sigma^{2}\exp\!\left(-c\frac{\Gamma_{K}^{2}\eta^{\star 2}(K)}{\sigma^{2}}\right)+\frac{\sigma^{3}}{\Gamma_{K}\eta^{\star}(K)}\\ &\lesssim\Gamma_{K}^{2}\eta^{\star 2}(K),\end{split}

log⁡(R/σ)≤log⁡(R/r)+12​log⁡n,\displaystyle\log(R/\sigma)\leq\log(R/r)+\tfrac{1}{2}\log n,

3 Quadratic Form Maximization (QFM)

In this section, we review some of the results of Bhattiprolu et al. (2021), and in addition, we establish some new results regarding QFM over convex bodies. Coupled with the results from Section 2 this demonstrates that our algorithm works unconditionally for plenty of type-2, well-balanced convex bodies.

The main problem of interest in this section is QFM over an origin-symmetric type-2 body KK. Specifically given a matrix XX we want to approximately maximize

maxp∈K⁡p⊤​X​p.\displaystyle\max_{p\in K}p^{\top}Xp.

Here, by approximate maximization, we mean finding a point 𝒪⁡(X)∈K\mathcal{O}(X)\in K such that 𝒪​(X)⊤​X​𝒪​(X)≥κ−1​maxp∈K​p⊤​X​p\mathcal{O}(X)^{\top}X\mathcal{O}(X)\geq\kappa^{-1}\max_{p\in K}p^{\top}Xp, for some κ≥1\kappa\geq 1 which may vary with the set KK but is sufficiently small.

This is a complicated problem, but fortunately the paper Bhattiprolu et al. (2021) studied it in great detail and provided polynomial-time algorithms based on the ellipsoid algorithm for a plethora of origin symmetric type-2 convex bodies. In our case the matrix XX is symmetric psd. In Bhattiprolu et al. (2021), the authors considered the same setting, and even the broader setting when XX is simply symmetric.

We will now review some of their results. In addition, in appendix A.1 we review all of their results which we subsequently use in this section. Bhattiprolu et al. propose two relaxations of the problem. Let g∼N⁡(0,I)g\sim N(0,I) be a standard Gaussian vector. They look at the following non-convex but approximately convex problem:

argmaxW⟨X,W⟩\displaystyle\mathop{\mathrm{argmax}}_{W}\langle X,W\rangle
subject to ​𝔼​ρK2​(W1/2​g)≤1\displaystyle\mbox{subject to }\mathbb{E}\rho^{2}_{K}(W^{1/2}g)\leq 1
W≥0,W⊤=W\displaystyle~~~~~~~~~~~~~~W\geq 0,W^{\top}=W

The second problem they formulate is:

argmaxWρK∘​(X1/2​W1/2​g)\displaystyle\mathop{\mathrm{argmax}}_{W}\rho_{K^{\circ}}(X^{1/2}W^{1/2}g)
subject to ​tr⁡(W)≤1\displaystyle\mbox{subject to }\operatorname{tr}(W)\leq 1
W≥0,W⊤=W,\displaystyle~~~~~~~~~~~~~~W\geq 0,W^{\top}=W,

where K∘={v∈ℝn:supx∈K⟨v,x⟩≤1}K^{\circ}=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\sup_{x\in K}\langle v,x\rangle\leq 1\} is the polar body of KK so that ρK∘\rho_{K^{\circ}} is the dual norm of ρK\rho_{K}, and X1/2X^{1/2} is a symmetric square root of XX which is symmetric and psd. It is proved that these two problems, have optimal values equal to that of the corresponding QFM problem. After approximately solving one of the the two problems, rounding algorithms are proposed to obtain the vectors 𝒪⁡(X)\mathcal{O}(X) from the optimal matrix W⋆​(X)W^{\star}(X).

In order to solve the two problems, Bhattiprolu et al. (2021) proceed to define the lower and upper covariance regions. The upper covariance region is defined as:

𝒰⁡(K):={W​ symmetric psd:𝔼​ρK2​(W1/2​g)≤1}\displaystyle\mathcal{U}(K):=\{W\text{ symmetric psd}:\mathbb{E}\rho^{2}_{K}(W^{1/2}g)\leq 1\}

while the lower covariance region is

ℒ⁡(K):={W​ symmetric psd:𝔼​ρK∘2​(W1/2​g)≥1}.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(K):=\{W\text{ symmetric psd}:\mathbb{E}\rho^{2}_{K^{\circ}}(W^{1/2}g)\geq 1\}.

Bhattiprolu et al. (2021) observe that

𝒰⁡(K)⊆conv⁡(𝒰⁡(K))⊆T2​(K)2⋅𝒰⁡(K)\displaystyle\mathcal{U}(K)\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal{U}(K))\subseteq T_{2}(K)^{2}\cdot\mathcal{U}(K)
ℒ⁡(K)⊆conv⁡(ℒ⁡(K))⊆1C2​(K∘)⋅ℒ⁡(K),\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(K)\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal{L}(K))\subseteq\frac{1}{C_{2}(K^{\circ})}\cdot\mathcal{L}(K),

where C2​(K∘)C_{2}(K^{\circ}) is the cotype constant of K∘K^{\circ} which is known to satisfy

C2​(K∘)≤T2​(K)≤C2​(K∘)​log⁡(n+1),\displaystyle C_{2}(K^{\circ})\leq T_{2}(K)\leq C_{2}(K^{\circ})\log(n+1),

where, as above, K∘K^{\circ} is the polar body of KK. In that sense the upper and lower covariance sets are approximately convex. In their sections 3 and 4 the authors of Bhattiprolu et al. (2021) establish conditional polynomial-time algorithms. These algorithms, which are based on an (approximate) ellipsoid algorithms, require the existence of an approximate separation oracle for (at least) one of the two sets 𝒰⁡(K),ℒ⁡(K)\mathcal{U}(K),\mathcal{L}(K). The reader is kindly referred to Definitions 1.6 and 1.11 in Bhattiprolu et al. (2021) for what an approximate separation oracle means. The conditional1111 11 Here the word conditional means that these algorithms work assuming separation oracles for one of the upper or lower covariance bodies. maximization polynomial-time algorithms guarantees are given in Propositions 4.2 and 4.4 of Bhattiprolu et al. (2021) (see also Appendix A.1). Importantly, we note that the algorithms in Propositions 4.2 and 4.4 not only can provide a near optimal value but also have rounding algorithms which produce near optimal vectors with high probability after polynomially many rounds. In addition to the approximate separation oracles for 𝒰⁡(K)\mathcal{U}(K) or ℒ⁡(K)\mathcal{L}(K), these results require the set KK to be balanced in the sense that r​B2⊆K⊆R​B2rB_{2}\subseteq K\subseteq RB_{2} for some known constants R,r∈ℝ+R,r\in\mathbb{R}_{+}. The complexity of the algorithms is polynomial in n,log⁡(R/r)n,\log(R/r) and bit⁡(X)\operatorname{bit}(X). Section 6 of Bhattiprolu et al. (2021) shows that the class of convex bodies for which we can evaluate an approximate separation oracle of the upper covariance region 𝒰⁡(K)\mathcal{U}(K) is closed under variety of operations including intersection, Minkowski addition, subspaces and quotients. This implies in particular that if one has a separation oracle for 𝒰⁡(K)\mathcal{U}(K) one is able to maximize over the set K∩c​B2K\cap cB_{2} for any c≥rc\geq r, since it is easy to see1212 12 Indeed results in Section 7 of Bhattiprolu et al. (2021) show that any type-2 exactly 2-convex and sign-invariant norm like ‖x‖2/c\|x\|_{2}/c (the Minkowski gauge of c​B2cB_{2}), admits an approximate separation oracle of 𝒰⁡(c​B2)\mathcal{U}(cB_{2}), and hence by results of Section 6 the intersection set K∩c​B2K\cap cB_{2} also admits such an oracle). See also the proof of Theorem 3.3 where we explain why explicit separation oracle of the convex set 𝒰⁡(c​B2)\mathcal{U}(cB_{2}) exists. that the set 𝒰⁡(c​B2)\mathcal{U}(cB_{2}) admits a separation oracle. Next, in Section 7 Bhattiprolu et al. (2021) exhibit unconditional algorithms for a plethora of convex bodies KK, where one has to have an oracle computing ρK​(x)\rho_{K}(x) for any x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} (see Theorem 7.6 and Theorem 7.12 and Appendix A.1). In other words, the authors are able to construct the approximate separation oracles for the upper and lower covariance regions of these sets. Specifically, the assumptions on the Minkowski gauges of the convex bodies in the latter theorems are as follows:

  • •

    ρK\rho_{K} is a sign-invariant (i.e. ρK​((,,,,,))=ρK​((ηj​xj)j∈[n])\rho_{K}((x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}))=\rho_{K}((\eta_{j}x_{j})_{j\in[n]}) for any x=(x1,…,xn)∈ℝnx=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and any ηj∈{±1}\eta_{j}\in\{\pm 1\}), and exactly 2-convex norm:

    ρK​((∑i∈[m]|xi|2)1/2)≤(∑i∈[m]ρK2​(xi))1/2,\displaystyle\rho_{K}((\sum_{i\in[m]}|x_{i}|^{2})^{1/2})\leq(\sum_{i\in[m]}\rho^{2}_{K}(x_{i}))^{1/2},

    for any m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} and vectors xi∈ℝnx_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, where |⋅|2|\cdot|^{2} is applied entry-wise.

  • •

    ρK\rho_{K} is a symmetric norm, i.e.,

    ρK​((,,,,,))=ρK​((ηj​xπj)j∈[n]),\displaystyle\rho_{K}((x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}))=\rho_{K}((\eta_{j}x_{\pi_{j}})_{j\in[n]}),

    for any x=(x1,…,xn)∈ℝnx=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, any ηj∈{±1}\eta_{j}\in\{\pm 1\} and an arbitrary permutation π\pi.

If ρK\rho_{K} is symmetric, then one can construct a separation oracle for ℒ⁡(K)\mathcal{L}(K), and hence can perform QFM over KK. Observe also that when ρK​(⋅)\rho_{K}(\cdot) is symmetric, the Minkowski gauge1313 13 We have ρK∩B⁡(0,c)​(x)=ρK​(x)∨‖x‖2/c\rho_{K\cap B(0,c)}(x)=\rho_{K}(x)\vee\|x\|_{2}/c. of the intersection of K∩B⁡(0,c)K\cap B(0,c) for some c∈ℝ+c\in\mathbb{R}^{+}, is also symmetric. Thus if the original set KK is given by a symmetric norm ρK\rho_{K} one can implement the algorithm from Section 2 unconditionally in polynomial-time.

If ρK\rho_{K} is sign-invariant and exactly 2-convex (such as any ℓp\ell_{p} norm with p≥2p\geq 2), one can find a separation oracle to 𝒰⁡(K)\mathcal{U}(K). Hence by our comment above, it follows that one can perform QFM over K∩c​B2K\cap cB_{2} for any r≤c≤Rr\leq c\leq R and thus one can implement the algorithm from Section 2 unconditionally in polynomial-time.

In conjunction with Section 2, these results imply that for any such convex bodies we can find the mean vector at a nearly minimax optimal rate. We now expand the class of bodies for which unconditional algorithms exist.

Theorem 3.1.

Let ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| be an exactly 22-convex sign-symmetric norm on ℝnA\mathbb{R}^{n_{A}} for nA≥nn_{A}\geq n which is also a type-2 norm with small constant which we denote by T2​(nA)T_{2}(n_{A}). Assume that we have an oracle for evaluating ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\|. Suppose our convex body K={x∈ℝn:‖A​x‖≤1}K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\|Ax\|\leq 1\} for some A∈ℝnA×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{A}\times n}, where we additionally assume that there are known r,R∈ℝ+r,R\in\mathbb{R}_{+} such that r​B2⊆K⊆R​B2rB_{2}\subseteq K\subseteq RB_{2}. subject to ​𝔼​ρK2​(W1/2​g)=𝔼​‖(A​W​A⊤)1/2​g′‖2≤1\displaystyle\mbox{subject to }\mathbb{E}\rho_{K}^{2}(W^{1/2}g)=\mathbb{E}\|(AWA^{\top})^{1/2}g^{\prime}\|^{2}\leq 1

Theorem 3.3.

Assume we have a symmetric type-2 norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| and an oracle for evaluation of ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\|. Denote the type-2 constant of ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| with T2​(n)T_{2}(n). Let the Minkowski gauge of the body KK be given by ρK​(x)=‖A​x‖\rho_{K}(x)=\|Ax\| where An×nA_{n\times n} is a given full rank matrix. Suppose that the set KK is balanced in the sense that there are known (r,R)(r,R) so that r​B2⊆K⊆R​B2rB_{2}\subseteq K\subseteq RB_{2}. Then for any r≤c≤Rr\leq c\leq R, we can find an approximate maximizer of argmaxp∈K∩c​B2p⊤​X​p\mathop{\mathrm{argmax}}_{p\in K\cap cB_{2}}p^{\top}Xp: 𝒪⁡(X)\mathcal{O}(X) for any psd matrix XX in polynomial-time operations: poly⁡(n,log⁡1/q,log⁡(R/r),bit⁡(X),bit⁡(A))\operatorname{poly}(n,\log 1/q,\log(R/r),\operatorname{bit}(X),\operatorname{bit}(A)) with probability at least 1−q1-q. Here κ⁡(K∩c​B2)≲2​T210​(K)​log4⁡(e​T2​(K))≤2​T210​(n)​log4⁡(e​T2​(n))\kappa(K\cap cB_{2})\lesssim 2T_{2}^{10}(K)\log^{4}(eT_{2}(K))\leq 2T_{2}^{10}(n)\log^{4}(eT_{2}(n)).

Proof.

For any input psd symmetric matrix XX we have the following identity:

maxp∈Kp⊤Xp=maxp:‖A​p‖≤1p⊤Xp=maxx:‖x‖≤1x⊤A−1⊤XA−1x.\displaystyle\max_{p\in K}p^{\top}Xp=\max_{p:\|Ap\|\leq 1}p^{\top}Xp=\max_{x:\|x\|\leq 1}x^{\top}A^{-1\top}XA^{-1}x.

Thus, we can approximately optimize the above problem by the results of Section 7 of Bhattiprolu et al. (2021), see Theorem 7.12 (see Theorem A.9 in the appendix). Here κ≲T26​(K)​log4⁡(e​T2​(K))\kappa\lesssim T_{2}^{6}(K)\log^{4}(eT_{2}(K)).

We now use a chain of results of Bhattiprolu et al. (2021). This chain of implications is described in greater detail in Remark A.11 in the appendix. Using Proposition 4.13 of Bhattiprolu et al. (2021) (see Proposition A.5 in the appendix) we can now claim that we have a α≲T28​(K)​log4⁡(e​T2​(K))\alpha\lesssim T_{2}^{8}(K)\log^{4}(eT_{2}(K))-approximate separation oracle for the set 𝒰⁡(K)\mathcal{U}(K) where K={x∈ℝn:‖A​x‖≤1}K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\|Ax\|\leq 1\}. Next, using Proposition 6.5 of Bhattiprolu et al. (2021) (see Proposition A.6 in the appendix) we know we can obtain a polynomial-time approximate quadratic maximization algorithm over the set K∩c​B2K\cap cB_{2} for any r≤c≤Rr\leq c\leq R. Not only that but we will also have rounding algorithms to obtain 𝒪⁡(X)\mathcal{O}(X) (we can simply replicate the rounding algorithms logic from the proof of Theorem 3.1 above which describes how to obtain rounding algorithms with the probability guarantees that we require). Here the constant κ≲2​max⁡(α,1)⋅max⁡(T22​(K),1)\kappa\lesssim 2\max(\alpha,1)\cdot\max(T^{2}_{2}(K),1).

In the above we used the fact that we can find an exact separation oracle for 𝒰⁡(c​B2)\mathcal{U}(cB_{2}). This is easy to see since 𝒰(cB2)={W≥0,W=W⊤:tr(W)≤c2}\mathcal{U}(cB_{2})=\{W\geq 0,W=W^{\top}:\operatorname{tr}(W)\leq c^{2}\} is convex and admits a simple explicit separation oracle.
