4 Robust Heavy-Tailed Extension

Consider the data Y~i=μ+ξi\tilde{Y}_{i}=\mu+\xi_{i}, i∈[N]i\in[N] where ξi\xi_{i} are i.i.d. vectors on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} such that 𝔼​ξi​ξi⊤=Σ\mathbb{E}\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{\top}=\Sigma with ‖Σ‖op≤σ2\|\Sigma\|_{\operatorname{op}}\leq\sigma^{2} where σ2\sigma^{2} (or an upper bound) is known to the statistician. Next the data is manipulated by a malicious and all-powerful adversary so that a (known) fraction ε≤c0<1/2\varepsilon\leq c_{0}<1/2 for a sufficiently small constant c0>0c_{0}>0 (c0≤1/300c_{0}\leq 1/300 suffices) of the observations can be arbitrary. This adversary is allowed to inspect all samples first, pick the ones to switch, and is also given oracle knowledge to all parameters of the model including μ\mu, KK, σ\sigma and oracle knowledge of our algorithm. We denote the observations after the adversary has tampered with the data as (Yi)i∈[N](Y_{i})_{i\in[N]}.

We are interested in estimating μ\mu in a minimax optimal way. In order to derive the rate Peng et al. (2026), suppose that N≳supδ>0log⁡MKloc​(δ)N\gtrsim\sup_{\delta>0}\log M^{\operatorname{loc}}_{K}(\delta). Since n≳log⁡MKloc​(δ)n\gtrsim\log M^{\operatorname{loc}}_{K}(\delta) this assumption is implied if N≳nN\gtrsim n. On the other hand, since we assume that the set KK is well-balanced, we have that r​B2⊆KrB_{2}\subseteq K and therefore, when δ≲r\delta\lesssim r, log⁡MKloc​(δ)≳n\log M^{\operatorname{loc}}_{K}(\delta)\gtrsim n. Thus, throughout this section we assume that N≳nN\gtrsim n. In that case, as shown by Peng et al. (2026) the minimax rate infμ^supμ∈Ksup𝒞𝔼​‖μ^−μ‖22\inf_{\hat{\mu}}\sup_{\mu\in K}\sup_{\mathcal{C}}\mathbb{E}\|\hat{\mu}-\mu\|_{2}^{2} is ≍η⋆2∧d2\asymp\eta^{\star 2}\wedge d^{2} where η⋆=(δ⋆∨ε​σ)\eta^{\star}=(\delta^{\star}\vee\sqrt{\varepsilon}\sigma) where δ⋆:=sup{δ≥0:N​δ2/σ2≤log⁡MKloc​(δ)}\delta^{\star}:=\sup\{\delta\geq 0:N\delta^{2}/\sigma^{2}\leq\log M^{\operatorname{loc}}_{K}(\delta)\}, and where the innermost supremum over 𝒞\mathcal{C} is taken over all admissible adversarial contamination schemes.

By substituting the σ\sigma with σ/N\sigma/\sqrt{N} in Lemma 2.1 we obtain the following corollary.

Corollary 4.1.

Let KK be a type-2 convex body with type-2 constant T2​(K)T_{2}(K), such that r​B2⊆K⊆R​B2rB_{2}\subseteq K\subseteq RB_{2} for some known r,Rr,R. Let κ:=κ⁡(K)\kappa:=\kappa(K) be a given scalar which can depend on KK. Let δ⋆:=δ⋆​(K)\delta^{\star}:=\delta^{\star}(K) be defined through the equation δ⋆=supδ{δ≥0:N​δ2/σ2≤log⁡MKloc​(δ)}\delta^{\star}=\sup_{\delta}\{\delta\geq 0:N\delta^{2}/\sigma^{2}\leq\log M_{K}^{\operatorname{loc}}(\delta)\}. Assume that κ−1/2d~/T2(K)≥2δ⋆\kappa^{-1/2}\tilde{d}/T_{2}(K)\geq 2\delta^{\star} and ⌈⌈logc⁡(κ1/2⋅T2​(K))⌉⋅4​δ⋆2⋅N/σ2⌉≤N⋅d~2/(σ2​C2)\lceil\lceil\log_{c}(\kappa^{1/2}\cdot T_{2}(K))\rceil\cdot 4\delta^{\star 2}\cdot N/\sigma^{2}\rceil\leq N\cdot\tilde{d}^{2}/(\sigma^{2}C^{2}) for d~=2​R≥d\tilde{d}=2R\geq d and where C>0C>0 is some absolute constant. Then for m=⌈N⋅d~2/(σ2​C2)⌉∧nm=\lceil N\cdot\tilde{d}^{2}/(\sigma^{2}C^{2})\rceil\wedge n, we have

dm(K)≲κ−1/2⋅d~/c,\displaystyle d_{m}(K)\lesssim\kappa^{-1/2}\cdot\tilde{d}/c,

We will modify several steps in our algorithm. Specifically, after obtaining the matrix A⋆⁣⋆A^{\star\star} for the set K′=K∩B2​(0,d~/2)K^{\prime}=K\cap B_{2}(0,\tilde{d}/2) we transform the data to (A⋆⁣⋆​Yi)i∈[N](A^{\star\star}Y_{i})_{i\in[N]} and we apply the polynomial-time algorithm of Depersin and Lecué (2022) to the data with k=u=⌈N​d~2/(C2​σ2)⌉∧Nk=u=\lceil N\tilde{d}^{2}/(C^{2}\sigma^{2})\rceil\wedge N blocks. In addition, when we obtain the matrix A⋆⁣⋆A^{\star\star} we use N−1/2σN^{-1/2}\sigma in place of σ\sigma in Theorem 2.7 and Algorithm 2.

Now we prove the following lemma

Lemma 4.2.

The estimator f⁡((A⋆⁣⋆​Yi)i∈[N])f((A^{\star\star}Y_{i})_{i\in[N]}), where ff denotes the procedure of Depersin and Lecué (2022) with k=u=⌈N​d~2/(C2​σ2)⌉∧Nk=u=\lceil N\tilde{d}^{2}/(C^{2}\sigma^{2})\rceil\wedge N, of A⋆⁣⋆​μA^{\star\star}\mu satisfies

‖f⁡((A⋆⁣⋆​Yi)i∈[N])−A⋆⁣⋆​μ‖22≤d~2/T2,\displaystyle\|f((A^{\star\star}Y_{i})_{i\in[N]})-A^{\star\star}\mu\|_{2}^{2}\leq\tilde{d}^{2}/T^{2},

with probability at least 1−exp(−k/C′)1-\exp(-k/C^{\prime}) provided that k≳ε​Nk\gtrsim\varepsilon N, and d~≥C​σ/N\tilde{d}\geq C\sigma/\sqrt{N}.

Proof.

From d~≥C​σ/N\tilde{d}\geq C\sigma/\sqrt{N} we have that ⌈N​d~2/(C2​σ2)⌉≍N​d~2/(C2​σ2)\lceil N\tilde{d}^{2}/(C^{2}\sigma^{2})\rceil\asymp N\tilde{d}^{2}/(C^{2}\sigma^{2}). Since A⋆⁣⋆​Y~=A⋆⁣⋆​μ+A⋆⁣⋆​ξA^{\star\star}\tilde{Y}=A^{\star\star}\mu+A^{\star\star}\xi, we will first evaluate tr⁡(Var⁡(A⋆⁣⋆​ξ))\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Var}(A^{\star\star}\xi)) and ‖Var⁡(A⋆⁣⋆​ξ)‖op\|\operatorname{Var}(A^{\star\star}\xi)\|_{\operatorname{op}} as they appear on the right hand side of the main inequality in Theorem 2 of Depersin and Lecué (2022) (see also Theorem A.14 where we state this result in our notation).

For the first term, we see that

tr⁡(Var⁡(A⋆⁣⋆​ξ))\displaystyle\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Var}(A^{\star\star}\xi)) =tr(𝔼A⋆⁣⋆ξξ⊤A⋆⁣⋆)=tr(ΣA⋆⋆2)\displaystyle=\operatorname{tr}(\mathbb{E}A^{\star\star}\xi\xi^{\top}A^{\star\star})=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma A^{\star\star 2})
≤∥Σ∥op∥A⋆⋆2∥∗≤∥Σ∥op∑i∈[n](1−λi)=∥Σ∥opm\displaystyle\leq\|\Sigma\|_{\operatorname{op}}\|A^{\star\star 2}\|_{*}\leq\|\Sigma\|_{\operatorname{op}}\sum_{i\in[n]}(1-\lambda_{i})=\|\Sigma\|_{\operatorname{op}}m
≲N​‖Σ‖op​d~2/(σ2​C2)≤N​d~2/C2,\displaystyle\lesssim N\|\Sigma\|_{\operatorname{op}}\tilde{d}^{2}/(\sigma^{2}C^{2})\leq N\tilde{d}^{2}/C^{2},

where we remind the reader that ‖Σ‖op≤σ2\|\Sigma\|_{\operatorname{op}}\leq\sigma^{2}, and in addition X⋆⁣⋆=V​Λ​V⊤=∑i∈[n]λi​vi​vi⊤X^{\star\star}=V\Lambda V^{\top}=\sum_{i\in[n]}\lambda_{i}v_{i}v_{i}^{\top}, while A⋆⁣⋆=(I−X⋆⁣⋆)1/2=∑i∈[n]1−λi​vi​vi⊤A^{\star\star}=(I-X^{\star\star})^{1/2}=\sum_{i\in[n]}\sqrt{1-\lambda_{i}}v_{i}v_{i}^{\top}. Furthermore, it is clear that

‖Var⁡(A⋆⁣⋆​ξ)‖op=‖𝔼​A⋆⁣⋆​ξ​ξ⊤​A⋆⁣⋆‖op≤‖Σ‖op.\displaystyle\|\operatorname{Var}(A^{\star\star}\xi)\|_{\operatorname{op}}=\|\mathbb{E}A^{\star\star}\xi\xi^{\top}A^{\star\star}\|_{\operatorname{op}}\leq\|\Sigma\|_{\operatorname{op}}.

This, in conjunction with the result of Depersin and Lecué (2022), completes the proof, after the use of the union bound. ∎

Clearly, we can now prove an analogous result to Lemma 2.12 for this setting, with Aj⋆⁣⋆​YA_{j}^{\star\star}Y substituted with f⁡((Aj⋆⁣⋆​Yi)i∈[N])f((A_{j}^{\star\star}Y_{i})_{i\in[N]}) with k=uk=u as specified in Lemma 4.2. For the sake of brevity we defer this to the appendix (see Lemma C.1 and its proof). In addition, using Theorem 2 of Depersin and Lecué (2022) with k=u=Nk=u=N, on the untransformed data (Yi)i∈[N](Y_{i})_{i\in[N]}, provided that ε\varepsilon is smaller than an absolute constant c0c_{0}, with probability at least 1−exp(−N/C0)1-\exp(-N/C_{0}) we have

‖f⁡((Yi)i∈[N])−μ‖2≲n/N​σ+σ≲σ.\displaystyle\|f((Y_{i})_{i\in[N]})-\mu\|_{2}\lesssim\sqrt{n/N}\sigma+\sigma\lesssim\sigma. (4.1)

Thus, instead of starting at the 00 vector, we can start at μ^0:=ΠK​f​((Yi)i∈[N])\hat{\mu}_{0}:=\Pi_{K}f((Y_{i})_{i\in[N]}), and set d~1=2​R∧C′​σ\tilde{d}_{1}=2R\wedge C^{\prime}\sigma for some absolute constant C′>0C^{\prime}>0, and K(1)=K∩B2​(0,d~1/2)K_{(1)}=K\cap B_{2}(0,\tilde{d}_{1}/2). Here when we write ΠK​f​((Yi)i∈[N])\Pi_{K}f((Y_{i})_{i\in[N]}), we mean weak projection as usual. By (4.1) and Lemma E.1 with ϵ=σ\epsilon=\sigma, we have

‖ΠK​f​((Yi)i∈[N])−μ‖2≲σ,\displaystyle\|\Pi_{K}f((Y_{i})_{i\in[N]})-\mu\|_{2}\lesssim\sigma,

while ΠK​f​((Yi)i∈[N])∈K\Pi_{K}f((Y_{i})_{i\in[N]})\in K. Since we are setting ϵ=σ\epsilon=\sigma1414 14 Note the distinction between ε\varepsilon and ϵ\epsilon: the former is the fraction of outliers, while the latter is simply the parameter of Lemma E.1 in Lemma E.1 this means σ\sigma cannot be too small. Specifically, we will assume that log⁡(1+1/σ)\log(1+1/\sigma) is polynomial in nn and NN.

The updated algorithm is given in the following:

 

Algorithm 4 Near-optimal Robust Mean Estimation Algorithm

 
0:  Convex body KK, r,R∈ℝ+r,R\in\mathbb{R}_{+} such that r​B2⊆K⊆R​B2rB_{2}\subseteq K\subseteq RB_{2}, observations (Yi)i∈[N](Y_{i})_{i\in[N]}, constant L~=L/(3+1)\tilde{L}=L/(\sqrt{3}+1) where LL is from the robust version of Lemma 2.12; We assume L~>2​(3+1)\tilde{L}>2(\sqrt{3}+1)
0:  Estimator μ^\hat{\mu} of μ\mu which belongs to the set KK
1:  Overwrite r:=(n/N​σ∨ε​σ)∧rr:=(\sqrt{n/N}\sigma\vee\sqrt{\varepsilon}\sigma)\wedge r
2:  Set d~1=2​R∧(C′​σ)\tilde{d}_{1}=2R\wedge(C^{\prime}\sigma), K(1):=K∩B2​(0,d~1/2)K_{(1)}:=K\cap B_{2}(0,\tilde{d}_{1}/2), set number of iterations M=⌈logL~/(2​(3+1))⁡d~1/(2​r)⌉M=\lceil\log_{\tilde{L}/(2(\sqrt{3}+1))}\tilde{d}_{1}/(2r)\rceil
3:  Set μ^1:=ΠK​f​((Yi)i∈[N])\hat{\mu}_{1}:=\Pi_{K}f((Y_{i})_{i\in[N]}) with ϵ=σ\epsilon=\sigma in Lemma E.1 and k=u=Nk=u=N (here ff denotes the procedure of Depersin and Lecué (2022))
4:  for j = 1, …, M do
5:   Find m=⌈N​d~j2/(C2​σ2)⌉∧nm=\lceil N\tilde{d}_{j}^{2}/(C^{2}\sigma^{2})\rceil\wedge n, and calculate the matrix Aj⋆⁣⋆A_{j}^{\star\star} for the set K(j)K_{(j)}
6:   Find μ~j+1=(f⁡((Aj⋆⁣⋆​Yi)i∈[N])−Aj⋆⁣⋆​μ^j)/2\tilde{\mu}_{j+1}=(f((A_{j}^{\star\star}Y_{i})_{i\in[N]})-A_{j}^{\star\star}\hat{\mu}_{j})/2 with k=u=⌈N​d~j2/(C2​σ2)⌉∧Nk=u=\lceil N\tilde{d}_{j}^{2}/(C^{2}\sigma^{2})\rceil\wedge N for some large constant C>C′C>C^{\prime} (here ff denotes the procedure of Depersin and Lecué (2022))
7:   Set μ¯j+1=ΠK(j)​μ~j+1\bar{\mu}_{j+1}=\Pi_{K_{(j)}}\tilde{\mu}_{j+1}1515 15 Here we set ϵ=d~j/L\epsilon=\tilde{d}_{j}/L in Lemma E.1 when evaluating the weak projection.
8:   Lift back to KK: μ^j+1=ΠK​(2​μ¯j+1+μ^j)\hat{\mu}_{j+1}=\Pi_{K}(2\bar{\mu}_{j+1}+\hat{\mu}_{j})1616 16 Here we set ϵ=2​d~j/L~\epsilon=2\tilde{d}_{j}/\tilde{L} in Lemma E.1 when evaluating the weak projection.
9:   Set d~j+1=2​(3+1)​d~j/L~\tilde{d}_{j+1}=2(\sqrt{3}+1)\tilde{d}_{j}/\tilde{L}
10:   Set K(j+1):=K∩B2​(0,d~j+1/2)K_{(j+1)}:=K\cap B_{2}(0,\tilde{d}_{j+1}/2)
11:   if d~j+1≤(2​r)∨(C​σ/N)\tilde{d}_{j+1}\leq(2r)\vee(C\sigma/\sqrt{N}) then
12:    return μ^:=μ^j+1\hat{\mu}:=\hat{\mu}_{j+1}
13:   end if
14:  end for
15:  return μ^:=μ^M+1\hat{\mu}:=\hat{\mu}_{M+1}
 

The main theorem of this section resembles the main result of Section 2 with slight modifications.

Theorem 4.3.

Suppose that T2​(K)T_{2}(K) and κ¯:=maxk∈[M]⁡κ⁡(K(k))\overline{\kappa}:=\max_{k\in[M]}\kappa(K_{(k)}) grow at most polylogarithmically in nn and NN. Assume also that N≳nN\gtrsim n, and log⁡d~1/r\log\tilde{d}_{1}/r (with the overwritten value of rr) and log⁡(1+1/σ)\log(1+1/\sigma) are polynomial in n,Nn,N. Furthermore, let d2σ2=diam​(K)2σ2≲exp⁡(N/C0)/N\frac{d^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}=\frac{\mathrm{diam}(K)^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\lesssim\exp(N/C_{0})/N. Define Υ⁡(K)=(1∨(2​2​T2​(K)​κ¯1/2)∨(2​C​ΛK))2\Upsilon(K)=(1\vee\left(2\sqrt{2}\,T_{2}(K)\overline{\kappa}^{1/2}\right)\vee\left(2C\sqrt{\Lambda_{K}}\right))^{2} with ΛK:=1+⌈logc⁡(κ¯1/2​2​T2​(K))⌉\Lambda_{K}:=1+\left\lceil\log_{c}\!\left(\overline{\kappa}^{1/2}\sqrt{2}\,T_{2}(K)\right)\right\rceil. Then the output μ^\hat{\mu} of Algorithm 4 satisfies

𝔼​‖μ^−μ‖22≲Υ⁡(K)​η⋆2​(K)∧d2,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\hat{\mu}-\mu\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim\Upsilon(K)\eta^{\star 2}(K)\wedge d^{2},

and is thus nearly minimax optimal.

The proof follows the same general strategy as that of Theorem 2.14, with several modifications specific to the robust setting, and is deferred to the appendix.

5 Linear Regression

In this section we consider the problem of linear regression with random design. Suppose we are given NN i.i.d. observations from the model:

Yi=Zi⊤​β+ξi,\displaystyle Y_{i}=Z_{i}^{\top}\beta+\xi_{i},

where β∈K⊆ℝn\beta\in K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} and KK is a type-2 set satisfying the assumptions of the preceding sections. We work in a moderate-dimensional regime in which N≳nN\gtrsim n, with a sufficiently large absolute implicit constant. We assume that the covariates ZiZ_{i} are independent of the noise variables ξi\xi_{i}. We also assume that the diameter of KK is bounded by an absolute constant, i.e., d:=diam⁡(K)=O⁡(1)d:=\mathrm{diam}(K)=O(1). Accordingly, we assume that the known outer radius RR in r​B2⊆K⊆R​B2rB_{2}\subseteq K\subseteq RB_{2} satisfies R=O⁡(1)R=O(1). Further, let ξi\xi_{i} be a centered sub-Gaussian variable with sub-Gaussian parameter γ\gamma of constant order, i.e., 𝔼​exp⁡(λ⋅ξi)≤exp⁡(λ2​γ2/2)\mathbb{E}\exp(\lambda\cdot\xi_{i})\leq\exp(\lambda^{2}\gamma^{2}/2), for all λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R} where γ=O⁡(1)\gamma=O(1). It may seem that the condition R=O⁡(1)R=O(1) is quite restrictive at first glance. We observe later (see Remark 5.4) that this can be significantly relaxed at almost no algorithmic cost. For simplicity we keep the R=O⁡(1)R=O(1) in the main theorem.

Suppose the covariates ZiZ_{i} are centered1717 17 If the predictors ZiZ_{i} are not centered one can consider (Y2​i−Y2​i−1,Z2​i−Z2​i−1)i∈[⌊N/2⌋](Y_{2i}-Y_{2i-1},Z_{2i}-Z_{2i-1})_{i\in[\lfloor N/2\rfloor]} to center the predictors while leave the β\beta unchanged. We note that this operation prevents the model from having an intercept. sub-Gaussian variables with a well conditioned covariance matrix 𝔼​Zi​Zi⊤=Σ\mathbb{E}Z_{i}Z_{i}^{\top}=\Sigma, i.e., c′≤λmin​(Σ)≤λmax​(Σ)≤C′c^{\prime}\leq\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\leq\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\leq C^{\prime} for some c′,C′>0c^{\prime},C^{\prime}>0, and sub-Gaussian parameter of constant order, i.e. supv∈Sn−1𝔼​exp⁡(λ​v⊤​Zi)≤exp⁡(λ2​ζ2/2)\sup_{v\in S^{n-1}}\mathbb{E}\exp(\lambda v^{\top}Z_{i})\leq\exp(\lambda^{2}\zeta^{2}/2) for ζ=O⁡(1)\zeta=O(1). Then the minimax rate η⋆2\eta^{\star 2}, in the case when ξi∼N⁡(0,1)\xi_{i}\sim N(0,1), is given by the entropy equation η⋆=supη{η≥0:N​η2≤log⁡MKloc​(η)}\eta^{\star}=\sup_{\eta}\{\eta\geq 0:N\eta^{2}\leq\log M_{K}^{\operatorname{loc}}(\eta)\}, as shown in Prasadan and Neykov (2025a).

Returning to Lemma 2.1, and plugging in N−1/2N^{-1/2} for σ\sigma we obtain the following corollary.

Corollary 5.1.

Let KK be a type-2 convex body with type-2 constant T2​(K)T_{2}(K), such that r​B2⊆K⊆R​B2rB_{2}\subseteq K\subseteq RB_{2} for some known r,Rr,R with R=O⁡(1)R=O(1). Let κ:=κ⁡(K)\kappa:=\kappa(K) be a given scalar which can depend on KK. Let η⋆:=η⋆​(K)\eta^{\star}:=\eta^{\star}(K) be the minimax rate defined by equation η⋆=supη{η≥0:N​η2≤log⁡MKloc​(η)}\eta^{\star}=\sup_{\eta}\{\eta\geq 0:N\eta^{2}\leq\log M_{K}^{\operatorname{loc}}(\eta)\}. Assume that κ−1/2d~/T2(K)≥2η⋆\kappa^{-1/2}\tilde{d}/T_{2}(K)\geq 2\eta^{\star} and ⌈⌈logc⁡(κ1/2⋅T2​(K))⌉⋅4​η⋆2⋅N⌉≤N⋅d~2/C2\lceil\lceil\log_{c}(\kappa^{1/2}\cdot T_{2}(K))\rceil\cdot 4\eta^{\star 2}\cdot N\rceil\leq N\cdot\tilde{d}^{2}/C^{2} for d~=2​R≥d\tilde{d}=2R\geq d and where C>0C>0 is some absolute constant. Then for m=⌈N⋅d~2/C2⌉∧nm=\lceil N\cdot\tilde{d}^{2}/C^{2}\rceil\wedge n, we have

dm(K)≲κ−1/2⋅d~/c,\displaystyle d_{m}(K)\lesssim\kappa^{-1/2}\cdot\tilde{d}/c,

We now state a lemma analogous to Lemma 2.12. However, the proof is more involved and uses an estimator adapted to the regression setting. We also mention that we are using Theorem 2.7 and Algorithm 2 with N−1/2N^{-1/2} for σ\sigma.

Lemma 5.2.

Suppose that we have an estimator β^j\hat{\beta}_{j} of β\beta such that ‖β^j−β‖2≤d~j\|\hat{\beta}_{j}-\beta\|_{2}\leq\tilde{d}_{j} happens with high probability, for some d~j∈ℝ+\tilde{d}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}_{+} such that d~j≥(2​r)∨(C/N)\tilde{d}_{j}\geq(2r)\vee(C/\sqrt{N}). Assume also N≳nN\gtrsim n for some absolute constant. Let K(j)=K∩B⁡(0,d~j/2)K_{(j)}=K\cap B(0,\tilde{d}_{j}/2). Obtain mm and the matrix Aj⋆⁣⋆A_{j}^{\star\star} from Corollary 5.1 and Algorithm 2 for the set K(j)K_{(j)}. Let

βj+1′:=argminν∈K(j)∑i∈[N]((Yi−Zi⊤​β^j)/2−Zi⊤​Aj⋆⁣⋆​ν)2\displaystyle\beta^{\prime}_{j+1}:=\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}_{\nu\in K_{(j)}}\sum_{i\in[N]}((Y_{i}-Z_{i}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{j})/2-Z_{i}^{\top}A_{j}^{\star\star}\nu)^{2} (5.1)

and define the estimator β~j+1:=Aj⋆⁣⋆​βj+1′\tilde{\beta}_{j+1}:=A^{\star\star}_{j}\beta^{\prime}_{j+1}. Then solving program (5.1) can be approximated in polynomial-time and the estimator β~j+1\tilde{\beta}_{j+1} satisfies:

ℙ⁡(‖β~j+1−(β−β^j)/2‖2≥d~j/L,‖β^j−β‖2≤d~j)≤exp⁡(−N​c′​d~j2)+(1+N3/2​d~j3)−1.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\|\tilde{\beta}_{j+1}-(\beta-\hat{\beta}_{j})/2\|_{2}\geq\tilde{d}_{j}/L,\|\hat{\beta}_{j}-\beta\|_{2}\leq\tilde{d}_{j})\leq\exp(-Nc^{\prime}\tilde{d}_{j}^{2})+(1+N^{3/2}\tilde{d}_{j}^{3})^{-1}.

for some absolute constant LL which can be made large provided that the constant CC is selected to be sufficiently large.

Due to space constraints the proof is relegated to the appendix. Now that we have established Lemma 5.2, all that remains is to state the algorithm for estimating β\beta. The algorithm is very similar to the one in the mean estimation setting:

 

Algorithm 5 Near-optimal Regression Estimation Algorithm

 
0:  Convex body KK, r,R∈ℝ+r,R\in\mathbb{R}_{+} such that r​B2⊆K⊆R​B2rB_{2}\subseteq K\subseteq RB_{2}, with R=O⁡(1)R=O(1); observations (Yi,Zi)i∈[N](Y_{i},Z_{i})_{i\in[N]}, constant L~=L/(3+1)\tilde{L}=L/(\sqrt{3}+1) where LL is from Lemma 5.2; We assume L~>2​(3+1)\tilde{L}>2(\sqrt{3}+1)
0:  Estimator β^\hat{\beta} of β\beta
1:  Set r=r∧(12​n/N)r=r\wedge(\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{n/N})
2:  Set d~1=2​R\tilde{d}_{1}=2R, K(1):=KK_{(1)}:=K, number of iterations M=⌈logL~/(2​(3+1))⁡R/r⌉M=\lceil\log_{\tilde{L}/(2(\sqrt{3}+1))}R/r\rceil
3:  Set β^1:=0\hat{\beta}_{1}:=0
4:  for j = 1, …, M do
5:   Find m=⌈N​d~j2/C2⌉∧nm=\lceil N\tilde{d}_{j}^{2}/C^{2}\rceil\wedge n, and calculate the matrix Aj⋆⁣⋆A_{j}^{\star\star} for the set K(j)K_{(j)}
6:   Find β~j+1\tilde{\beta}_{j+1}, the estimator from Lemma 5.2
7:   Set β¯j+1=ΠK(j)​β~j+1\bar{\beta}_{j+1}=\Pi_{K_{(j)}}\tilde{\beta}_{j+1}1818 18 Here we set ϵ=d~j/L\epsilon=\tilde{d}_{j}/L in Lemma E.1 when evaluating the weak projection.
8:   Lift back to KK: β^j+1=ΠK​(2​β¯j+1+β^j)\hat{\beta}_{j+1}=\Pi_{K}(2\bar{\beta}_{j+1}+\hat{\beta}_{j})1919 19 Here we set ϵ=2​d~j/L~\epsilon=2\tilde{d}_{j}/\tilde{L} in Lemma E.1 when evaluating the weak projection.
9:   Set d~j+1=2​(3+1)​d~j/L~\tilde{d}_{j+1}=2(\sqrt{3}+1)\tilde{d}_{j}/\tilde{L}
10:   Set K(j+1):=K∩B2​(0,d~j+1/2)K_{(j+1)}:=K\cap B_{2}(0,\tilde{d}_{j+1}/2)
11:   if d~j+1≤(2​r)∨(C/N)\tilde{d}_{j+1}\leq(2r)\vee(C/\sqrt{N}) then
12:    return β^:=β^j+1\hat{\beta}:=\hat{\beta}_{j+1}
13:   end if
14:  end for
15:  return β^:=β^M+1\hat{\beta}:=\hat{\beta}_{M+1}
 

We can now state the main theorem of this section.

Theorem 5.3.

Suppose that the assumptions of Section 5 hold. Set

κ¯:=maxj∈[M]⁡κ⁡(K(j)),\displaystyle\overline{\kappa}:=\max_{j\in[M]}\kappa(K_{(j)}),

and suppose that T2​(K)T_{2}(K) and κ¯\overline{\kappa} are polylogarithmic in n,Nn,N, while log⁡(R/r)\log(R/r) is polynomial in n,Nn,N. Assume also that N≳nN\gtrsim n for a sufficiently large absolute constant. Then there exists a factor

Υ⁡(K)=(1∨(2​2​T2​(K)​κ¯1/2)∨(2​C​ΛK))2,\displaystyle\Upsilon(K)=\left(1\vee\left(2\sqrt{2}\,T_{2}(K)\overline{\kappa}^{1/2}\right)\vee\left(2C\sqrt{\Lambda_{K}}\right)\right)^{2},

with ΛK=1+⌈logc⁡(κ¯1/2​2​T2​(K))⌉\Lambda_{K}=1+\left\lceil\log_{c}\!\left(\overline{\kappa}^{1/2}\sqrt{2}\,T_{2}(K)\right)\right\rceil, such that the output β^\widehat{\beta} of Algorithm 5 satisfies

𝔼​‖β^−β‖22≲Υ⁡(K)​η⋆2​(K).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\widehat{\beta}-\beta\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim\Upsilon(K)\eta^{\star 2}(K).

In particular, Algorithm 5 is nearly minimax rate optimal and runs in polynomial time.

The proof of Theorem 5.3 is deferred to the appendix since it follows a similar strategy to the proof of Theorem 2.14. Since ellipsoids are type-2 sets with small type-2 constant, we note that our method provides efficient implementation for linear regression problem under ellipsoidal constraints considered in the recent paper Pathak et al. (2024), provided that our further assumptions on the constraint set, covariates and noise vector are satisfied. Finally we remark how the assumption R=O⁡(1)R=O(1) can be significantly relaxed at almost no algorithmic cost.

Remark 5.4 (On the bounded-diameter assumption).

The assumption diam⁡(K)=O⁡(1)\mathrm{diam}(K)=O(1) in this section is mainly a convenient normalization and can be relaxed by a preliminary localization step. We describe one way to do this. The sample splitting below is useful because it ensures that, conditional on the pilot estimator, the observations used in the main procedure still form an independent linear-regression sample.

Split the observations into two subsamples I0I_{0} and I1I_{1} of comparable cardinality, say |I0|=⌊N/2⌋|I_{0}|=\lfloor N/2\rfloor and |I1|=N−|I0||I_{1}|=N-|I_{0}|. Using the first subsample, form the ordinary least-squares estimator

β^OLS=(∑i∈I0Zi​Zi⊤)−1​∑i∈I0Zi​Yi.\displaystyle\widehat{\beta}_{\rm OLS}=\left(\sum_{i\in I_{0}}Z_{i}Z_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_{0}}Z_{i}Y_{i}.

Under the assumptions of this section, standard concentration for sub-Gaussian random matrices implies that, provided N≳nN\gtrsim n,

λmin​(1|I0|​∑i∈I0Zi​Zi⊤)≳1\displaystyle\lambda_{\min}\!\left(\frac{1}{|I_{0}|}\sum_{i\in I_{0}}Z_{i}Z_{i}^{\top}\right)\gtrsim 1

with probability at least 1−exp⁡(−c​N)1-\exp(-cN). Conditional on the design,

β^OLS−β=(∑i∈I0Zi​Zi⊤)−1​∑i∈I0Zi​ξi.\displaystyle\widehat{\beta}_{\rm OLS}-\beta=\left(\sum_{i\in I_{0}}Z_{i}Z_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_{0}}Z_{i}\xi_{i}.

Since the ξi\xi_{i} are independent centered sub-Gaussian random variables with sub-Gaussian parameter γ=O⁡(1)\gamma=O(1), an ε\varepsilon-net argument, together with the preceding lower bound on the empirical covariance, gives

ℙ⁡(‖β^OLS−β‖2>C0​γ)≤exp⁡(−c0​N)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\!\left(\|\widehat{\beta}_{\rm OLS}-\beta\|_{2}>C_{0}\gamma\right)\leq\exp(-c_{0}N)

for sufficiently large absolute constants C0,c0>0C_{0},c_{0}>0. More precisely, one has the usual bound

‖β^OLS−β‖2≲γ​nN+t\displaystyle\|\widehat{\beta}_{\rm OLS}-\beta\|_{2}\lesssim\gamma\sqrt{\frac{n}{N}}+t

with probability at least 1−exp(−cNt2/γ2)−exp(−cN)1-\exp(-cNt^{2}/\gamma^{2})-\exp(-cN), and the displayed constant-radius bound follows from N≳nN\gtrsim n and γ=O⁡(1)\gamma=O(1). For more details on the last two statements please refer to Lemma D.1 in the appendix. Let

β¯:=ΠK​β^OLS,\displaystyle\overline{\beta}:=\Pi_{K}\widehat{\beta}_{\rm OLS},

where, as elsewhere in the paper, ΠK\Pi_{K} may be taken to be a weak Euclidean projection with accuracy of order γ\gamma. Lemma E.1 then implies that, on the preceding event,

‖β¯−β‖2≤C1​γ\displaystyle\|\overline{\beta}-\beta\|_{2}\leq C_{1}\gamma

for an absolute constant C1C_{1}, while β¯∈K\overline{\beta}\in K. Define

θ:=β−β¯2.\displaystyle\theta:=\frac{\beta-\overline{\beta}}{2}.

Since KK is origin-symmetric and convex, β,−β¯∈K\beta,-\overline{\beta}\in K, and therefore

θ=β+(−β¯)2∈K.\displaystyle\theta=\frac{\beta+(-\overline{\beta})}{2}\in K.

Moreover,

‖θ‖2≤C1​γ/2.\displaystyle\|\theta\|_{2}\leq C_{1}\gamma/2.

Thus, on the pilot-good event, the new coefficient belongs to the bounded convex body

K0:=K∩B2​(0,C2​γ),\displaystyle K_{0}:=K\cap B_{2}(0,C_{2}\gamma),

where C2C_{2} is a sufficiently large absolute constant. Notice that K0K_{0} is again origin-symmetric and convex, and

(r∧C2​γ)​B2⊆K0⊆C2​γ​B2.\displaystyle(r\wedge C_{2}\gamma)B_{2}\subseteq K_{0}\subseteq C_{2}\gamma B_{2}.

Furthermore, by the same intersection argument used earlier in the paper,

T2​(K0)≤2​max⁡{T2​(K),1},\displaystyle T_{2}(K_{0})\leq\sqrt{2}\max\{T_{2}(K),1\},

and

log⁡MK0loc​(δ)≤log⁡MKloc​(δ).\displaystyle\log M_{K_{0}}^{\operatorname{loc}}(\delta)\leq\log M_{K}^{\operatorname{loc}}(\delta).

Hence the corresponding entropy rate satisfies η⋆​(K0)≲η⋆​(K)\eta^{\star}(K_{0})\lesssim\eta^{\star}(K), where replacing NN by |I1|≍N|I_{1}|\asymp N changes the entropy fixed point by at most an absolute constant factor. Indeed, if

ηN⋆:=sup{η:N​η2≤log⁡MKloc​(η)},\displaystyle\eta_{N}^{\star}:=\sup\{\eta:N\eta^{2}\leq\log M_{K}^{\operatorname{loc}}(\eta)\},

then monotonicity of the local entropy immediately gives ηN/2⋆≤2​ηN⋆\eta_{N/2}^{\star}\leq\sqrt{2}\,\eta_{N}^{\star}. For the classes considered in Section 3, the QFM assumptions are also preserved under intersection with a Euclidean ball.

Now use only the second subsample I1I_{1} and define

Yi′:=Yi−Zi⊤​β¯2,i∈I1.\displaystyle Y_{i}^{\prime}:=\frac{Y_{i}-Z_{i}^{\top}\overline{\beta}}{2},\qquad i\in I_{1}.

Conditional on the first subsample,

Yi′=Zi⊤​θ+ξi2,i∈I1,\displaystyle Y_{i}^{\prime}=Z_{i}^{\top}\theta+\frac{\xi_{i}}{2},\qquad i\in I_{1},

and the observations on the right-hand side are independent of the pilot estimator. Thus they satisfy exactly the regression assumptions of this section, but with parameter θ∈K0\theta\in K_{0}, a constraint set of bounded diameter. Applying the bounded-diameter procedure to this transformed problem produces an estimator θ^\widehat{\theta} satisfying, on the pilot-good event,

𝔼⁡[‖θ^−θ‖22|(Yi,Zi)i∈I0]≲Υ⁡(K0)​η⋆2​(K0)≲Υ⁡(K)​η⋆2​(K),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widehat{\theta}-\theta\|_{2}^{2}\,\middle|\,(Y_{i},Z_{i})_{i\in I_{0}}\right]\lesssim\Upsilon(K_{0})\eta^{\star 2}(K_{0})\lesssim\Upsilon(K)\eta^{\star 2}(K),

up to the same logarithmic factors as in the main theorem.

Finally, lift the estimator back to the original parameterization by setting

β~:=2​θ^+β¯\displaystyle\widetilde{\beta}:=2\widehat{\theta}+\overline{\beta}

and weakly projecting β~\widetilde{\beta} onto KK. Taking the accuracy of this last weak projection to be, for example,

ϵproj≲r∧N−1/2,\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm proj}\lesssim r\wedge N^{-1/2},

does not affect the statistical rate. Indeed, since r​B2⊆KrB_{2}\subseteq K,

η⋆(K)≳r∧nN≳r∧N−1/2,\displaystyle\eta^{\star}(K)\gtrsim r\wedge\sqrt{\frac{n}{N}}\gtrsim r\wedge N^{-1/2},

while Lemma E.1 shows that this final projection changes the estimation error by at most an absolute constant factor at the relevant scale. The resulting estimator is proper, i.e., it belongs to KK.

The only additional contribution to the expected risk comes from failure of the OLS localization event. Since the final estimator belongs to KK, its squared error is always at most d2d^{2}, where d=diam⁡(K)d=\mathrm{diam}(K). Consequently the preceding reduction yields

𝔼​‖β^−β‖22≲Υ⁡(K)​η⋆2​(K)+d2​exp⁡(−c0​N).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\widehat{\beta}-\beta\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim\Upsilon(K)\eta^{\star 2}(K)+d^{2}\exp(-c_{0}N).

Therefore the bounded-diameter assumption may be removed whenever

d2​exp⁡(−c0​N)≲η⋆2​(K).d^{2}\exp(-c_{0}N)\lesssim\eta^{\star 2}(K). (5.2)

A completely explicit sufficient condition follows from r​B2⊆KrB_{2}\subseteq K, which implies

η⋆2​(K)≳η⋆2​(r​B2)≍r2∧nN.\displaystyle\eta^{\star 2}(K)\gtrsim\eta^{\star 2}(rB_{2})\asymp r^{2}\wedge\frac{n}{N}.

Thus it suffices to assume

d2​exp⁡(−c0​N)≲r2∧nN.\displaystyle d^{2}\exp(-c_{0}N)\lesssim r^{2}\wedge\frac{n}{N}.

6 Some Remarks

In this section, we give an example of a type of convex bodies that obey all conditions previously required. It has long been known Donoho et al. (1990) that for convex Quadratically Convex Orthosymmetric (QCO) sets, the minimax rate is given by an equation involving the Kolmogorov widths. In fact, the truncated series estimator is rate optimal over any QCO set. However, it was not previously known how one can compute a minimax optimal estimator (including the truncated series one) for QCO sets in generality. Here we argue that any orthosymmetric QCO set induces a norm which is of type-2 with small type-2 constant and is exactly 2-convex.

Lemma 6.1.

Let K⊂ℝnK\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a quadratically convex orthosymmetric (QCO) set, i.e.

  1. 1.

    KK is convex, origin-symmetric, and sign-invariant;

  2. 2.

    the set K(2):={x2:x∈K}K^{(2)}:=\{x^{2}:x\in K\} is convex, where squaring is done coordinatewise.

Then the norm ρK​(⋅)\rho_{K}(\cdot) induced by KK satisfies a type-2 inequality with constant C​log⁡n\sqrt{C\log n}, i.e., T2​(K)≲log⁡nT_{2}(K)\lesssim\sqrt{\log n}:

𝔼​ρK​(∑i=1mεi​xi)2≤C⁡(log⁡n)​∑i=1mρK​(xi)2,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\rho_{K}(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\varepsilon_{i}x_{i})^{2}\;\leq\;C(\log n)\sum_{i=1}^{m}\rho_{K}(x_{i})^{2},

for all x1,…,xm∈ℝnx_{1},\dots,x_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, where εi\varepsilon_{i} are i.i.d. Rademacher signs.

We note furthermore that the Minkowski gauges of QCO sets are necessarily 2-convex. To show this define

K2:={sign⁡(x)∘x2:x∈K}.\displaystyle K^{2}:=\{\operatorname{sign}(x)\circ x^{2}:x\in K\}.

Since KK is convex, sign-invariant and quadratically convex, K2K^{2} is convex and sign-invariant (see Lemma E.3 for a short proof). By direct inspection,

|x|∈t​K⇔x2∈t2​K2,\displaystyle|x|\in tK\iff x^{2}\in t^{2}K^{2},

and therefore

ρK​(x)=ρK2​(x2).\rho_{K}(x)=\sqrt{\rho_{K^{2}}(x^{2})}.

Thus, by the triangle inequality:

ρK2​((∑i∈[m]|xi|2)1/2)=ρK2​(∑i∈[m]|xi|2)≤∑i∈[m]ρK2​(|xi|2)=∑i∈[m]ρK2​(xi)\displaystyle\rho_{K}^{2}((\sum_{i\in[m]}|x_{i}|^{2})^{1/2})=\rho_{K^{2}}(\sum_{i\in[m]}|x_{i}|^{2})\leq\sum_{i\in[m]}\rho_{K^{2}}(|x_{i}|^{2})=\sum_{i\in[m]}\rho_{K}^{2}(x_{i})

It follows immediately that if K⊂ℝmK\subset\mathbb{R}^{m} is a QCO set (with mm being “small”), we can implement our algorithm over bounded, well-balanced sets K′={x∈ℝn:ρK​(A​x)≤1}K^{\prime}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\rho_{K}(Ax)\leq 1\} for some full rank matrix A∈ℝm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} (provided that we can evaluate ρK\rho_{K}). Clearly in the special case when A=InA=I_{n}, this implies that we can implement our algorithm for any well-balanced QCO set with oracle evaluating its Minkowski gauge. Examples of QCO include ellipsoids, hyperrectangles and sets of the type {x∈ℝn:∑i∈[n]θi​ψ​(xi2)≤1}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\sum_{i\in[n]}\theta_{i}\psi(x_{i}^{2})\leq 1\} for some convex function ψ\psi and constants θi∈ℝ+\theta_{i}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}.

It is easy to see that not all bodies with small type-2 constant are QCO sets. We attach the following proposition which verifies this fact.

Proposition 6.2.

Let n≥2n\geq 2 and define, for x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

‖x‖=(‖x‖22+1n​‖x‖12)1/2.\displaystyle\|x\|=\Big(\|x\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{n}\|x\|_{1}^{2}\Big)^{1/2}.

Then ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| is a norm which is convex, sign–symmetric, permutation–invariant, and has type–2 constant bounded by an absolute constant. However, its unit ball

K={x∈ℝn:‖x‖≤1}\displaystyle K=\bigl\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\|x\|\leq 1\bigr\}

is not quadratically convex.

Hence our algorithm can be implemented for well-balanced sets K′={x∈ℝn:‖A​x‖≤1}K^{\prime}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\|Ax\|\leq 1\} where A∈ℝn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is a full rank matrix. We conclude that our algorithm applies not only to transformed QCO sets, but also to a broader class of constraint sets.

7 Discussion

To the best of our knowledge, this paper proposed the first computationally efficient algorithm for constrained mean estimation in a Gaussian sequence model setting, heavy-tailed robust mean estimation and linear regression under type-2 convex constraints, where the constraint set satisfies further regularity assumptions as outlined in Sections 2 and 3. There is one central open question that remains: can one develop near optimal polynomial-time algorithms for other (convex) constraints. Notably our algorithm does not work for ℓp\ell_{p} balls for 1≤p<21\leq p<2, for which efficient near-minimax optimal soft and hard thresholding algorithms do exist Johnstone (2019). We further had to assume that the set KK is origin-symmetric. The hypothetical efficient algorithm will likely have to use a fundamentally different approach as we are no longer guaranteed that the Kolmogorov widths decay as in the origin-symmetric type-2 sets considered in this paper.

Another interesting open question is whether our algorithm is meaningful for misspecified scenarios, i.e., when μ\mu or β\beta do not belong to the set KK.

Yet another question is as follows. In the work of Neykov (2022) when the constraint set is convex, one can show that the estimator is adaptive to the location of the true mean μ∈K\mu\in K. However, we suspect that the estimator provided in this paper is not adaptive. It will be interesting to look into this rigorously: either establish that the estimator proposed here is adaptive, or refute it and provide an adaptive estimator.

Another avenue for future research is to try to remove the condition d2/σ2≲exp⁡(N/C0)/Nd^{2}/\sigma^{2}\lesssim\exp(N/C_{0})/N in the robust algorithm. We believe this assumption is not necessary, but we will likely need to develop a new algorithm which converges without the need of the pilot estimator based on the work of Depersin and Lecué (2022).

In the regression setting we had to assume the dimension is smaller than the sample size up to an absolute constant. It will be interesting if one can remove this condition. We crucially used in the proof of Lemma 5.2, to show that the eigenvalues of the sample covariance matrix are upper and lower bounded, and we do not know presently how to remove it.

Finally, our mean estimation procedures require knowledge of σ\sigma, or an accurate upper bound. Whether one can develop near optimal adaptive computationally tractable algorithms is an open problem.

Appendix A External results used in the proofs

For the reader’s convenience, in this appendix we collect the external results that are used as black boxes in the paper. We state them in the notation used throughout the manuscript and, when the statement in the cited source uses a slightly different normalization, we explicitly record the translation. We only include the portions of the cited results that are used in our arguments.

A.1 Quadratic-form maximization results of Bhattiprolu–Lee–Naor

We first collect the results from [1]. For an origin-symmetric convex body K⊂ℝnK\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} and a symmetric matrix X∈𝕊nX\in\mathbb{S}^{n}, write

QK​(X):=maxp∈K⁡p⊤​X​p.\displaystyle Q_{K}(X):=\max_{p\in K}p^{\top}Xp. (A.1)

Thus, a κ\kappa-approximate search oracle for quadratic-form maximization (QFM) over KK is an oracle that, on input XX, returns a point 𝒪K​(X)∈K\mathcal{O}_{K}(X)\in K satisfying

𝒪K​(X)⊤​X​𝒪K​(X)≥κ−1​QK​(X).\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{K}(X)^{\top}X\mathcal{O}_{K}(X)\geq\kappa^{-1}Q_{K}(X). (A.2)

This is the convention used in (2.5) in the main text.

Let g∼N⁡(0,In)g\sim N(0,I_{n}). Recall the upper and lower covariance regions

𝒰⁡(K)\displaystyle\mathcal{U}(K) :={W∈𝕊n:W≥0,𝔼ρK2(W1/2g)≤1},\displaystyle:=\left\{W\in\mathbb{S}^{n}:\ W\geq 0,\ \mathbb{E}\rho_{K}^{2}(W^{1/2}g)\leq 1\right\}, (A.3)
ℒ⁡(K)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(K) :={W∈𝕊n:W≥0,𝔼ρK∘2(W1/2g)≥1}.\displaystyle:=\left\{W\in\mathbb{S}^{n}:\ W\geq 0,\ \mathbb{E}\rho_{K^{\circ}}^{2}(W^{1/2}g)\geq 1\right\}. (A.4)

We use the notion of an approximate separation oracle from [1]. Concretely, if a star-shaped set SS satisfies conv⁡(S)⊆α​S\operatorname{conv}(S)\subseteq\alpha S, then an α\alpha-approximate separation oracle, on input xx, either returns “Inside,” in which case x∈α​Sx\in\alpha S, or returns an affine hyperplane separating xx from SS. For an outward-closed set TT satisfying conv⁡(T)⊆α−1​T\operatorname{conv}(T)\subseteq\alpha^{-1}T, the analogous convention is that “Inside” certifies x∈α−1​Tx\in\alpha^{-1}T, while a returned hyperplane separates xx from TT. These are Definitions 1.6 and 1.11 of [1], respectively.

The source [1] formulates several of the results below using the Gaussian type-22 constant T~2\widetilde{T}_{2}. Our paper uses the Rademacher type-22 constant T2​(K)T_{2}(K) from (1.3). By the standard Gaussian–Rademacher comparison (equivalently, Kahane–Khintchine), these two constants are equivalent up to an absolute multiplicative constant. Accordingly, when translating a bound involving T~2\widetilde{T}_{2} into our convention, we write ≲T2​(K)\lesssim T_{2}(K) and absorb only a universal constant.

Remark A.1.

Although the results of [1] state the running time in terms of log⁡R\log R and log⁡(1/r)\log(1/r) for a body satisfying

r​B2⊆K⊆R​B2,rB_{2}\subseteq K\subseteq RB_{2},

the geometric dependence may equivalently be expressed in terms of log⁡(R/r)\log(R/r). Indeed, consider the rescaled body

K~:=r−1​K,\widetilde{K}:=r^{-1}K,

for which

B2⊆K~⊆(R/r)​B2.B_{2}\subseteq\widetilde{K}\subseteq(R/r)B_{2}.

Moreover,

ρK~​(x)=r​ρK​(x),\rho_{\widetilde{K}}(x)=r\rho_{K}(x),

so an evaluation oracle for the Minkowski gauge of KK immediately yields one for K~\widetilde{K}. Quadratic-form maximization is also invariant under this normalization up to the deterministic scaling

maxz∈K~⁡z⊤​X​z=r−2​maxp∈K​p⊤​X​p,\max_{z\in\widetilde{K}}z^{\top}Xz=r^{-2}\max_{p\in K}p^{\top}Xp,

and hence approximation factors are unchanged after mapping an output z∈K~z\in\widetilde{K} back to r​z∈Krz\in K. Finally, the type-22 constant is invariant under scalar dilations. Thus one may apply the corresponding results to K~\widetilde{K} with inner radius 11 and outer radius R/rR/r, so that the dependence on the balancing radii is through log⁡(R/r)\log(R/r) alone, apart from the ordinary bit complexity of the numerical input parameters. This observation was also confirmed by Vijay Bhattiprolu in personal communication.

Proposition A.2 ([1], Proposition 4.2).

Suppose that KK is well-balanced, so that the radii r,R>0r,R>0 are known and

r​B2⊆K⊆R​B2.rB_{2}\subseteq K\subseteq RB_{2}.

Assume that an α\alpha-approximate separation oracle for 𝒰⁡(K)\mathcal{U}(K) is available. Then, for every symmetric matrix X∈𝕊nX\in\mathbb{S}^{n}, there is a randomized algorithm running in

poly⁡(n,log⁡R,log⁡(1/r),bit⁡(X))\operatorname{poly}\!\left(n,\log R,\log(1/r),\operatorname{bit}(X)\right)

time which, with probability at least 1−2−Ω⁡(n)1-2^{-\Omega(n)}, returns p∈Kp\in K such that

p⊤​X​p≥1(1+o⁡(1))​α​QK​(X).\displaystyle p^{\top}Xp\geq\frac{1}{(1+o(1))\alpha}\,Q_{K}(X). (A.5)

In particular, the result is a search guarantee: the algorithm returns an approximately optimal vector, not only an approximation to the optimal value.

Proposition A.3 ([1], Proposition 4.4).

Suppose that r​B2⊆K⊆R​B2rB_{2}\subseteq K\subseteq RB_{2} with known r,R>0r,R>0, and assume that an α\alpha-approximate separation oracle for ℒ⁡(K)\mathcal{L}(K) is available. Then, for every symmetric psd matrix X∈𝕊nX\in\mathbb{S}^{n}, there is a randomized algorithm running in

poly⁡(n,log⁡R,log⁡(1/r),bit⁡(X))\operatorname{poly}\!\left(n,\log R,\log(1/r),\operatorname{bit}(X)\right)

time which, with probability at least 1−2−Ω⁡(n)1-2^{-\Omega(n)}, returns p∈Kp\in K such that

p⊤​X​p≥1(1+o⁡(1))​α​QK​(X).\displaystyle p^{\top}Xp\geq\frac{1}{(1+o(1))\alpha}\,Q_{K}(X). (A.6)
Corollary A.4 ([1], Corollary 4.12(1)).

Suppose that r​B2⊆K⊆R​B2rB_{2}\subseteq K\subseteq RB_{2} with known r,R>0r,R>0. Assume that there is an exactly computable convex function

f:{W∈𝕊n:W≥0}→ℝf:\{W\in\mathbb{S}^{n}:W\geq 0\}\to\mathbb{R}

and constants α1,α2≥1\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\geq 1 such that, for every W≥0W\geq 0,

α1−1​f​(W)≤𝔼​ρK2​(W1/2​g)≤α2​f​(W).\displaystyle\alpha_{1}^{-1}f(W)\leq\mathbb{E}\rho_{K}^{2}(W^{1/2}g)\leq\alpha_{2}f(W). (A.7)

Then for every symmetric X∈𝕊nX\in\mathbb{S}^{n} one can, in

poly⁡(n,log⁡R,log⁡(1/r),bit⁡(X))\operatorname{poly}\!\left(n,\log R,\log(1/r),\operatorname{bit}(X)\right)

time, return with probability at least 1−2−Ω⁡(n)1-2^{-\Omega(n)} a vector p∈Kp\in K such that

p⊤​X​p≳1α1​α2​T2​(K)2​QK​(X).\displaystyle p^{\top}Xp\gtrsim\frac{1}{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}T_{2}(K)^{2}}\,Q_{K}(X). (A.8)

Equivalently, under our Rademacher type-22 convention the approximation factor is ≲α1​α2​T2​(K)2\lesssim\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}T_{2}(K)^{2}. If one uses the Gaussian type-22 constant T~2\widetilde{T}_{2} of [1], the source states the factor exactly as α1​α2​T~2​(K)2\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\widetilde{T}_{2}(K)^{2}.

Proposition A.5 ([1], Proposition 4.13).

Suppose that r​B2⊆K⊆R​B2rB_{2}\subseteq K\subseteq RB_{2} with known r,R>0r,R>0, and suppose that a κ\kappa-approximate QFM search oracle over KK, in the sense of (A.2), is available. Then one can construct an approximate separation oracle for 𝒰⁡(K)\mathcal{U}(K) with approximation factor

α≲κ​T2​(K)2,\displaystyle\alpha\lesssim\kappa T_{2}(K)^{2}, (A.9)

whose running time is polynomial in n,log⁡R,log⁡(1/r)n,\log R,\log(1/r) and the bit complexity of the input matrix. More precisely, in the Gaussian type convention of [1] the factor is (1+o⁡(1))​κ​T~2​(K)2(1+o(1))\kappa\widetilde{T}_{2}(K)^{2}.

Proposition A.6 ([1], Proposition 6.5).

Let K1,K2⊂ℝnK_{1},K_{2}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be origin-symmetric, well-balanced convex bodies, and assume that both QFM problems admit α\alpha-approximate search oracles. Then the intersection K1∩K2K_{1}\cap K_{2}, whose Minkowski gauge is

ρK1∩K2​(x)=ρK1​(x)∨ρK2​(x),\rho_{K_{1}\cap K_{2}}(x)=\rho_{K_{1}}(x)\vee\rho_{K_{2}}(x),

admits a randomized polynomial-time QFM search algorithm with approximation factor

κ⁡(K1∩K2)≲2​α​max⁡{T2​(K1)2,T2​(K2)2},\displaystyle\kappa(K_{1}\cap K_{2})\lesssim 2\alpha\max\left\{T_{2}(K_{1})^{2},T_{2}(K_{2})^{2}\right\}, (A.10)

and success probability at least 1−2−Ω⁡(n)1-2^{-\Omega(n)}. If the two available QFM oracles have factors κ1\kappa_{1} and κ2\kappa_{2}, the same conclusion follows after setting α=κ1∨κ2\alpha=\kappa_{1}\vee\kappa_{2}.

In particular, for K2=c​B2K_{2}=cB_{2} we have T2​(c​B2)=1T_{2}(cB_{2})=1 and exact QFM over c​B2cB_{2}. Thus, if KK admits a κ\kappa-approximate QFM search oracle, then

κ⁡(K∩c​B2)≲2​κ​T2​(K)2.\displaystyle\kappa(K\cap cB_{2})\lesssim 2\kappa T_{2}(K)^{2}. (A.11)

Under the definition (A.3), one also has the explicit identity

𝒰(cB2)={W∈𝕊n:W≥0,tr(W)≤c2}.\displaystyle\mathcal{U}(cB_{2})=\left\{W\in\mathbb{S}^{n}:\ W\geq 0,\ \operatorname{tr}(W)\leq c^{2}\right\}. (A.12)

We next state the Banach-lattice results used to construct the separation oracles appearing above. Suppose that ρK\rho_{K} is sign-invariant. For 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty, define the pp-convexity constant M(p)​(K)M^{(p)}(K) as the smallest CC such that

ρK​((∑i|xi|p)1/p)≤C​(∑iρK​(xi)p)1/p\displaystyle\rho_{K}\!\left(\left(\sum_{i}|x_{i}|^{p}\right)^{1/p}\right)\leq C\left(\sum_{i}\rho_{K}(x_{i})^{p}\right)^{1/p} (A.13)

for every finite collection (xi)(x_{i}). Similarly, define the qq-concavity constant M(q)​(K)M_{(q)}(K) as the smallest CC such that

ρK​((∑i|xi|q)1/q)≥C−1​(∑iρK​(xi)q)1/q.\displaystyle\rho_{K}\!\left(\left(\sum_{i}|x_{i}|^{q}\right)^{1/q}\right)\geq C^{-1}\left(\sum_{i}\rho_{K}(x_{i})^{q}\right)^{1/q}. (A.14)

All powers and absolute values inside the vector in (A.13)–(A.14) are applied coordinatewise. The norm is exactly pp-convex when M(p)​(K)=1M^{(p)}(K)=1.

Theorem A.7 ([1], Theorem 7.4).

Let ρK\rho_{K} be sign-invariant, let 1≤p≤2≤q<∞1\leq p\leq 2\leq q<\infty, let x1,…,xm∈ℝnx_{1},\ldots,x_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, and let g1,…,gmg_{1},\ldots,g_{m} be independent standard Gaussian random variables. Put

γs:=(𝔼​|g1|s)1/s.\gamma_{s}:=\left(\mathbb{E}|g_{1}|^{s}\right)^{1/s}.

Then

γpM(p)​(K)​ρK​((∑i=1m|xi|2)1/2)\displaystyle\frac{\gamma_{p}}{M^{(p)}(K)}\rho_{K}\!\left(\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}|x_{i}|^{2}\right)^{1/2}\right) ≤(𝔼​ρK2​(∑i=1mgi​xi))1/2\displaystyle\leq\left(\mathbb{E}\rho_{K}^{2}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}g_{i}x_{i}\right)\right)^{1/2}
≤γq​M(q)​(K)​ρK​((∑i=1m|xi|2)1/2).\displaystyle\leq\gamma_{q}M_{(q)}(K)\rho_{K}\!\left(\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}|x_{i}|^{2}\right)^{1/2}\right). (A.15)

In particular, if ρK\rho_{K} is exactly 22-convex, then the constant in the left inequality can be taken to be 11.

Theorem A.8 ([1], Theorem 7.6).

Suppose that ρK\rho_{K} is an exactly computable, sign-invariant, exactly 22-convex norm and that KK is well-balanced. Then, for every symmetric matrix X∈𝕊nX\in\mathbb{S}^{n}, there is a randomized polynomial-time QFM search algorithm over KK which succeeds with probability at least 1−2−Ω⁡(n)1-2^{-\Omega(n)} and has approximation factor

κ⁡(K)=inf2≤q<∞M(q)​(K)2​γq2.\displaystyle\kappa(K)=\inf_{2\leq q<\infty}M_{(q)}(K)^{2}\gamma_{q}^{2}. (A.16)

In particular, for a sign-invariant norm on ℝnA\mathbb{R}^{n_{A}}, one may take q≍log⁡nAq\asymp\log n_{A}; using M(log⁡nA)​(K)≤eM_{(\log n_{A})}(K)\leq e gives the logarithmic-factor bound used in Section 3.

Theorem A.9 ([1], Theorem 7.12).

Suppose that ρK\rho_{K} is a symmetric norm, i.e., it is invariant under arbitrary coordinate permutations and sign changes, and assume that ρK​(x)\rho_{K}(x) can be evaluated in polynomial time. Then, for every symmetric matrix X∈𝕊nX\in\mathbb{S}^{n}, there is a randomized polynomial-time QFM search algorithm which succeeds with probability at least 1−2−Ω⁡(n)1-2^{-\Omega(n)} and whose approximation factor, in the type-22 convention of this paper, satisfies

κ⁡(K)≲T2​(K)6​log4⁡(e​T2​(K)).\displaystyle\kappa(K)\lesssim T_{2}(K)^{6}\log^{4}\!\bigl(eT_{2}(K)\bigr). (A.17)

The source gives the more refined intermediate bound in terms of the dual cotype-22 constant and then bounds it by the right-hand side of (A.17).

Corollary A.10 (Linear images of symmetric norm balls).

Let ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| be a symmetric norm on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, let A∈ℝn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be full rank, and let

K={x∈ℝn:‖A​x‖≤1}.K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\ \|Ax\|\leq 1\}.

Then Theorem A.9 applies after the change of variables z=A​xz=Ax. Indeed, for every symmetric matrix XX,

QK​(X)\displaystyle Q_{K}(X) =max‖z‖≤1⁡z⊤​A−⁣⊤​X​A−1​z.\displaystyle=\max_{\|z\|\leq 1}z^{\top}A^{-\top}XA^{-1}z. (A.18)

Moreover, the normed spaces (ℝn,ρK)(\mathbb{R}^{n},\rho_{K}) and (ℝn,∥⋅∥)(\mathbb{R}^{n},\|\cdot\|) are isometric via AA, and hence their type-22 constants agree. Consequently one obtains a QFM search oracle over KK with

κ⁡(K)≲T2​(K)6​log4⁡(e​T2​(K)),\displaystyle\kappa(K)\lesssim T_{2}(K)^{6}\log^{4}\!\bigl(eT_{2}(K)\bigr), (A.19)

with polynomial running time (including the bit complexity of AA and XX).

Remark A.11 (The composition used for symmetric norms).

The chain used in the proof of Theorem 3.3 is now explicit. Theorem A.9 first gives

κ⁡(K)≲T2​(K)6​log4⁡(e​T2​(K)).\kappa(K)\lesssim T_{2}(K)^{6}\log^{4}\!\bigl(eT_{2}(K)\bigr).

Proposition A.5 then gives an approximate separation oracle for 𝒰⁡(K)\mathcal{U}(K) with factor

α≲T2​(K)8​log4⁡(e​T2​(K)).\alpha\lesssim T_{2}(K)^{8}\log^{4}\!\bigl(eT_{2}(K)\bigr).

Finally, Proposition A.6, applied to KK and c​B2cB_{2}, yields

κ⁡(K∩c​B2)≲2​T2​(K)10​log4⁡(e​T2​(K)),\displaystyle\kappa(K\cap cB_{2})\lesssim 2T_{2}(K)^{10}\log^{4}\!\bigl(eT_{2}(K)\bigr), (A.20)

which is precisely the approximation factor used in Theorem 3.3.

Remark on numbering.

In the version of [1] used above, item 4.12 is a corollary, not a proposition. We therefore refer to it as Corollary 4.12 throughout this appendix.

A.2 Weak convex optimization and weak Euclidean projection

We next record the convex-optimization result from [8] that we use to implement weak Euclidean projections and the convex minimizations in the regression section.

Theorem A.12 ([8], Theorem 2.5.9).

Let K⊂ℝnK\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a convex body for which there are known a0∈ℝna_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and r,R>0r,R>0 such that

a0+r​B2⊆K⊆a0+R​B2,a_{0}+rB_{2}\subseteq K\subseteq a_{0}+RB_{2},

and suppose that a weak membership oracle for KK is available. Let f:ℝn→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} be a convex LL-Lipschitz function. Assume that ff is available through an evaluation oracle which, given x∈ℚnx\in\mathbb{Q}^{n} and δ>0\delta>0, returns a rational number tt satisfying

|t−f⁡(x)|≤δ.|t-f(x)|\leq\delta.

Then, for every ϵ>0\epsilon>0, one can compute in polynomial time a rational number ww and a point p∈Kp\in K such that

w−ϵ≤minx∈K⁡f⁡(x)≤f⁡(p)≤w.\displaystyle w-\epsilon\leq\min_{x\in K}f(x)\leq f(p)\leq w. (A.21)

The running time is polynomial in the encoding lengths of the input parameters and the corresponding oracle accuracies.

Since our sets are origin-symmetric and well-balanced, we take a0=0a_{0}=0. Moreover, our oracle for the Minkowski gauge ρK\rho_{K} gives a weak membership oracle for KK; in particular, membership is determined by the condition ρK​(x)≤1\rho_{K}(x)\leq 1 up to the requested numerical tolerance.

The following is the specialization used repeatedly in the paper.

Corollary A.13 (Weak Euclidean projection).

Let KK satisfy the assumptions above. Given z∈ℝnz\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and ϵ>0\epsilon>0, one can compute in polynomial time a rational number ww and p∈Kp\in K such that

w−ϵ≤‖z−Π¯K​(z)‖2≤‖z−p‖2≤w,\displaystyle w-\epsilon\leq\|z-\overline{\Pi}_{K}(z)\|_{2}\leq\|z-p\|_{2}\leq w, (A.22)

where Π¯K​(z)\overline{\Pi}_{K}(z) denotes the exact Euclidean projection of zz onto KK. Furthermore, for every ν∈K\nu\in K,

‖p−ν‖2≤‖z−ν‖2+ϵ2+2​ϵ​‖z−ν‖2.\displaystyle\|p-\nu\|_{2}\leq\|z-\nu\|_{2}+\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}+2\epsilon\|z-\nu\|_{2}}. (A.23)
Proof.

Apply Theorem A.12 to f⁡(x)=‖z−x‖2f(x)=\|z-x\|_{2}, which is convex and 11-Lipschitz. This gives (A.22). Put z0=Π¯K​(z)z_{0}=\overline{\Pi}_{K}(z). The projection inequality for convex sets implies

‖p−z0‖22+‖z−z0‖22≤‖z−p‖22.\|p-z_{0}\|_{2}^{2}+\|z-z_{0}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|z-p\|_{2}^{2}.

Using ‖z−p‖2≤‖z−z0‖2+ϵ\|z-p\|_{2}\leq\|z-z_{0}\|_{2}+\epsilon gives

‖p−z0‖2≤ϵ2+2​ϵ​‖z−z0‖2≤ϵ2+2​ϵ​‖z−ν‖2.\|p-z_{0}\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}+2\epsilon\|z-z_{0}\|_{2}}\leq\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}+2\epsilon\|z-\nu\|_{2}}.

Also, by the projection inequality, ‖z0−ν‖2≤‖z−ν‖2\|z_{0}-\nu\|_{2}\leq\|z-\nu\|_{2}. The triangle inequality therefore yields (A.23). ∎

A.3 The robust mean estimator of Depersin–Lecue

We state the result in the notation of Section 4. The theorem appears as Theorem 2.1 in the published version of [9] (and is the result referred to as Theorem 2 in the main text).

Theorem A.14 ([9], Theorem 2.1).

Let Y~1,…,Y~N∈ℝn\widetilde{Y}_{1},\ldots,\widetilde{Y}_{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} be independent random vectors with common mean μ\mu and covariance matrix Σ\Sigma. An adversary is allowed to replace arbitrarily the observations indexed by a set ℐout⊆[N]\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{out}}\subseteq[N], producing the observed vectors Y1,…,YNY_{1},\ldots,Y_{N}. No moment assumption beyond the existence of Σ\Sigma is required.

Let k∈{1,…,N}k\in\{1,\ldots,N\} be the number of equal-sized blocks in the Depersin–Lecue procedure and assume

k≥300​|ℐout|.\displaystyle k\geq 300|\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{out}}|. (A.24)

Let u∈ℕu\in\mathbb{N} be the parameter of the covering SDP used at each descent step. Then their algorithm runs in time

O~​(N​n+k​u​n)\displaystyle\widetilde{O}\!\left(Nn+kun\right) (A.25)

and, with probability at least

1−exp(−k/180000)−10−u,\displaystyle 1-\exp(-k/180000)-10^{-u}, (A.26)

returns an estimator, which we denote by f⁡((Yi)i∈[N])f((Y_{i})_{i\in[N]}), satisfying

‖f⁡((Yi)i∈[N])−μ‖2≤808​(1200​tr⁡(Σ)N+1200​‖Σ‖op​kN).\displaystyle\bigl\|f((Y_{i})_{i\in[N]})-\mu\bigr\|_{2}\leq 808\left(1200\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)}{N}}+\sqrt{\frac{1200\|\Sigma\|_{\operatorname{op}}k}{N}}\right). (A.27)

The form used in our proofs is the immediate universal-constant consequence

‖f⁡((Yi)i∈[N])−μ‖2≲tr⁡(Σ)N+‖Σ‖op​kN.\displaystyle\bigl\|f((Y_{i})_{i\in[N]})-\mu\bigr\|_{2}\lesssim\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)}{N}}+\sqrt{\frac{\|\Sigma\|_{\operatorname{op}}k}{N}}. (A.28)

For example, under the standing assumption ‖Σ‖op≤σ2\|\Sigma\|_{\operatorname{op}}\leq\sigma^{2}, we also have tr⁡(Σ)≤n​σ2\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)\leq n\sigma^{2}. Taking k=u=Nk=u=N and assuming the contamination fraction is smaller than a sufficiently small absolute constant therefore gives

‖f⁡((Yi)i∈[N])−μ‖2≲n/N​σ+σ≲σ\displaystyle\bigl\|f((Y_{i})_{i\in[N]})-\mu\bigr\|_{2}\lesssim\sqrt{n/N}\,\sigma+\sigma\lesssim\sigma (A.29)

with probability at least 1−exp(−N/C0)1-\exp(-N/C_{0}) for an absolute constant C0>0C_{0}>0. This is the pilot-estimator guarantee used in (4.1). Likewise, applying (A.28) after the linear transformation A⋆⁣⋆A^{\star\star} gives the bound used in Lemma 4.2.

A.4 Carl’s inequality

We next record Theorem 5 of [5] and its specialization to the identity embedding associated with KK. For a bounded linear operator S:E→FS:E\to F, let sj​(S)s_{j}(S) denote either its jj-th Kolmogorov number or its jj-th Gelfand number, and let

gm​(S):=infk≥1k1/m​εk​(S),\displaystyle g_{m}(S):=\inf_{k\geq 1}k^{1/m}\varepsilon_{k}(S), (A.30)

where εk​(S)\varepsilon_{k}(S) is the non-dyadic entropy number, i.e., the smallest radius for which S⁡(BE)S(B_{E}) can be covered by kk translates of that radius times BFB_{F}.

Theorem A.15 ([5], Theorem 5, real case).

Let S:E→FS:E\to F be a bounded linear operator between real Banach spaces. Suppose that EE has Rademacher type pp with type constant τp​(E)\tau_{p}(E) and F∗F^{*} has Rademacher type qq with type constant τq​(F∗)\tau_{q}(F^{*}). Then, for every m≥1m\geq 1,

(∏j=1msj​(S))1/m≤ρ​τp​(E)​τq​(F∗)​m−1+1/p+1/q​gm​(S),\displaystyle\left(\prod_{j=1}^{m}s_{j}(S)\right)^{1/m}\leq\rho\,\tau_{p}(E)\tau_{q}(F^{*})\,m^{-1+1/p+1/q}g_{m}(S), (A.31)

where ρ\rho is an absolute numerical constant in the real case.

We now take

E=(ℝn,ρK),F=(ℝn,∥⋅∥2),S=I.E=(\mathbb{R}^{n},\rho_{K}),\qquad F=(\mathbb{R}^{n},\|\cdot\|_{2}),\qquad S=I.

Then S⁡(BE)=KS(B_{E})=K, F∗=FF^{*}=F is Hilbert and has type-22 constant one, and εk​(S)=ek​(K)\varepsilon_{k}(S)=e_{k}(K) under Definition 1.2. Taking p=q=2p=q=2 in Theorem A.15, and using the equivalence between Carl’s first-moment type-22 convention and the second-moment convention (1.3), gives

(∏j=1mdj​(K))1/m≲T2​(K)​infk≥1k1/m​ek​(K).\displaystyle\left(\prod_{j=1}^{m}d_{j}(K)\right)^{1/m}\lesssim T_{2}(K)\inf_{k\geq 1}k^{1/m}e_{k}(K). (A.32)

Carl’s operator-theoretic Kolmogorov numbers use subspaces of dimension strictly less than the index, whereas Definition 1.1 uses a kk-dimensional subspace. The resulting shift by one is absorbed by the monotonicity of the widths. Equation (A.32) is therefore exactly the form of Carl’s inequality used in (1.7).

A.5 The global-to-local packing inequality of Yang–Barron

Finally, we record the elementary packing inequality used in the proof of Lemma 2.1. Recall that M⁡(η,K)M(\eta,K) denotes the maximal cardinality of an η\eta-packing of KK, while for the fixed constant c>1c>1 from Definition 1.3,

MKloc​(η)=supν∈KM⁡(η/c,B2​(ν,η)∩K).M_{K}^{\operatorname{loc}}(\eta)=\sup_{\nu\in K}M\!\left(\eta/c,B_{2}(\nu,\eta)\cap K\right).

The original statement in [33] is written with the constant 22; the same proof gives the version with an arbitrary fixed c>1c>1 used here.

Lemma A.16 (Yang–Barron global-to-local packing inequality).

For every η>0\eta>0,

log⁡M⁡(η/c,K)−log⁡M⁡(η,K)≤log⁡MKloc​(η)≤log⁡M⁡(η/c,K).\displaystyle\log M(\eta/c,K)-\log M(\eta,K)\leq\log M_{K}^{\operatorname{loc}}(\eta)\leq\log M(\eta/c,K). (A.33)

In particular, for every integer j≥0j\geq 0 and every Υ>0\Upsilon>0,

log⁡M⁡(Υ​cj−1,K)−log⁡M⁡(Υ​cj,K)≤log⁡MKloc​(Υ​cj),\displaystyle\log M(\Upsilon c^{j-1},K)-\log M(\Upsilon c^{j},K)\leq\log M_{K}^{\operatorname{loc}}(\Upsilon c^{j}), (A.34)

which is the form used in the proof of Lemma 2.1.

Proof.

Let {a1,…,aM}\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{M}\} be a maximal η\eta-packing of KK, so that M=M⁡(η,K)M=M(\eta,K). Maximality implies that the balls B2​(ai,η)B_{2}(a_{i},\eta) cover KK. Next let {b1,…,bL}\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{L}\} be an η/c\eta/c-packing of KK of maximal cardinality, so that L=M⁡(η/c,K)L=M(\eta/c,K). Assign every bℓb_{\ell} to an index ii for which bℓ∈B2​(ai,η)b_{\ell}\in B_{2}(a_{i},\eta). By the pigeonhole principle, for at least one ii, B2​(ai,η)∩KB_{2}(a_{i},\eta)\cap K contains at least L/ML/M of the points bℓb_{\ell}. These points remain η/c\eta/c-separated, and therefore

MKloc​(η)≥M⁡(η/c,K)M⁡(η,K).M_{K}^{\operatorname{loc}}(\eta)\geq\frac{M(\eta/c,K)}{M(\eta,K)}.

Taking logarithms gives the first inequality in (A.33). The second inequality is immediate because B2​(ν,η)∩K⊆KB_{2}(\nu,\eta)\cap K\subseteq K for every ν∈K\nu\in K. ∎

Proof of Lemma 2.5.

We form the Lagrangian

ℒ⁡(w,θ,α,β)=12​‖w−v‖22+θ⁡(∑i=1nwi−k)−∑i=1nαi​wi+∑i=1nβi​(wi−1),\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(w,\theta,\alpha,\beta)=\frac{1}{2}\|w-v\|_{2}^{2}+\theta\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}-k\Big)-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}w_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\beta_{i}(w_{i}-1),

where αi,βi≥0\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}\geq 0 are the multipliers for the box constraints wi≥0w_{i}\geq 0 and wi≤1w_{i}\leq 1, respectively.

Stationarity gives

0=∇wℒ=w−v+θ​𝟏−α+β,i.e.wi=vi−θ+αi−βi.\displaystyle 0=\nabla_{w}\mathcal{L}=w-v+\theta\mathbf{1}-\alpha+\beta,\quad\text{i.e.}\quad w_{i}=v_{i}-\theta+\alpha_{i}-\beta_{i}.

The complementary slackness conditions are:

αi​wi=0,βi​(wi−1)=0.\displaystyle\alpha_{i}w_{i}=0,\qquad\beta_{i}(w_{i}-1)=0.

Hence, for each coordinate ii:

  • •

    If 0<wi<10<w_{i}<1, then αi=βi=0\alpha_{i}=\beta_{i}=0 and wi=vi−θw_{i}=v_{i}-\theta.

  • •

    If wi=0w_{i}=0, then αi≥0\alpha_{i}\geq 0 and vi−θ≤0v_{i}-\theta\leq 0.

  • •

Therefore,

wi=min⁡{1,max⁡{0,vi−θ⋆}}.\displaystyle w_{i}=\min\{1,\max\{0,v_{i}-\theta^{\star}\}\}.

The equality constraint ∑iwi=k\sum_{i}w_{i}=k then becomes

f⁡(θ)=∑i=1nmin⁡{1,max⁡{0,vi−θ}}=k.\displaystyle f(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\min\{1,\max\{0,v_{i}-\theta\}\}=k.

The function f⁡(θ)f(\theta) is continuous, nonincreasing, and piecewise linear. As f⁡(min⁡(v)−1)=nf(\min(v)-1)=n and f⁡(max⁡(v))=0f(\max(v))=0, by the intermediate value theorem there exists a θ⋆\theta^{\star} such that f⁡(θ⋆)=kf(\theta^{\star})=k. Although θ⋆\theta^{\star} need not be unique, the resulting projected vector is unique because the Euclidean projection problem has a strictly convex objective over a convex feasible set. Substituting the value of θ⋆\theta^{\star} yields the claimed projection. Convexity of both the objective and constraint set ensures uniqueness. The last implication is obvious due to the formula for wiw_{i}. ∎

B.1 Removing the global diameter dependence by Gaussian sample splitting

In Remark 2.3, the passage from local metric entropy to global metric entropy introduces the factor

1+log⁡diam⁡(K)η⋆.\displaystyle 1+\log\frac{\mathrm{diam}(K)}{\eta^{\star}}.

For a general convex body this quantity need not be logarithmic in the ambient dimension, since diam⁡(K)\mathrm{diam}(K) may be arbitrarily large compared with the noise level. In the Gaussian sequence model, however, one can remove this dependence on the global diameter by a sample-splitting localization argument. We give the details below.

Throughout this appendix, let

Y=μ+σ​Z,Z∼N⁡(0,In),μ∈K,\displaystyle Y=\mu+\sigma Z,\qquad Z\sim N(0,I_{n}),\qquad\mu\in K,

where K⊂ℝnK\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is a compact, origin-symmetric convex body. Recall that

η⋆=sup{η≥0:η2σ2≤log⁡MKloc​(η)}.\displaystyle\eta^{\star}=\sup\left\{\eta\geq 0:\frac{\eta^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\leq\log M_{K}^{\operatorname{loc}}(\eta)\right\}.

We assume σ>0\sigma>0 and that KK is not a singleton; the remaining cases are immediate.

We first record two elementary observations.

Lemma B.1 (A crude lower bound on the critical radius).

Let d=diam⁡(K)d=\mathrm{diam}(K). Then

η⋆≳d∧σ.\displaystyle\eta^{\star}\gtrsim d\wedge\sigma.
Proof.

To be self contained we spell the details of this lemma. The same result can be found in [25]. Since KK is compact and origin-symmetric, there exists v∈Kv\in K with ‖v‖2=d/2\|v\|_{2}=d/2. By convexity,

[−v,v]⊆K.\displaystyle[-v,v]\subseteq K.

Consequently, for every

0<t≤d/2,\displaystyle 0<t\leq d/2,

the set B2​(0,t)∩KB_{2}(0,t)\cap K contains the two points ±tv/∥v∥2\pm t\,v/\|v\|_{2}. Their Euclidean distance is 2​t2t, so, for the sufficiently large absolute constant cc appearing in the definition of local metric entropy,

MKloc​(t)≥2.\displaystyle M_{K}^{\operatorname{loc}}(t)\geq 2.

Choose

t0=min⁡{d4,log⁡22​σ}.\displaystyle t_{0}=\min\left\{\frac{d}{4},\,\frac{\sqrt{\log 2}}{2}\sigma\right\}.

Then

t02σ2≤log⁡2≤log⁡MKloc​(t0),\displaystyle\frac{t_{0}^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\leq\log 2\leq\log M_{K}^{\operatorname{loc}}(t_{0}),

and therefore t0≤η⋆t_{0}\leq\eta^{\star}. This proves η⋆≳d∧σ\eta^{\star}\gtrsim d\wedge\sigma. ∎

Lemma B.2 (Type-22 is preserved by Euclidean localization).

For every R>0R>0, define

LR:=2​K∩R​B2.\displaystyle L_{R}:=2K\cap RB_{2}.

Then LRL_{R} is an origin-symmetric convex body and

T2​(LR)≤T2​(K)2+1≲T2​(K).\displaystyle T_{2}(L_{R})\leq\sqrt{T_{2}(K)^{2}+1}\lesssim T_{2}(K).
Proof.

The Minkowski gauge of LRL_{R} is

ρLR​(x)=max⁡{12​ρK​(x),‖x‖2R}.\displaystyle\rho_{L_{R}}(x)=\max\left\{\frac{1}{2}\rho_{K}(x),\,\frac{\|x\|_{2}}{R}\right\}.

Hence, for arbitrary x1,…,xN∈ℝnx_{1},\ldots,x_{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and independent Rademacher variables ϵ1,…,ϵN\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{N},

𝔼ϵ​ρLR2​(∑i=1Nϵi​xi)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}\rho_{L_{R}}^{2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\epsilon_{i}x_{i}\right) ≤14​𝔼ϵ​ρK2​(∑i=1Nϵi​xi)+1R2​𝔼ϵ​‖∑i=1Nϵi​xi‖22\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{4}\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}\rho_{K}^{2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\epsilon_{i}x_{i}\right)+\frac{1}{R^{2}}\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\epsilon_{i}x_{i}\right\|_{2}^{2}
≤T2​(K)24​∑i=1NρK2​(xi)+1R2​∑i=1N‖xi‖22\displaystyle\leq\frac{T_{2}(K)^{2}}{4}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\rho_{K}^{2}(x_{i})+\frac{1}{R^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|x_{i}\|_{2}^{2}
≤(T2​(K)2+1)​∑i=1NρLR2​(xi).\displaystyle\leq\bigl(T_{2}(K)^{2}+1\bigr)\sum_{i=1}^{N}\rho_{L_{R}}^{2}(x_{i}).

The claim follows. ∎

We next record the deterministic consequence of the local-to-global entropy argument that we will use. The point is that the critical radius in the following lemma is the critical radius of the original body KK, not that of the localized body.

Lemma B.3 (A small width for the localized error body).

m\displaystyle m ≲η⋆2σ2​(1+log+⁡DRη⋆),\displaystyle\lesssim\frac{\eta^{\star 2}}{\sigma^{2}}\left(1+\log_{+}\frac{D_{R}}{\eta^{\star}}\right), (B.1)
suph∈LR‖(I−Pm)​h‖2\displaystyle\sup_{h\in L_{R}}\|(I-P_{m})h\|_{2} ≲T2​(LR)​η⋆.\displaystyle\lesssim T_{2}(L_{R})\eta^{\star}. (B.2)

We can now give the sample-splitting construction.

Proposition B.4 (Gaussian sample-splitting localization).

There exists a randomized estimator μ^\widehat{\mu} such that

supμ∈K𝔼μ​‖μ^−μ‖22≲(T2​(K)2+log⁡(e​n))​η⋆2.\sup_{\mu\in K}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\|\widehat{\mu}-\mu\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim\left(T_{2}(K)^{2}+\log(en)\right)\eta^{\star 2}. (B.5)

The estimator constructed below is not a single fixed linear estimator of YY; rather, it is a sample-split estimator consisting of a pilot estimate followed by a linear correction.

Proof.

Let G∼N⁡(0,In)G\sim N(0,I_{n}) be independent of YY, and define

Y(1)=Y+σ​G,Y(2)=Y−σ​G.Y^{(1)}=Y+\sigma G,\qquad Y^{(2)}=Y-\sigma G. (B.6)

Y=μ+σ​Z,\displaystyle Y=\mu+\sigma Z,

Y(1)−μ=σ⁡(Z+G),Y(2)−μ=σ⁡(Z−G).\displaystyle Y^{(1)}-\mu=\sigma(Z+G),\qquad Y^{(2)}-\mu=\sigma(Z-G).

The two vectors Z+GZ+G and Z−GZ-G are jointly Gaussian and have zero cross-covariance. Therefore

Y(1),Y(2)∼indN⁡(μ,2​σ2​In).Y^{(1)},Y^{(2)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\operatorname{ind}}}{{\sim}}N(\mu,2\sigma^{2}I_{n}). (B.7)

μ~:=ΠK​(Y(1)).\displaystyle\widetilde{\mu}:=\Pi_{K}(Y^{(1)}).

Because Euclidean projection onto a closed convex set is non-expansive and ΠK​(μ)=μ\Pi_{K}(\mu)=\mu,

‖μ~−μ‖2≤‖Y(1)−μ‖2.\|\widetilde{\mu}-\mu\|_{2}\leq\|Y^{(1)}-\mu\|_{2}. (B.8)

Moreover, since both μ~\widetilde{\mu} and μ\mu belong to KK,

h:=μ−μ~∈K−K=2​K.h:=\mu-\widetilde{\mu}\in K-K=2K. (B.9)

Fix a sufficiently large absolute constant AA and set

R=A​n​σ,LR=2​K∩R​B2.\displaystyle R=A\sqrt{n}\,\sigma,\qquad L_{R}=2K\cap RB_{2}.

Let PmP_{m} be the projection furnished by Lemma B.3, and define

μ^:=μ~+Pm​(Y(2)−μ~).\widehat{\mu}:=\widetilde{\mu}+P_{m}\bigl(Y^{(2)}-\widetilde{\mu}\bigr). (B.10)

Conditional on Y(1)Y^{(1)}, the vector hh is fixed, while Y(2)−μ∼N⁡(0,2​σ2​In)Y^{(2)}-\mu\sim N(0,2\sigma^{2}I_{n}) is independent of Y(1)Y^{(1)}. Therefore

μ^−μ\displaystyle\widehat{\mu}-\mu =−(I−Pm)​h+Pm​(Y(2)−μ),\displaystyle=-(I-P_{m})h+P_{m}(Y^{(2)}-\mu), (B.11)

and hence

𝔼⁡[‖μ^−μ‖22|Y(1)]=‖(I−Pm)​h‖22+2​σ2​m.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widehat{\mu}-\mu\|_{2}^{2}\,\middle|\,Y^{(1)}\right]=\|(I-P_{m})h\|_{2}^{2}+2\sigma^{2}m. (B.12)

Let

ℰ:={∥h∥2≤R}.\displaystyle\mathcal{E}:=\{\|h\|_{2}\leq R\}.

On ℰ\mathcal{E}, (B.9) implies h∈LRh\in L_{R}, and therefore

‖(I−Pm)​h‖22≲T2​(LR)2​η⋆2.\displaystyle\|(I-P_{m})h\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim T_{2}(L_{R})^{2}\eta^{\star 2}.

On ℰc\mathcal{E}^{c}, since PmP_{m} is an orthogonal projection,

‖(I−Pm)​h‖22≤‖h‖22.\displaystyle\|(I-P_{m})h\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|h\|_{2}^{2}.

Taking expectations in (B.12) gives

𝔼μ​‖μ^−μ‖22\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\|\widehat{\mu}-\mu\|_{2}^{2} ≤2σ2m+CT2(LR)2η⋆2+𝔼μ[∥h∥22𝟏{∥h∥2>R}].\displaystyle\leq 2\sigma^{2}m+CT_{2}(L_{R})^{2}\eta^{\star 2}+\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\left[\|h\|_{2}^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\{\|h\|_{2}>R\}}\right]. (B.13)

We first control the deterministic terms. Since

DR=diam⁡(LR)≤2​min⁡{d,R},\displaystyle D_{R}=\mathrm{diam}(L_{R})\leq 2\min\{d,R\},

DRη⋆\displaystyle\frac{D_{R}}{\eta^{\star}} ≲min⁡{d,n​σ}d∧σ≲n.\displaystyle\lesssim\frac{\min\{d,\sqrt{n}\,\sigma\}}{d\wedge\sigma}\lesssim\sqrt{n}. (B.14)

Consequently,

1+log+⁡DRη⋆≲log⁡(e​n).\displaystyle 1+\log_{+}\frac{D_{R}}{\eta^{\star}}\lesssim\log(en).

Combining this with Lemma B.3 and Lemma B.2,

2​σ2​m+C​T2​(LR)2​η⋆2≲(T2​(K)2+log⁡(e​n))​η⋆2.2\sigma^{2}m+CT_{2}(L_{R})^{2}\eta^{\star 2}\lesssim\left(T_{2}(K)^{2}+\log(en)\right)\eta^{\star 2}. (B.15)

‖h‖2≤‖Y(1)−μ‖2.\displaystyle\|h\|_{2}\leq\|Y^{(1)}-\mu\|_{2}.

supx∈2​K‖x‖2=d.\displaystyle\sup_{x\in 2K}\|x\|_{2}=d.

η⋆≳σ.\displaystyle\eta^{\star}\gtrsim\sigma. (B.16)

Y(1)−μ2​σ∼N⁡(0,In).\displaystyle\frac{Y^{(1)}-\mu}{\sqrt{2}\sigma}\sim N(0,I_{n}).

𝔼μ[∥Y(1)−μ∥22𝟏{∥Y(1)−μ∥2>R}]≲nσ2e−c​n.\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\left[\|Y^{(1)}-\mu\|_{2}^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\{\|Y^{(1)}-\mu\|_{2}>R\}}\right]\lesssim n\sigma^{2}e^{-cn}. (B.17)

ℙ(∥Z∥2≥n+t)≤e−t2/2,\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\|Z\|_{2}\geq\sqrt{n}+t)\leq e^{-t^{2}/2},

together with Cauchy–Schwarz and 𝔼​‖Z‖24=n⁡(n+2)\mathbb{E}\|Z\|_{2}^{4}=n(n+2). Using (B.8), (B.16), and the elementary bound n​e−c​n≲1ne^{-cn}\lesssim 1, we obtain

𝔼μ[∥h∥22𝟏{∥h∥2>R}]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\left[\|h\|_{2}^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\{\|h\|_{2}>R\}}\right] ≤𝔼μ[∥Y(1)−μ∥22𝟏{∥Y(1)−μ∥2>R}]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\left[\|Y^{(1)}-\mu\|_{2}^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\{\|Y^{(1)}-\mu\|_{2}>R\}}\right]
≲n​σ2​e−c​n≲σ2≲η⋆2.\displaystyle\lesssim n\sigma^{2}e^{-cn}\lesssim\sigma^{2}\lesssim\eta^{\star 2}. (B.18)

Corollary B.5 (The auxiliary randomization can be removed).

There exists a deterministic estimator μ¯=μ¯​(Y)\overline{\mu}=\overline{\mu}(Y) satisfying the same risk bound (B.5).

Proof.

Write the estimator in Proposition  B.4 as μ^​(Y,G)\widehat{\mu}(Y,G), where G∼N⁡(0,In)G\sim N(0,I_{n}) is the auxiliary Gaussian randomization, independent of YY. Define

μ¯​(Y):=𝔼G​[μ^​(Y,G)∣Y].\displaystyle\overline{\mu}(Y):=\mathbb{E}_{G}\!\left[\widehat{\mu}(Y,G)\mid Y\right].

This is a genuine estimator depending only on the observed data YY; in particular, the averaging distribution of GG does not involve the unknown parameter μ\mu. Conditional Jensen’s inequality gives, for every μ∈K\mu\in K,

‖μ¯​(Y)−μ‖22\displaystyle\|\overline{\mu}(Y)-\mu\|_{2}^{2} =‖𝔼G​[μ^​(Y,G)−μ|Y]‖22\displaystyle=\left\|\mathbb{E}_{G}\!\left[\widehat{\mu}(Y,G)-\mu\,\middle|\,Y\right]\right\|_{2}^{2}
≤𝔼G​[‖μ^​(Y,G)−μ‖22|Y].\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{G}\!\left[\|\widehat{\mu}(Y,G)-\mu\|_{2}^{2}\,\middle|\,Y\right].

Taking expectation with respect to YY proves the claim.

For the particular construction above one may write this deterministic estimator more explicitly as

μ¯​(Y)=Pm​Y+(I−Pm)​𝔼G​[ΠK​(Y+σ​G)],\displaystyle\overline{\mu}(Y)=P_{m}Y+(I-P_{m})\mathbb{E}_{G}\!\left[\Pi_{K}(Y+\sigma G)\right],

because 𝔼G​G=0\mathbb{E}_{G}G=0. ∎

Remark B.6.

The construction above should be viewed as a statistical localization argument rather than as a proof that a single deterministic linear estimator is near-minimax. Indeed, the estimator (B.10) can be written as

μ^=Pm​Y(2)+(I−Pm)​μ~,\displaystyle\widehat{\mu}=P_{m}Y^{(2)}+(I-P_{m})\widetilde{\mu},

and its offset depends on the independent pilot sample Y(1)Y^{(1)}. Thus the argument removes the dependence on the global diameter at the price of leaving the class of fixed linear estimators. By Corollary B.5, the auxiliary randomization itself is inessential, but the resulting deterministic estimator remains nonlinear. The argument also does not, by itself, address the computational problem of finding the appropriate Kolmogorov-width projection PmP_{m}.

Appendix C Proofs of Section 4

Lemma C.1 (Robust refinement lemma).

Suppose that μ^j∈K\hat{\mu}_{j}\in K is an estimator of μ\mu and let

Hj:={∥μ^j−μ∥2≤d~j}.\displaystyle H_{j}:=\left\{\|\hat{\mu}_{j}-\mu\|_{2}\leq\tilde{d}_{j}\right\}.

Set

K(j):=K∩B2​(0,d~j/2),kj:=⌈N​d~j2C2​σ2⌉∧N.\displaystyle K_{(j)}:=K\cap B_{2}(0,\tilde{d}_{j}/2),\qquad k_{j}:=\left\lceil\frac{N\tilde{d}_{j}^{2}}{C^{2}\sigma^{2}}\right\rceil\wedge N.

K(j)=K∩B2​(0,d~j/2).\displaystyle K_{(j)}=K\cap B_{2}(0,\widetilde{d}_{j}/2).

As in the proof of Theorem 2.14,

We first record two elementary consequences of the entropy definition that will be useful below. Let d:=diam⁡(K)d:=\mathrm{diam}(K). d≳N−1/2,and henceη⋆(K)≳N−1/2.d\gtrsim N^{-1/2},\qquad\text{and hence}\qquad\eta^{\star}(K)\gtrsim N^{-1/2}. (D.16)

We also need to justify the rr-part of the stopping rule. Denote by r0r_{0} the original inner radius and by

ralg:=r0∧12​nN\displaystyle r_{\rm alg}:=r_{0}\wedge\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{n}{N}}

the value after the overwrite in Algorithm 5. Then ralg​B2⊆Kr_{\rm alg}B_{2}\subseteq K and

log⁡MKloc​(a0​ralg)≳n≳N​(a0​ralg)2,\displaystyle\log M_{K}^{\operatorname{loc}}(a_{0}r_{\rm alg})\gtrsim n\gtrsim N(a_{0}r_{\rm alg})^{2},

where a0a_{0} is chosen sufficiently small. By the definition of η⋆\eta^{\star},

ralg≲η⋆​(K).r_{\rm alg}\lesssim\eta^{\star}(K). (D.17)

Notice that this argument uses the overwritten radius. We do not claim that the minimax risk is always bounded below by r02r_{0}^{2}; rather, the overwrite ensures precisely that the Euclidean-ball local entropy at scale ralgr_{\rm alg} is large enough for (D.17).

We now make the inductive probability argument explicit. Define the trapping events

Hj:={∥β^j−β∥2≤d~j}.\displaystyle H_{j}:=\left\{\|\widehat{\beta}_{j}-\beta\|_{2}\leq\widetilde{d}_{j}\right\}.

‖β‖2≤R≤d~1=2​R.\displaystyle\|\beta\|_{2}\leq R\leq\widetilde{d}_{1}=2R.

Whenever the two assumptions of Corollary 5.1 hold for K(j)K_{(j)} and

d~j≥(2ralg)∨(CN−1/2),\widetilde{d}_{j}\geq(2r_{\rm alg})\vee(CN^{-1/2}), (D.18)

define the good refinement event

Ej:={‖β~j+1−β−β^j2‖2≤d~jL}.\displaystyle E_{j}:=\left\{\left\|\widetilde{\beta}_{j+1}-\frac{\beta-\widehat{\beta}_{j}}{2}\right\|_{2}\leq\frac{\widetilde{d}_{j}}{L}\right\}.

Lemma 5.2 gives

ℙ⁡(Hj∩Ejc)≤exp⁡(−c1​N​d~j2)+11+N3/2​d~j3\begin{split}\mathbb{P}(H_{j}\cap E_{j}^{c})\leq\exp(-c_{1}N\widetilde{d}_{j}^{2})+\frac{1}{1+N^{3/2}\widetilde{d}_{j}^{3}}\end{split} (D.19)

for an absolute constant c1>0c_{1}>0. We stress that this is an unconditional bound on the intersection Hj∩EjcH_{j}\cap E_{j}^{c}; no independence between iterations is required.

We next verify that, on Hj∩EjH_{j}\cap E_{j}, the same deterministic contraction as in the proof of Theorem 2.14 holds. On HjH_{j},

νj:=β−β^j2∈K∩B2​(0,d~j/2)=K(j).\displaystyle\nu_{j}:=\frac{\beta-\widehat{\beta}_{j}}{2}\in K\cap B_{2}(0,\widetilde{d}_{j}/2)=K_{(j)}.

Indeed, β,−β^j∈K\beta,-\widehat{\beta}_{j}\in K and KK is convex and origin-symmetric. Applying Lemma E.1 to the weak projection of β~j+1\widetilde{\beta}_{j+1} onto K(j)K_{(j)}, with ϵ=d~j/L\epsilon=\widetilde{d}_{j}/L, gives on Hj∩EjH_{j}\cap E_{j}

‖β¯j+1−νj‖2≤‖β~j+1−νj‖2+ϵ2+2​ϵ​‖β~j+1−νj‖2≤(1+3)​d~jL=d~jL~.\displaystyle\begin{split}\|\overline{\beta}_{j+1}-\nu_{j}\|_{2}&\leq\|\widetilde{\beta}_{j+1}-\nu_{j}\|_{2}+\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}+2\epsilon\|\widetilde{\beta}_{j+1}-\nu_{j}\|_{2}}\\ &\leq\frac{(1+\sqrt{3})\widetilde{d}_{j}}{L}=\frac{\widetilde{d}_{j}}{\widetilde{L}}.\end{split}

Consequently,

‖2​β¯j+1+β^j−β‖2≤2​d~jL~.\displaystyle\|2\overline{\beta}_{j+1}+\widehat{\beta}_{j}-\beta\|_{2}\leq\frac{2\widetilde{d}_{j}}{\widetilde{L}}.

A second application of Lemma E.1, now to the weak projection onto KK with ϵ=2​d~j/L~\epsilon=2\widetilde{d}_{j}/\widetilde{L}, yields

‖β^j+1−β‖2≤2​d~jL~+4​d~j2L~2+8​d~j2L~2=2​(3+1)​d~jL~=d~j+1.\displaystyle\begin{split}\|\widehat{\beta}_{j+1}-\beta\|_{2}&\leq\frac{2\widetilde{d}_{j}}{\widetilde{L}}+\sqrt{\frac{4\widetilde{d}_{j}^{2}}{\widetilde{L}^{2}}+\frac{8\widetilde{d}_{j}^{2}}{\widetilde{L}^{2}}}\\ &=\frac{2(\sqrt{3}+1)\widetilde{d}_{j}}{\widetilde{L}}=\widetilde{d}_{j+1}.\end{split}

As in the proof of Theorem 2.14, we also need a deterministic stability statement after the first scale at which the contraction argument can no longer be invoked. Let

aℓ:=‖β^ℓ−β‖2.\displaystyle a_{\ell}:=\|\widehat{\beta}_{\ell}-\beta\|_{2}.

for an absolute constant C6C_{6}. Hence, after the first unsuccessful refinement, or after the first deterministic scale at which the width argument ceases to apply, all later iterates remain within a constant multiple of the last valid scale.

We now identify the deterministic scales at which the induction can stop. First, suppose the first condition of Corollary 5.1 fails for K(j)K_{(j)}. Then

κ(K(j))−1/2d~jT2​(K(j))<2η⋆(K(j)),\displaystyle\kappa(K_{(j)})^{-1/2}\frac{\widetilde{d}_{j}}{T_{2}(K_{(j)})}<2\eta^{\star}(K_{(j)}),

Lj:=⌈logc⁡(κ​(K(j))1/2​T2​(K(j)))⌉.\displaystyle L_{j}:=\left\lceil\log_{c}\!\left(\kappa(K_{(j)})^{1/2}T_{2}(K_{(j)})\right)\right\rceil.

so, using ⌈x⌉≤x+1\lceil x\rceil\leq x+1,

d~j≲C​ΛK​η⋆​(K)≲ΓK​η⋆​(K).\widetilde{d}_{j}\lesssim C\sqrt{\Lambda_{K}}\,\eta^{\star}(K)\lesssim\Gamma_{K}\eta^{\star}(K). (D.23)

We can now accumulate the failure probabilities. Let

t0:=C7​ΓK​η⋆​(K),\displaystyle t_{0}:=C_{7}\Gamma_{K}\eta^{\star}(K),

where C7C_{7} is a sufficiently large absolute constant, depending only on the constant in (D.21). By (D.22)–(D.24), a purely deterministic termination of the contraction argument cannot lead to final error exceeding tt for t≥t0t\geq t_{0}. Hence, if

Because t≥t0≳η⋆(K)≳N−1/2t\geq t_{0}\gtrsim\eta^{\star}(K)\gtrsim N^{-1/2} in the regime under consideration,

∑j:d~j≳texp(−c1Nd~j2)≤∑s=0∞exp⁡(−c2​ρ−2​s​N​t2)≲exp⁡(−c3​N​t2).\displaystyle\begin{split}\sum_{j:\,\widetilde{d}_{j}\gtrsim t}\exp(-c_{1}N\widetilde{d}_{j}^{2})&\leq\sum_{s=0}^{\infty}\exp(-c_{2}\rho^{-2s}Nt^{2})\\ &\lesssim\exp(-c_{3}Nt^{2}).\end{split}

∑j:d~j≳t11+N3/2​d~j3≤1N3/2∑j:d~j≳t1d~j3≲1N3/2​t3.\displaystyle\begin{split}\sum_{j:\,\widetilde{d}_{j}\gtrsim t}\frac{1}{1+N^{3/2}\widetilde{d}_{j}^{3}}&\leq\frac{1}{N^{3/2}}\sum_{j:\,\widetilde{d}_{j}\gtrsim t}\frac{1}{\widetilde{d}_{j}^{3}}\\ &\lesssim\frac{1}{N^{3/2}t^{3}}.\end{split}

Thus, for every t≥t0t\geq t_{0},

ℙ⁡(‖β^−β‖2≥t)≲exp⁡(−c3​N​t2)+C8N3/2​t3.\mathbb{P}\left(\|\widehat{\beta}-\beta\|_{2}\geq t\right)\lesssim\exp(-c_{3}Nt^{2})+\frac{C_{8}}{N^{3/2}t^{3}}. (D.26)

The second term is exactly the accumulated failure probability coming from the randomized QFM oracle.

We finally integrate the tail. Since the estimator is proper, ‖β^−β‖2≤d\|\widehat{\beta}-\beta\|_{2}\leq d, so (D.26) may harmlessly be integrated to infinity. Using

𝔼​‖β^−β‖22=2​∫0∞t​ℙ​(‖β^−β‖2≥t)​𝑑t,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\widehat{\beta}-\beta\|_{2}^{2}=2\int_{0}^{\infty}t\,\mathbb{P}(\|\widehat{\beta}-\beta\|_{2}\geq t)\,dt,

𝔼​‖β^−β‖22≲t02+∫t0∞t​exp⁡(−c3​N​t2)​𝑑t+1N3/2​∫t0∞d​tt2≲ΓK2​η∗2​(K)+1N​exp⁡(−c4​N​t02)+1N3/2​t0.\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathbb{E}\|\widehat{\beta}-\beta\|_{2}^{2}&\lesssim t_{0}^{2}+\int_{t_{0}}^{\infty}t\exp(-c_{3}Nt^{2})\,dt+\frac{1}{N^{3/2}}\int_{t_{0}}^{\infty}\frac{dt}{t^{2}}\\ &\lesssim\Gamma_{K}^{2}\eta^{*2}(K)+\frac{1}{N}\exp(-c_{4}Nt_{0}^{2})+\frac{1}{N^{3/2}t_{0}}.\end{split}
