1N≲η∗2​(K),1N3/2​t0≲1N3/2​η⋆​(K)≲η∗2​(K).\displaystyle\frac{1}{N}\lesssim\eta^{*2}(K),\qquad\frac{1}{N^{3/2}t_{0}}\lesssim\frac{1}{N^{3/2}\eta^{\star}(K)}\lesssim\eta^{*2}(K).

It follows that

𝔼​‖β^−β‖22≲ΓK2​η∗2​(K).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\widehat{\beta}-\beta\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim\Gamma_{K}^{2}\eta^{*2}(K).

Thus the theorem holds with, for example,

Υ⁡(K)≍ΓK2,\displaystyle\Upsilon(K)\asymp\Gamma_{K}^{2},

which depends polynomially, up to logarithmic factors, on T2​(K)T_{2}(K) and maxj∈[M]⁡κ⁡(K(j))\max_{j\in[M]}\kappa(K_{(j)}).

It remains only to note the computational complexity. Since R=O⁡(1)R=O(1) and

ralg=r0∧12​nN,\displaystyle r_{\rm alg}=r_{0}\wedge\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{n}{N}},

the number of iterations is

M=O⁡(log⁡Rralg)=O⁡(log⁡Rr0+log⁡N),\displaystyle M=O\!\left(\log\frac{R}{r_{\rm alg}}\right)=O\!\left(\log\frac{R}{r_{0}}+\log N\right),

up to absolute constants. The weak projections, the SDP/QFM computations, and the approximate convex optimization in Lemma 5.2 are polynomial-time under the assumptions of Section 5. The required oracle failure probability at scale d~j\widetilde{d}_{j} has logarithm O⁡(log⁡(1+N3/2​d~j3))O(\!\log(1+N^{3/2}\widetilde{d}_{j}^{3})), which is polynomially bounded over the active scales. Hence the entire procedure runs in polynomial time. This completes the proof. ∎

Lemma D.1 (High-probability bound for the OLS pilot estimator).

Consider the linear model

Yi=Zi⊤β+ξi,i=1,…,m,\displaystyle Y_{i}=Z_{i}^{\top}\beta+\xi_{i},\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,

where the noise variables ξi\xi_{i} are independent of the design, centered, and sub-Gaussian with parameter γ2\gamma^{2}. Let

G:=∑i=1mZi​Zi⊤,β^OLS:=G−1​∑i=1mZi​Yi.\displaystyle G:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}Z_{i}Z_{i}^{\top},\qquad\widehat{\beta}_{\rm OLS}:=G^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{m}Z_{i}Y_{i}.

Suppose that the event

ℰZ:={λmin(1mG)≥c0}\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{Z}:=\left\{\lambda_{\min}\!\left(\frac{1}{m}G\right)\geq c_{0}\right\}

holds for some absolute constant c0>0c_{0}>0. Then, conditional on the design, for every t≥0t\geq 0,

ℙ(∥β^OLS−β∥2>C(γnm+t)|Z1,…,Zm)≤2exp(−cm​t2γ2)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\!\left(\left.\|\widehat{\beta}_{\rm OLS}-\beta\|_{2}>C\left(\gamma\sqrt{\frac{n}{m}}+t\right)\,\right|\,Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{m}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-c\frac{mt^{2}}{\gamma^{2}}\right)

on ℰZ\mathcal{E}_{Z}, where c,C>0c,C>0 are absolute constants depending only on c0c_{0}.

In particular, if

ℙ⁡(ℰZc)≤δ,\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{Z}^{c})\leq\delta,

then

ℙ⁡(‖β^OLS−β‖2>C⁡(γ​nm+t))≤2​exp⁡(−c​m​t2γ2)+δ.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\!\left(\|\widehat{\beta}_{\rm OLS}-\beta\|_{2}>C\left(\gamma\sqrt{\frac{n}{m}}+t\right)\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-c\frac{mt^{2}}{\gamma^{2}}\right)+\delta.
Proof.

Conditional on the design,

β^OLS−β=G−1​∑i=1mZi​ξi.\displaystyle\widehat{\beta}_{\rm OLS}-\beta=G^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{m}Z_{i}\xi_{i}.

Fix u∈Sn−1u\in S^{n-1}. Then

⟨u,β^OLS−β⟩=∑i=1m⟨G−1​u,Zi⟩​ξi.\displaystyle\left\langle u,\widehat{\beta}_{\rm OLS}-\beta\right\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left\langle G^{-1}u,Z_{i}\right\rangle\xi_{i}.

Since the ξi\xi_{i} are independent centered sub-Gaussian random variables, the right-hand side is conditionally sub-Gaussian with variance proxy

γ2​∑i=1m⟨G−1​u,Zi⟩2=γ2​u⊤​G−1​(∑i=1mZi​Zi⊤)​G−1​u=γ2​u⊤​G−1​u.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \gamma^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left\langle G^{-1}u,Z_{i}\right\rangle^{2}&=\gamma^{2}u^{\top}G^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}Z_{i}Z_{i}^{\top}\right)G^{-1}u\\ &=\gamma^{2}u^{\top}G^{-1}u.\end{aligned}

On ℰZ\mathcal{E}_{Z}, we have G⪰c0​m​InG\succeq c_{0}mI_{n}, and hence

u⊤​G−1​u≤1c0​m.\displaystyle u^{\top}G^{-1}u\leq\frac{1}{c_{0}m}.

Therefore, for every s≥0s\geq 0,

ℙ(|⟨u,β^OLS−β⟩|>s|Z1,…,Zm)≤2exp(−cm​s2γ2).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\!\left(\left.\left|\left\langle u,\widehat{\beta}_{\rm OLS}-\beta\right\rangle\right|>s\,\right|\,Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{m}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-c\frac{ms^{2}}{\gamma^{2}}\right).

Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be a 1/21/2-net of Sn−1S^{n-1} with |𝒩|≤5n|\mathcal{N}|\leq 5^{n}. By the standard net inequality,

‖x‖2≤2​maxu∈𝒩​|⟨u,x⟩|.\displaystyle\|x\|_{2}\leq 2\max_{u\in\mathcal{N}}|\langle u,x\rangle|.

Applying the preceding tail bound to every u∈𝒩u\in\mathcal{N} and taking a union bound yields

ℙ(∥β^OLS−β∥2>C(γnm+t)|Z1,…,Zm)≤2exp(−cm​t2γ2)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\!\left(\left.\|\widehat{\beta}_{\rm OLS}-\beta\|_{2}>C\left(\gamma\sqrt{\frac{n}{m}}+t\right)\,\right|\,Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{m}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-c\frac{mt^{2}}{\gamma^{2}}\right)

on ℰZ\mathcal{E}_{Z}. The unconditional statement follows by adding ℙ⁡(ℰZc)\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{Z}^{c}). ∎

Under the sub-Gaussian random-design assumptions of Section 5, standard concentration for sub-Gaussian sample covariance matrices gives ℙ⁡(ℰZc)≤2​exp⁡(−c​m)\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{Z}^{c})\leq 2\exp(-cm) provided m≳nm\gtrsim n. Thus, for m≍Nm\asymp N,

‖β^OLS−β‖2≲γ​nN+t\displaystyle\|\widehat{\beta}_{\rm OLS}-\beta\|_{2}\lesssim\gamma\sqrt{\frac{n}{N}}+t

with probability at least

1−2​exp⁡(−c​N​t2γ2)−2​exp⁡(−c​N).\displaystyle 1-2\exp\left(-c\frac{Nt^{2}}{\gamma^{2}}\right)-2\exp(-cN).

Appendix E Supplemental Results

Lemma E.1.

Given a convex body with a weak separation oracle, we can weakly project on KK, in the sense that for any z∈ℝnz\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, and ϵ>0\epsilon>0 we can find a rational number ww and a point p∈Kp\in K in polynomial-time, such that

w−ϵ≤‖z−Π¯K​(z)‖2≤‖z−p‖2≤w,\displaystyle w-\epsilon\leq\|z-\overline{\Pi}_{K}(z)\|_{2}\leq\|z-p\|_{2}\leq w,

where Π¯K​(z)\overline{\Pi}_{K}(z) denotes the true Euclidean projection of zz on KK. Moreover, for any point ν∈K\nu\in K we have

‖p−ν‖2≤‖z−ν‖2+ϵ2+2​ϵ​‖z−ν‖.\displaystyle\|p-\nu\|_{2}\leq\|z-\nu\|_{2}+\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}+2\epsilon\|z-\nu\|}.
Corollary E.2.

Hence if ‖z−ν‖≤L\|z-\nu\|\leq L and ϵ≤L\epsilon\leq L we have

‖p−ν‖2≤(3+1)​L\displaystyle\|p-\nu\|_{2}\leq(\sqrt{3}+1)L
Proof.

This is a direct corollary of Theorem 2.5.9 of [8], see also [18] using the fact that the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm is 11-Lipschitz.

For the second part we first observe that

‖ν−ΠK​(z)‖2≤‖z−ν‖2\displaystyle\|\nu-\Pi_{K}(z)\|_{2}\leq\|z-\nu\|_{2}

Next by the properties of the Euclidean projection on convex bodies we have:

‖p−ΠK​(z)‖22+‖z−ΠK​(z)‖22≤‖z−p‖22≤‖z−ΠK​(z)‖22+ϵ2+2​ϵ​‖z−ΠK​(z)‖2\displaystyle\|p-\Pi_{K}(z)\|_{2}^{2}+\|z-\Pi_{K}(z)\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|z-p\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|z-\Pi_{K}(z)\|_{2}^{2}+\epsilon^{2}+2\epsilon\|z-\Pi_{K}(z)\|_{2}

Thus

‖p−ΠK​(z)‖2≤ϵ2+2​ϵ​‖z−ΠK​(z)‖2≤ϵ2+2​ϵ​‖z−ν‖2≤3​L,\displaystyle\|p-\Pi_{K}(z)\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}+2\epsilon\|z-\Pi_{K}(z)\|_{2}}\leq\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}+2\epsilon\|z-\nu\|_{2}}\leq\sqrt{3}L,

where we used the inequlity ‖z−ν‖2∨ϵ≤L\|z-\nu\|_{2}\vee\epsilon\leq L. By the triangle inequality

‖ν−p‖≤‖ν−ΠK​(z)‖2+‖p−ΠK​(z)‖2≤‖z−ν‖2+3​L≤(3+1)​L.\displaystyle\|\nu-p\|\leq\|\nu-\Pi_{K}(z)\|_{2}+\|p-\Pi_{K}(z)\|_{2}\leq\|z-\nu\|_{2}+\sqrt{3}L\leq(\sqrt{3}+1)L.

∎

Proof of Lemma 6.1.

Step 1: Quadratic representation of the norm. Let ∥⋅∥K=ρK(⋅)\|\cdot\|_{K}=\rho_{K}(\cdot). Define

K2:={sign⁡(x)∘x2:x∈K}.\displaystyle K^{2}:=\{\operatorname{sign}(x)\circ x^{2}:x\in K\}.

Since KK is sign-invariant and quadratically convex, K2K^{2} is convex, sign-invariant, and symmetric. By direct inspection,

|x|∈t​K⇔x2∈t2​K2,\displaystyle|x|\in tK\iff x^{2}\in t^{2}K^{2},

and therefore

‖x‖K=‖x2‖K2.\|x\|_{K}=\sqrt{\|x^{2}\|_{K^{2}}}. (E.1)

Step 2: Reduction to Gaussian averages. By [17, Lemma 4.5],

𝔼​‖∑i=1mεi​xi‖K2≤π2​𝔼​‖∑i=1mgi​xi‖K2,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big\|\sum_{i=1}^{m}\varepsilon_{i}x_{i}\Big\|_{K}^{2}\leq\frac{\pi}{2}\,\mathbb{E}\Big\|\sum_{i=1}^{m}g_{i}x_{i}\Big\|_{K}^{2},

where gi∼N⁡(0,1)g_{i}\sim N(0,1) are independent Gaussians.

Step 3: Coordinatewise representation. Let S:=∑i=1mgi​xi∈ℝnS:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}g_{i}x_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Then for each coordinate jj,

Sj=∑i=1mgi​xi​j∼N⁡(0,σj2),σj2=∑ixi​j2.\displaystyle S_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}g_{i}x_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma_{j}^{2}),\quad\sigma_{j}^{2}=\sum_{i}x_{ij}^{2}.

Hence Sj2=σj2​χj2S_{j}^{2}=\sigma_{j}^{2}\chi_{j}^{2}, where χj2∼χ12\chi_{j}^{2}\sim\chi^{2}_{1}, and in vector form

S2=χ2∘(∑ixi2),\displaystyle S^{2}=\chi^{2}\circ\Big(\sum_{i}x_{i}^{2}\Big),

where “∘\circ” denotes coordinatewise multiplication.

Step 4: Monotonicity of sign-invariant norms. For any unconditional norm,

|u|≤|v|⟹‖u‖K2≤‖v‖K2.\displaystyle|u|\leq|v|\implies\|u\|_{K^{2}}\leq\|v\|_{K^{2}}.

Therefore,

‖S2‖K2≤(maxj⁡χj2)​‖∑ixi2‖K2.\displaystyle\|S^{2}\|_{K^{2}}\leq\big(\max_{j}\chi_{j}^{2}\big)\,\Big\|\sum_{i}x_{i}^{2}\Big\|_{K^{2}}.

𝔼​‖S2‖K2≤𝔼​maxj​χj2⋅‖∑ixi2‖K2,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|S^{2}\|_{K^{2}}\leq\mathbb{E}\max_{j}\chi_{j}^{2}\cdot\Big\|\sum_{i}x_{i}^{2}\Big\|_{K^{2}},

𝔼​max1≤j≤n​χj2≲log⁡n.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\max_{1\leq j\leq n}\chi_{j}^{2}\lesssim\log n.

𝔼​‖S2‖K2≲(log⁡n)​‖∑ixi2‖K2.\mathbb{E}\|S^{2}\|_{K^{2}}\lesssim(\log n)\Big\|\sum_{i}x_{i}^{2}\Big\|_{K^{2}}. (E.2)

‖∑ixi2‖K2≤∑i‖xi2‖K2.\displaystyle\Big\|\sum_{i}x_{i}^{2}\Big\|_{K^{2}}\leq\sum_{i}\|x_{i}^{2}\|_{K^{2}}.

Using (E.1) and (E.2),

𝔼​‖S‖K2=𝔼​‖S2‖K2≲(log⁡n)​∑i‖xi‖K2.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|S\|_{K}^{2}=\mathbb{E}\|S^{2}\|_{K^{2}}\lesssim(\log n)\sum_{i}\|x_{i}\|_{K}^{2}.

Lemma E.3.

Let K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be convex, sign-invariant, and quadratically convex. Define

K2:={sign⁡(x)∘x2:x∈K}.\displaystyle K^{2}:=\{\operatorname{sign}(x)\circ x^{2}:x\in K\}.

Then K2K^{2} is convex and sign-invariant.

Proof.

Sign-invariance is immediate. Let

C:={x2:x∈K}⊆ℝ+n.\displaystyle C:=\{x^{2}:x\in K\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}.

By quadratic convexity, CC is convex. Moreover, since KK is convex and sign-invariant, it is coordinatewise solid: if x∈Kx\in K and |y|≤|x||y|\leq|x| coordinatewise, then y∈Ky\in K. Hence CC is downward closed in ℝ+n\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}.

Now let a,b∈K2a,b\in K^{2} and t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]. Since |a|,|b|∈C|a|,|b|\in C,

|t​a+(1−t)​b|≤t​|a|+(1−t)​|b|∈C.\displaystyle|ta+(1-t)b|\leq t|a|+(1-t)|b|\in C.

By downward closedness, |t​a+(1−t)​b|∈C|ta+(1-t)b|\in C. Sign-invariance then implies

t​a+(1−t)​b∈K2.\displaystyle ta+(1-t)b\in K^{2}.

Thus K2K^{2} is convex. ∎

Appendix F A Counterexample for the Posterior Mean under the Uniform Prior

Consider the Gaussian sequence model

Y=μ+Z,Z∼N⁡(0,In),\displaystyle Y=\mu+Z,\qquad Z\sim N(0,I_{n}),

with parameter constrained to the ellipsoid

Kn:={μ=(u,t)∈ℝn−1×ℝ:‖u‖22+t2n≤1}.\displaystyle K_{n}:=\left\{\mu=(u,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times\mathbb{R}:\|u\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{t^{2}}{\sqrt{n}}\leq 1\right\}.

Write

Ln:=n1/4,\displaystyle L_{n}:=n^{1/4},

so that equivalently

Kn={(u,t):‖u‖22+t2Ln2≤1}.\displaystyle K_{n}=\left\{(u,t):\|u\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{t^{2}}{L_{n}^{2}}\leq 1\right\}.

Let Πn=Unif⁡(Kn)\Pi_{n}=\operatorname{Unif}(K_{n}), and let

μ^unif​(Y):=𝔼​Πn​[μ∣Y]\displaystyle\widehat{\mu}^{\,\mathrm{unif}}(Y):=\mathbb{E}{\Pi_{n}}[\mu\mid Y]

denote the corresponding posterior mean. We note that the set KnK_{n} is a type-2 body with constant T2​(Kn)=1T_{2}(K_{n})=1, which implies our algorithm works optimally on KnK_{n}.

Proposition F.1 (The uniform-prior posterior mean can be polynomially suboptimal).

There exist universal constants c>0c>0 and n0<∞n_{0}<\infty such that, for every n≥n0n\geq n_{0},

supμ∈Kn𝔼​μ​‖μ^unif​(Y)−μ‖22≥c​n.\displaystyle\sup_{\mu\in K_{n}}\mathbb{E}\mu\bigl\|\widehat{\mu}^{\,\mathrm{unif}}(Y)-\mu\bigr\|_{2}^{2}\geq c\sqrt{n}.

On the other hand,

infμ^supμ∈Kn𝔼​μ​‖μ^​(Y)−μ‖22≤2.\displaystyle\inf_{\widehat{\mu}}\sup_{\mu\in K_{n}}\mathbb{E}\mu\|\widehat{\mu}(Y)-\mu\|_{2}^{2}\leq 2.

Consequently the posterior mean under the uniform prior is not minimax, and its worst-case risk can exceed the minimax risk by a factor of order n\sqrt{n}.

More concretely, one may take c=1/32c=1/32 for all sufficiently large nn.

μ⋆:=Ln​en.\displaystyle\mu^{\star}:=L_{n}e_{n}.

exp⁡(−12​‖Y−μ‖22)=exp⁡(⟨Y,μ⟩−12​‖μ‖22).\displaystyle\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\|Y-\mu\|_{2}^{2}\right)=\exp\left(\langle Y,\mu\rangle-\frac{1}{2}\|\mu\|_{2}^{2}\right).

qy​(μ):=⟨y,μ⟩−12​‖μ‖22.\displaystyle q_{y}(\mu):=\langle y,\mu\rangle-\frac{1}{2}\|\mu\|_{2}^{2}.

Remark F.2 (Geometric reason for the failure).

The last semiaxis of KnK_{n} has length Ln=n1/4L_{n}=n^{1/4}, but under the uniform measure on KnK_{n} the marginal density of the last coordinate tt is proportional to

(1−t2Ln2)(n−1)/2,|t|≤Ln.\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{t^{2}}{L_{n}^{2}}\right)^{(n-1)/2},\qquad|t|\leq L_{n}.

Thus the uniform prior places exponentially little mass near the two tips ±Ln​en\pm L_{n}e_{n}. At the same time, these tips are statistically easy to estimate by retaining the last observation YnY_{n}. The posterior associated with the uniform prior therefore overweights the enormous central volume of the ellipsoid and shrinks strongly away from the extremal points. This volume effect is precisely what makes the uniform-prior posterior mean non-minimax.

Appendix G Construction and conditional computational lower bound

We describe a centrally symmetric convex body whose gauge is computable by a polynomial-size semidefinite program, but for which minimax-rate estimation in the Gaussian sequence model would imply recovery in the planted-submatrix model in the computationally hard regime identified by Schramm and Wein [28]. The resulting computational lower bound is conditional on the usual low-degree heuristic/conjecture: Schramm and Wein prove a rigorous low-degree lower bound, rather than an unconditional lower bound against all polynomial-time algorithms.

Fix a sparsity parameter ρ=ρn∈(0,1/2)\rho=\rho_{n}\in(0,1/2) and write

k=ρ​n.\displaystyle k=\rho n.

For simplicity we ignore integer-rounding issues. Let δn↓0\delta_{n}\downarrow 0 satisfy

δn2​k⟶∞,\displaystyle\delta_{n}^{2}k\longrightarrow\infty,

for example δn=k−1/4\delta_{n}=k^{-1/4}, and define

k−=(1−δn)​k,k+=(1+δn)​k.\displaystyle k_{-}=(1-\delta_{n})k,\qquad k_{+}=(1+\delta_{n})k.

Define the convex cone

𝒞n,k={X∈𝕊n:X⪰0,Xi​j≥0,Xi​j≤Xi​i,Xi​j≤Xj​jfor all i,j,k−​Xi​i≤∑j=1nXi​j≤k+​Xi​ifor every ​i}.\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{n,k}=\left\{X\in\mathbb{S}^{n}:\begin{array}[]{l}X\succeq 0,\qquad X_{ij}\geq 0,\\[2.84526pt] X_{ij}\leq X_{ii},\qquad X_{ij}\leq X_{jj}\quad\text{for all }i,j,\\[2.84526pt] k_{-}X_{ii}\leq\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_{ij}\leq k_{+}X_{ii}\quad\text{for every }i\end{array}\right\}.

Let

Kn,k+={X∈𝒞n,k:tr⁡(X)≤1},\displaystyle K_{n,k}^{+}=\left\{X\in\mathcal{C}_{n,k}:\operatorname{tr}(X)\leq 1\right\},

and take the centrally symmetric convex body

Kn,k=conv⁡(Kn,k+∪(−Kn,k+)).K_{n,k}=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(K_{n,k}^{+}\cup(-K_{n,k}^{+})\bigr). (G.1)

G.1 The gauge is efficiently computable

Lemma G.1 (SDP representation of the gauge).

For every X∈𝕊nX\in\mathbb{S}^{n},

‖X‖Kn,k=infX=X+−X−X+,X−∈𝒞n,k{tr⁡(X+)+tr⁡(X−)}.\|X\|_{K_{n,k}}=\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}X=X_{+}-X_{-}\\ X_{+},X_{-}\in\mathcal{C}_{n,k}\end{subarray}}\left\{\operatorname{tr}(X_{+})+\operatorname{tr}(X_{-})\right\}. (G.2)

In particular, the gauge of Kn,kK_{n,k} is computable by a polynomial-size semidefinite program.

Proof.

Since 𝒞n,k\mathcal{C}_{n,k} is a convex cone, the absolute convexification in (G.1) can equivalently be written as

Kn,k={X+−X−:X±∈𝒞n,k,tr(X+)+tr(X−)≤1}.\displaystyle K_{n,k}=\left\{X_{+}-X_{-}:X_{\pm}\in\mathcal{C}_{n,k},\;\operatorname{tr}(X_{+})+\operatorname{tr}(X_{-})\leq 1\right\}.

Indeed, if X=t​X+−(1−t)​X−X=tX_{+}-(1-t)X_{-} with X±∈Kn,k+X_{\pm}\in K_{n,k}^{+} and t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], then t​X+,(1−t)​X−∈𝒞n,ktX_{+},(1-t)X_{-}\in\mathcal{C}_{n,k} and the sum of their traces is at most one. The converse follows by normalizing the two summands by their total trace, i.e. take X∈{X+−X−:X±∈𝒞n,k,tr(X+)+tr(X−)≤1}X\in\left\{X_{+}-X_{-}:X_{\pm}\in\mathcal{C}_{n,k},\;\operatorname{tr}(X_{+})+\operatorname{tr}(X_{-})\leq 1\right\} and observe that

X=s⁡(tr⁡(X+)s​X+tr⁡(X+)−tr⁡(X−)s​X−tr⁡(X−)).\displaystyle X=s\bigg(\frac{\operatorname{tr}(X_{+})}{s}\frac{X_{+}}{\operatorname{tr}(X_{+})}-\frac{\operatorname{tr}(X_{-})}{s}\frac{X_{-}}{\operatorname{tr}(X_{-})}\bigg).

where s:=tr⁡(X+)+tr⁡(X−)≤1s:=\operatorname{tr}(X_{+})+\operatorname{tr}(X_{-})\leq 1. Since s≤1s\leq 1 it follows X∈Kn,kX\in K_{n,k}. Taking the Minkowski functional gives (G.2). All constraints defining 𝒞n,k\mathcal{C}_{n,k} are linear matrix inequalities or linear inequalities, so (G.2) is an SDP of polynomial size. ∎

G.2 Embedding the Schramm–Wein planted submatrix

Schramm and Wein consider the planted-submatrix model

Y=λ​v​v⊤+W,vi∼iidBernoulli⁡(ρ),Y=\lambda vv^{\top}+W,\qquad v_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\rho), (G.3)

with Gaussian noise WW; see [28]. Their theorem is stated in the parameterization

ρ=n−b,λ=n−a,\displaystyle\rho=n^{-b},\qquad\lambda=n^{-a},

with a>0a>0 and 0<b<1/20<b<1/2.

Let

m=‖v‖0.\displaystyle m=\|v\|_{0}.

By the Chernoff bound and the assumption δn2​k→∞\delta_{n}^{2}k\to\infty,

ℙ{k−≤m≤k+}=1−o(1).\mathbb{P}\{k_{-}\leq m\leq k_{+}\}=1-o(1). (G.4)

On the event in (G.4), set

Av=v​v⊤k+.\displaystyle A_{v}=\frac{vv^{\top}}{k_{+}}.

Then

tr⁡(Av)=mk+≤1.\displaystyle\operatorname{tr}(A_{v})=\frac{m}{k_{+}}\leq 1.

Moreover, if vi=1v_{i}=1, then

∑j(Av)i​j(Av)i​i=m∈[k−,k+],\displaystyle\frac{\sum_{j}(A_{v})_{ij}}{(A_{v})_{ii}}=m\in[k_{-},k_{+}],

while if vi=0v_{i}=0, the entire iith row and column are zero. Also Av⪰0A_{v}\succeq 0, Av≥0A_{v}\geq 0 entrywise, and

(Av)i​j≤(Av)i​i,(Av)i​j≤(Av)j​j.\displaystyle(A_{v})_{ij}\leq(A_{v})_{ii},\qquad(A_{v})_{ij}\leq(A_{v})_{jj}.

Thus

Av∈Kn,k+⊂Kn,kwith probability ​1−o⁡(1).A_{v}\in K_{n,k}^{+}\subset K_{n,k}\qquad\text{with probability }1-o(1). (G.5)

Consequently, if

θ=λ​k+,\theta=\lambda k_{+}, (G.6)

then

λ​v​v⊤=θ​Av∈θ​Kn,kwith probability ​1−o⁡(1).\lambda vv^{\top}=\theta A_{v}\in\theta K_{n,k}\qquad\text{with probability }1-o(1). (G.7)

The Gaussian matrix observation can be identified with an ordinary Gaussian sequence model on the upper-triangular coordinates. Any difference between the standard normalization used for a symmetric Gaussian matrix and iid N⁡(0,1)N(0,1) sequence noise amounts only to a fixed linear rescaling of the diagonal coordinates and therefore changes all Euclidean/Frobenius quantities by universal constants.

G.3 Metric entropy of the convex body

The particular linear inequalities in the definition of 𝒞n,k\mathcal{C}_{n,k} ensure that the relaxation remains statistically small.

Lemma G.2 (Large-scale entropy bound).

There exists a universal constant CC such that, for 0<ε<1/20<\varepsilon<1/2,

log⁡N⁡(Kn,k,ε​BF)≤C⁡[kε2​log⁡e​nk+kε4​log⁡Cε],\log N\!\left(K_{n,k},\varepsilon B_{F}\right)\leq C\left[\frac{k}{\varepsilon^{2}}\log\frac{en}{k}+\frac{k}{\varepsilon^{4}}\log\frac{C}{\varepsilon}\right], (G.8)

where BFB_{F} is the unit ball for the Frobenius norm.

Proof.

We first consider X∈Kn,k+X\in K_{n,k}^{+}. Put di=Xi​id_{i}=X_{ii}. Since 0≤Xi​j≤Xi​i=di0\leq X_{ij}\leq X_{ii}=d_{i} and ∑jXi​j≤k+​di\sum_{j}X_{ij}\leq k_{+}d_{i},

∑j=1nXi​j2≤di​∑j=1nXi​j≤k+​di2.\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_{ij}^{2}\leq d_{i}\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_{ij}\leq k_{+}d_{i}^{2}. (G.9)

Order the diagonal entries so that d1≥d2≥⋯≥0d_{1}\geq d_{2}\geq\cdots\geq 0. Because ∑idi=tr⁡(X)≤1\sum_{i}d_{i}=\operatorname{tr}(X)\leq 1, we have ds+1≤1/sd_{s+1}\leq 1/s and hence

∑i>sdi2≤ds+1​∑i>sdi≤1s.\displaystyle\sum_{i>s}d_{i}^{2}\leq d_{s+1}\sum_{i>s}d_{i}\leq\frac{1}{s}.

If TT is the set of the ss largest diagonal coordinates, then

‖X−XT​T‖F2\displaystyle\|X-X_{TT}\|_{F}^{2} ≤2​∑i∉T∑j=1nXi​j2\displaystyle\leq 2\sum_{i\notin T}\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_{ij}^{2}
≤2​k+​∑i∉Tdi2≤2​k+s.\displaystyle\leq 2k_{+}\sum_{i\notin T}d_{i}^{2}\leq\frac{2k_{+}}{s}. (G.10)

Thus, choosing

s≍k​ε−2\displaystyle s\asymp k\varepsilon^{-2}

makes XX O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon)-close to a matrix supported on an s×ss\times s principal block.

Next, XT​T⪰0X_{TT}\succeq 0 and tr⁡(XT​T)≤1\operatorname{tr}(X_{TT})\leq 1. If λ1≥λ2≥⋯≥0\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\cdots\geq 0 are its eigenvalues, then ∑jλj≤1\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}\leq 1, and therefore

∑j>rλj2≤λr+1​∑j>rλj≤1r.\displaystyle\sum_{j>r}\lambda_{j}^{2}\leq\lambda_{r+1}\sum_{j>r}\lambda_{j}\leq\frac{1}{r}.

Hence the best rank-rr approximation has Frobenius error at most r−1/2r^{-1/2}. Taking r≍ε−2r\asymp\varepsilon^{-2} reduces the covering problem to rank-O⁡(ε−2)O(\varepsilon^{-2}) positive semidefinite matrices on O⁡(k​ε−2)O(k\varepsilon^{-2}) coordinates.

There are at most

(ns)≤(e​ns)s\displaystyle\binom{n}{s}\leq\left(\frac{en}{s}\right)^{s}

choices of TT. For each fixed TT, a standard covering bound for rank-rr matrices [see Lemma 3.1 4, together with a trivial discretization of the Frobenius norm] in the Frobenius unit ball gives logarithmic covering number at most

C​s​r​log⁡Cε.\displaystyle Csr\log\frac{C}{\varepsilon}.

Substituting s≍k​ε−2s\asymp k\varepsilon^{-2} and r≍ε−2r\asymp\varepsilon^{-2} yields

log⁡N⁡(Kn,k+,ε​BF)≲kε2​log⁡e​nk+kε4​log⁡Cε,\displaystyle\log N(K_{n,k}^{+},\varepsilon B_{F})\lesssim\frac{k}{\varepsilon^{2}}\log\frac{en}{k}+\frac{k}{\varepsilon^{4}}\log\frac{C}{\varepsilon},

after harmless changes of constants.

Finally, every X∈Kn,kX\in K_{n,k} can be written as X=X+−X−X=X_{+}-X_{-} with X±∈Kn,k+X_{\pm}\in K_{n,k}^{+}. Covering the two summands separately only squares the covering number and changes constants. This proves (G.8). ∎

G.4 The statistical minimax rate is much smaller than the planted signal

Consider the Gaussian sequence model

Z=μ+ξ,ξ∼N⁡(0,σ2​I),μ∈θ​Kn,k.Z=\mu+\xi,\qquad\xi\sim N(0,\sigma^{2}I),\qquad\mu\in\theta K_{n,k}. (G.11)

Let

R∗​(θ​Kn,k)=infμ^supμ∈θ​Kn,k𝔼μ​‖μ^−μ‖F2\displaystyle R^{*}(\theta K_{n,k})=\inf_{\widehat{\mu}}\sup_{\mu\in\theta K_{n,k}}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\|\widehat{\mu}-\mu\|_{F}^{2}

denote the minimax squared-error risk, up to the harmless fixed linear identification between symmetric matrices and Gaussian sequence coordinates.

A minimum-distance estimator on an ε​θ\varepsilon\theta-net gives

R∗​(θ​Kn,k)≲θ2​ε2+σ2​log⁡N⁡(Kn,k,ε​BF).R^{*}(\theta K_{n,k})\lesssim\theta^{2}\varepsilon^{2}+\sigma^{2}\log N(K_{n,k},\varepsilon B_{F}). (G.12)

This is a folklore result that can be traced back to [33]; for completeness, we provide a short proof.

Lemma G.3 (Risk bound for a minimum-distance estimator on a net).

Let T⊆ℝdT\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} and suppose that

Y=μ+σ​Z,Z∼N⁡(0,Id),\displaystyle Y=\mu+\sigma Z,\qquad Z\sim N(0,I_{d}),

where μ∈T\mu\in T. Let 𝒩δ⊆T\mathcal{N}_{\delta}\subseteq T be a finite δ\delta-net of TT in Euclidean norm, and define

μ^∈arg⁡minν∈𝒩δ⁡‖Y−ν‖2.\displaystyle\widehat{\mu}\in\arg\min_{\nu\in\mathcal{N}_{\delta}}\|Y-\nu\|_{2}.

Then there exists a universal constant C>0C>0 such that

supμ∈T𝔼μ​‖μ^−μ‖22≤C⁡(δ2+σ2​log⁡|𝒩δ|).\displaystyle\sup_{\mu\in T}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\|\widehat{\mu}-\mu\|_{2}^{2}\leq C\left(\delta^{2}+\sigma^{2}\log|\mathcal{N}_{\delta}|\right).

Consequently,

R∗​(T)≲δ2+σ2​log⁡N⁡(T,δ​B2).\displaystyle R^{*}(T)\lesssim\delta^{2}+\sigma^{2}\log N(T,\delta B_{2}).

In particular, for T=θ​Kn,kT=\theta K_{n,k} and δ=θ​ε\delta=\theta\varepsilon,

R∗​(θ​Kn,k)≲θ2​ε2+σ2​log⁡N⁡(Kn,k,ε​BF).\displaystyle R^{*}(\theta K_{n,k})\lesssim\theta^{2}\varepsilon^{2}+\sigma^{2}\log N(K_{n,k},\varepsilon B_{F}).
Proof.

Fix μ∈T\mu\in T, and choose ν0∈𝒩δ\nu_{0}\in\mathcal{N}_{\delta} such that

‖μ−ν0‖2≤δ.\displaystyle\|\mu-\nu_{0}\|_{2}\leq\delta.

By the definition of μ^\widehat{\mu},

‖Y−μ^‖22≤‖Y−ν0‖22.\displaystyle\|Y-\widehat{\mu}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|Y-\nu_{0}\|_{2}^{2}.

Substituting Y=μ+σ​ZY=\mu+\sigma Z and expanding gives

‖μ^−ν0‖22≤2​⟨μ−ν0,μ^−ν0⟩+2​σ​⟨Z,μ^−ν0⟩.\displaystyle\|\widehat{\mu}-\nu_{0}\|_{2}^{2}\leq 2\langle\mu-\nu_{0},\widehat{\mu}-\nu_{0}\rangle+2\sigma\langle Z,\widehat{\mu}-\nu_{0}\rangle.

Define

M:=maxν∈𝒩δν≠ν0⁡⟨Z,ν−ν0⟩‖ν−ν0‖2,\displaystyle M:=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\nu\in\mathcal{N}_{\delta}\\ \nu\neq\nu_{0}\end{subarray}}\frac{\langle Z,\nu-\nu_{0}\rangle}{\|\nu-\nu_{0}\|_{2}},

with the convention M=0M=0 if 𝒩δ={ν0}\mathcal{N}_{\delta}=\{\nu_{0}\}. Since μ^∈𝒩δ\widehat{\mu}\in\mathcal{N}_{\delta}, Cauchy–Schwarz and the definition of MM imply

‖μ^−ν0‖22≤2​δ​‖μ^−ν0‖2+2​σ​M​‖μ^−ν0‖2.\displaystyle\|\widehat{\mu}-\nu_{0}\|_{2}^{2}\leq 2\delta\|\widehat{\mu}-\nu_{0}\|_{2}+2\sigma M\|\widehat{\mu}-\nu_{0}\|_{2}.

Therefore, either μ^=ν0\widehat{\mu}=\nu_{0}, or, after dividing by ‖μ^−ν0‖2\|\widehat{\mu}-\nu_{0}\|_{2},

‖μ^−ν0‖2≤2​δ+2​σ​M.\displaystyle\|\widehat{\mu}-\nu_{0}\|_{2}\leq 2\delta+2\sigma M.

Hence

‖μ^−ν0‖22≲δ2+σ2​M+2,\displaystyle\|\widehat{\mu}-\nu_{0}\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim\delta^{2}+\sigma^{2}M_{+}^{2},

where M+=max⁡{M,0}M_{+}=\max\{M,0\}.

For every fixed ν≠ν0\nu\neq\nu_{0},

⟨Z,ν−ν0⟩‖ν−ν0‖2∼N⁡(0,1).\displaystyle\frac{\langle Z,\nu-\nu_{0}\rangle}{\|\nu-\nu_{0}\|_{2}}\sim N(0,1).

Thus, by the standard Gaussian maximal inequality,

𝔼​M+2≲log⁡|𝒩δ|\displaystyle\mathbb{E}M_{+}^{2}\lesssim\log|\mathcal{N}_{\delta}|

whenever |𝒩δ|≥2|\mathcal{N}_{\delta}|\geq 2; the case |𝒩δ|=1|\mathcal{N}_{\delta}|=1 is immediate. Consequently,

𝔼μ​‖μ^−ν0‖22≲δ2+σ2​log⁡|𝒩δ|.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\|\widehat{\mu}-\nu_{0}\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim\delta^{2}+\sigma^{2}\log|\mathcal{N}_{\delta}|.

Finally,

‖μ^−μ‖22≤2​‖μ^−ν0‖22+2​‖ν0−μ‖22,\displaystyle\|\widehat{\mu}-\mu\|_{2}^{2}\leq 2\|\widehat{\mu}-\nu_{0}\|_{2}^{2}+2\|\nu_{0}-\mu\|_{2}^{2},

and therefore

supμ∈T𝔼μ​‖μ^−μ‖22≲δ2+σ2​log⁡|𝒩δ|.\displaystyle\sup_{\mu\in T}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\|\widehat{\mu}-\mu\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim\delta^{2}+\sigma^{2}\log|\mathcal{N}_{\delta}|.

Taking 𝒩δ\mathcal{N}_{\delta} to be a minimal δ\delta-net proves the entropy bound. Applying it with T=θ​Kn,kT=\theta K_{n,k} and δ=θ​ε\delta=\theta\varepsilon, and using

N⁡(θ​Kn,k,θ​ε​BF)=N⁡(Kn,k,ε​BF),\displaystyle N(\theta K_{n,k},\theta\varepsilon B_{F})=N(K_{n,k},\varepsilon B_{F}),

gives the claimed specialization. ∎

Combining (G.12) with (G.8), and choosing ε=εn↓0\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{n}\downarrow 0 sufficiently slowly, yields

R∗​(θ​Kn,k)=o⁡(θ2)wheneverθ2σ2​k​log⁡(e​n/k)⟶∞.R^{*}(\theta K_{n,k})=o(\theta^{2})\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad\frac{\theta^{2}}{\sigma^{2}k\log(en/k)}\longrightarrow\infty. (G.13)

For the planted signal in (G.7), θ≍λ​k\theta\asymp\lambda k, so the condition becomes

λ2​k≫σ2​log⁡e​nk.\lambda^{2}k\gg\sigma^{2}\log\frac{en}{k}. (G.14)

G.5 The Schramm–Wein computational regime

Schramm and Wein [28, Theorem 1.2] consider the planted submatrix model in the parametrization

ρ=n−b,λ=n−a,0<b<12.\displaystyle\rho=n^{-b},\qquad\lambda=n^{-a},\qquad 0<b<\frac{1}{2}.

Their lower bound is already an estimation lower bound. More precisely, letting 𝖬𝖬𝖲𝖤≤D\mathsf{MMSE}_{\leq D} denote the minimum mean-squared error among degree-DD polynomial estimators of a planted coordinate v1v_{1}, they prove that if

a>12−b,a>\frac{1}{2}-b, (G.15)

then, for some ϵ=ϵ⁡(a,b)>0\epsilon=\epsilon(a,b)>0,

𝖬𝖬𝖲𝖤≤nϵ=ρ−(1+o⁡(1))​ρ2.\mathsf{MMSE}_{\leq n^{\epsilon}}=\rho-(1+o(1))\rho^{2}. (G.16)

Thus no polynomial of degree nϵn^{\epsilon} can achieve mean-squared error o⁡(ρ)o(\rho) for estimating a planted coordinate; in particular, it cannot estimate the full planted vector vv with total squared error o⁡(ρ​n)=o⁡(k)o(\rho n)=o(k). Conversely, if a<1/2−ba<1/2-b, Schramm and Wein show that a constant-degree polynomial achieves mean-squared error o⁡(ρ)o(\rho). Hence a=1/2−ba=1/2-b is the sharp low-degree estimation threshold in their model.

On the other hand, our statistical condition (G.14) with σ≍1\sigma\asymp 1 reads

n−2​a​n1−b≫log⁡n,\displaystyle n^{-2a}n^{1-b}\gg\log n,

which holds whenever

a<1−b2=12−b2.a<\frac{1-b}{2}=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{b}{2}. (G.17)

Therefore the interval

12−b<a<12−b2\frac{1}{2}-b<a<\frac{1}{2}-\frac{b}{2} (G.18)

is nonempty for every 0<b<1/20<b<1/2. Throughout this interval, the full convex body θ​Kn,k\theta K_{n,k} is statistically estimable to vanishing relative error, while the embedded planted-submatrix instances lie in the Schramm–Wein low-degree hard regime for estimation.

For example, take

b=13,a=14.\displaystyle b=\frac{1}{3},\qquad a=\frac{1}{4}.

Then

ρ=n−1/3,k=n2/3,λ=n−1/4.\displaystyle\rho=n^{-1/3},\qquad k=n^{2/3},\qquad\lambda=n^{-1/4}.

We have

λ2​k=n1/6≫log⁡n,\displaystyle\lambda^{2}k=n^{1/6}\gg\log n,

so (G.13) holds, while

14>16=12−b,\displaystyle\frac{1}{4}>\frac{1}{6}=\frac{1}{2}-b,

placing the planted instance strictly in the Schramm–Wein low-degree hard regime.

G.6 Reduction from minimax-rate estimation to planted-submatrix estimation

Proposition G.4 (Conditional computational-statistical separation).

Fix constants a,ba,b satisfying (G.18), and let

ρ=n−b,k=ρ​n,λ=n−a,θ=λ​k+.\displaystyle\rho=n^{-b},\qquad k=\rho n,\qquad\lambda=n^{-a},\qquad\theta=\lambda k_{+}.

Let LnL_{n} be any polylogarithmic sequence, i.e.,

Ln≤(log⁡n)A\displaystyle L_{n}\leq(\log n)^{A}

for some fixed A<∞A<\infty. Suppose there exists a polynomial-time estimator μ^\widehat{\mu} for the Gaussian sequence model over θ​Kn,k\theta K_{n,k} satisfying

supμ∈θ​Kn,k𝔼μ​‖μ^−μ‖F2≤Ln​R∗​(θ​Kn,k).\sup_{\mu\in\theta K_{n,k}}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\|\widehat{\mu}-\mu\|_{F}^{2}\leq L_{n}R^{*}(\theta K_{n,k}). (G.19)

Then, from μ^\widehat{\mu}, one can construct in polynomial time an estimator v~=v~​(Y)∈[0,1]n\widetilde{v}=\widetilde{v}(Y)\in[0,1]^{n} of the planted vector in the Schramm–Wein model such that

𝔼​‖v~−v‖22=o⁡(k)=o⁡(ρ​n).\mathbb{E}\|\widetilde{v}-v\|_{2}^{2}=o(k)=o(\rho n). (G.20)

Consequently, after a permutation symmetrization, one obtains a polynomial-time estimator of a planted coordinate with mean-squared error o⁡(ρ)o(\rho).

Therefore, under the standard low-degree conjecture for planted-submatrix estimation—namely, that the degree-nΩ⁡(1)n^{\Omega(1)} estimation barrier of [28, Theorem 1.2] reflects a corresponding barrier for polynomial-time algorithms—there is no polynomial-time estimator satisfying (G.19) for any polylogarithmic approximation factor Ln=(log⁡n)O⁡(1)L_{n}=(\log n)^{O(1)}.

Proof.

We first strengthen the statistical estimate (G.13). Define

Δ:=1−b−2​a.\displaystyle\Delta:=1-b-2a.

Since a<1/2−b/2a<1/2-b/2 by (G.18), we have Δ>0\Delta>0. Moreover,

λ2​k=n−2​a​n1−b=nΔ.\displaystyle\lambda^{2}k=n^{-2a}n^{1-b}=n^{\Delta}.

Recall from (G.12) and (G.8) that, for every 0<ε<1/20<\varepsilon<1/2,

R∗​(θ​Kn,k)\displaystyle R^{*}(\theta K_{n,k}) ≲θ2​ε2+σ2​k​[ε−2​log⁡e​nk+ε−4​log⁡Cε].\displaystyle\lesssim\theta^{2}\varepsilon^{2}+\sigma^{2}k\left[\varepsilon^{-2}\log\frac{en}{k}+\varepsilon^{-4}\log\frac{C}{\varepsilon}\right]. (G.21)

For the planted-submatrix model under consideration, σ≍1\sigma\asymp 1, and θ=λ​k+≍λ​k\theta=\lambda k_{+}\asymp\lambda k. Hence

R∗​(θ​Kn,k)θ2≲ε2+1λ2​k​[ε−2​log⁡e​nk+ε−4​log⁡Cε].\displaystyle\frac{R^{*}(\theta K_{n,k})}{\theta^{2}}\lesssim\varepsilon^{2}+\frac{1}{\lambda^{2}k}\left[\varepsilon^{-2}\log\frac{en}{k}+\varepsilon^{-4}\log\frac{C}{\varepsilon}\right]. (G.22)

Choose

ε:=n−Δ/8.\displaystyle\varepsilon:=n^{-\Delta/8}.

For all sufficiently large nn, ε∈(0,1/2)\varepsilon\in(0,1/2). Since

log⁡e​nk=O⁡(log⁡n),log⁡Cε=O⁡(log⁡n),\displaystyle\log\frac{en}{k}=O(\log n),\qquad\log\frac{C}{\varepsilon}=O(\log n),

and λ2​k=nΔ\lambda^{2}k=n^{\Delta}, (G.22) yields

R∗​(θ​Kn,k)θ2\displaystyle\frac{R^{*}(\theta K_{n,k})}{\theta^{2}} ≲n−Δ/4+n−3Δ/4logn+n−Δ/2logn\displaystyle\lesssim n^{-\Delta/4}+n^{-3\Delta/4}\log n+n^{-\Delta/2}\log n
≲n−Δ/4.\displaystyle\lesssim n^{-\Delta/4}. (G.23)

Thus

R∗(θKn,k)≲θ2n−Δ/4.R^{*}(\theta K_{n,k})\lesssim\theta^{2}n^{-\Delta/4}. (G.24)

This polynomial slack absorbs every fixed polylogarithmic approximation factor. Indeed, if Ln≤(log⁡n)AL_{n}\leq(\log n)^{A} for some fixed A<∞A<\infty, then

Lnn−Δ/4⟶0.\displaystyle L_{n}n^{-\Delta/4}\longrightarrow 0.

Consequently, (G.19) and (G.24) imply

supμ∈θ​Kn,k𝔼μ​‖μ^−μ‖F2=o⁡(θ2).\sup_{\mu\in\theta K_{n,k}}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\|\widehat{\mu}-\mu\|_{F}^{2}=o(\theta^{2}). (G.25)

Now let

𝒢:={k−≤m≤k+},m=∥v∥0.\displaystyle\mathcal{G}:=\{k_{-}\leq m\leq k_{+}\},\qquad m=\|v\|_{0}.

By (G.4), ℙ⁡(𝒢)=1−o⁡(1)\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G})=1-o(1). On 𝒢\mathcal{G}, the embedding (G.7) gives

μ=λ​v​v⊤∈θ​Kn,k.\displaystyle\mu=\lambda vv^{\top}\in\theta K_{n,k}.

Therefore, uniformly over planted vectors satisfying 𝒢\mathcal{G},

𝔼W​‖μ^−λ​v​v⊤‖F2=o⁡(θ2)=o⁡(λ2​k2).\mathbb{E}_{W}\bigl\|\widehat{\mu}-\lambda vv^{\top}\bigr\|_{F}^{2}=o(\theta^{2})=o(\lambda^{2}k^{2}). (G.26)

Here the expectation is over the Gaussian noise conditional on vv.

Since the target matrix is symmetric, we may replace μ^\widehat{\mu} by its symmetrization

M^:=μ^+μ^⊤2,\displaystyle\widehat{M}:=\frac{\widehat{\mu}+\widehat{\mu}^{\top}}{2},

which is still computable in polynomial time and satisfies

‖M^−λ​v​v⊤‖F≤‖μ^−λ​v​v⊤‖F.\displaystyle\|\widehat{M}-\lambda vv^{\top}\|_{F}\leq\|\widehat{\mu}-\lambda vv^{\top}\|_{F}.

Let u^\widehat{u} be a leading unit eigenvector of M^\widehat{M}, and write

u:=vm.\displaystyle u:=\frac{v}{\sqrt{m}}.

The matrix λ​v​v⊤\lambda vv^{\top} has a single nonzero eigenvalue λ​m\lambda m. Combining Davis–Kahan with the trivial bound on the sine of the angle gives, for an absolute constant C0C_{0},

1−|⟨u^,u⟩|2≤C0​‖M^−λ​v​v⊤‖F2λ2​m2.1-|\langle\widehat{u},u\rangle|^{2}\leq C_{0}\frac{\|\widehat{M}-\lambda vv^{\top}\|_{F}^{2}}{\lambda^{2}m^{2}}. (G.27)

Since m≍km\asymp k on 𝒢\mathcal{G}, taking conditional expectations and using (G.26) yields

We now convert this normalized eigenvector estimate directly into an estimator of the planted vector. Let |u^||\widehat{u}| denote coordinatewise absolute value, and define

‖|u^|−u‖2≤mins∈{−1,1}⁡‖s​u^−u‖2.\displaystyle\bigl\||\widehat{u}|-u\bigr\|_{2}\leq\min_{s\in\{-1,1\}}\|s\widehat{u}-u\|_{2}.

mins∈{−1,1}⁡‖s​u^−u‖22=2​(1−|⟨u^,u⟩|)≤2​(1−|⟨u^,u⟩|2).\displaystyle\min_{s\in\{-1,1\}}\|s\widehat{u}-u\|_{2}^{2}=2\bigl(1-|\langle\widehat{u},u\rangle|\bigr)\leq 2\bigl(1-|\langle\widehat{u},u\rangle|^{2}\bigr).

≤2​k​‖|u^|−u‖22+2​(k−m)2.\displaystyle\leq 2k\bigl\||\widehat{u}|-u\bigr\|_{2}^{2}+2(\sqrt{k}-\sqrt{m})^{2}. (G.30)

By (G.28), the conditional expectation of the first term is o⁡(k)o(k). Furthermore, on 𝒢\mathcal{G} we have m/k=1+O⁡(δn)m/k=1+O(\delta_{n}), and therefore

(k−m)2=O⁡(δn2​k)=o⁡(k).\displaystyle(\sqrt{k}-\sqrt{m})^{2}=O(\delta_{n}^{2}k)=o(k).

𝔼⁡[‖v~−v‖22​𝟏𝒢]=o⁡(k).\mathbb{E}\left[\|\widetilde{v}-v\|_{2}^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{G}}\right]=o(k). (G.31)

and hence

≤2​k​ℙ​(𝒢c)+2​(𝔼​m2)1/2​ℙ​(𝒢c)1/2=o⁡(k),\displaystyle\leq 2k\,\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}^{c})+2(\mathbb{E}m^{2})^{1/2}\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}^{c})^{1/2}=o(k),

We now show a lemma about symmmetrizing the estimator.

Lemma G.5 (Deterministic permutation averaging).

Consider the planted-submatrix model

Y=λ​v​v⊤+W,vi∼iidBernoulli⁡(ρ),\displaystyle Y=\lambda vv^{\top}+W,\qquad v_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\rho),

where the distribution of WW is invariant under simultaneous permutations of its rows and columns. Let A⁡(Y)∈ℝnA(Y)\in\mathbb{R}^{n} be any estimator of vv.

For each i∈[n]i\in[n], choose a fixed permutation πi∈Sn\pi_{i}\in S_{n} satisfying

πi​(1)=i,\displaystyle\pi_{i}(1)=i,

and let PπiP_{\pi_{i}} denote its permutation matrix. Define

Aπi​(Y):=Pπi⊤​A​(Pπi​Y​Pπi⊤),\displaystyle A^{\pi_{i}}(Y):=P_{\pi_{i}}^{\top}A\!\left(P_{\pi_{i}}YP_{\pi_{i}}^{\top}\right),

A¯1​(Y):=1n​∑i=1nA1πi​(Y).\overline{A}_{1}(Y):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A^{\pi_{i}}_{1}(Y). (G.32)

Then

𝔼⁡[(A¯1​(Y)−v1)2]≤1n​𝔼​‖A⁡(Y)−v‖22.\mathbb{E}\left[\bigl(\overline{A}_{1}(Y)-v_{1}\bigr)^{2}\right]\leq\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\|A(Y)-v\|_{2}^{2}. (G.33)

Proof.

For each i∈[n]i\in[n], define

vπi:=Pπi​v,Yπi:=Pπi​Y​Pπi⊤.\displaystyle v^{\pi_{i}}:=P_{\pi_{i}}v,\qquad Y^{\pi_{i}}:=P_{\pi_{i}}YP_{\pi_{i}}^{\top}.

(Yπi,vπi)=d(Y,v).(Y^{\pi_{i}},v^{\pi_{i}})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}(Y,v). (G.34)

(vπi)i=v1.\displaystyle(v^{\pi_{i}})_{i}=v_{1}.

=𝔼⁡[(Ai​(Y)−vi)2].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\bigl(A_{i}(Y)-v_{i}\bigr)^{2}\right]. (G.35)

≤1n​∑i=1n𝔼⁡[(A1πi​(Y)−v1)2]\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\bigl(A^{\pi_{i}}_{1}(Y)-v_{1}\bigr)^{2}\right]
=1n​∑i=1n𝔼⁡[(Ai​(Y)−vi)2]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\bigl(A_{i}(Y)-v_{i}\bigr)^{2}\right]

Finally, A¯1\overline{A}_{1} requires only nn evaluations of AA, together with permutations of the rows and columns of YY. Hence if AA is polynomial-time computable, then A¯1\overline{A}_{1} is also polynomial-time computable. ∎

Application to the planted vector.

Apply the lemma to the polynomial-time estimator v~​(Y)∈[0,1]n\widetilde{v}(Y)\in[0,1]^{n} constructed above from the leading eigenvector of the matrix estimator. We have already shown that

𝔼​‖v~−v‖22=o⁡(k)=o⁡(ρ​n).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\widetilde{v}-v\|_{2}^{2}=o(k)=o(\rho n).

Therefore, defining

v¯1​(Y):=1n​∑i=1n[Pπi⊤​v~​(Pπi​Y​Pπi⊤)]1,\displaystyle\overline{v}_{1}(Y):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[P_{\pi_{i}}^{\top}\widetilde{v}\!\left(P_{\pi_{i}}YP_{\pi_{i}}^{\top}\right)\right]_{1},

the lemma gives

𝔼⁡[(v¯1​(Y)−v1)2]=o⁡(ρ).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\bigl(\overline{v}_{1}(Y)-v_{1}\bigr)^{2}\right]=o(\rho).

Moreover, v¯1\overline{v}_{1} is computable in polynomial time, since it requires only nn calls to the polynomial-time procedure producing v~\widetilde{v}. Thus a polynomial-time minimax-rate estimator over θ​Kn,k\theta K_{n,k} would yield a polynomial-time estimator of the planted coordinate v1v_{1} with mean-squared error o⁡(ρ)o(\rho). Under the standard low-degree conjecture interpreting the Schramm–Wein degree-nΩ⁡(1)n^{\Omega(1)} estimation lower bound as a polynomial-time barrier, this gives the desired contradiction. ∎

Remark G.6 (Scope of the Schramm–Wein result).

The final step is deliberately stated conditionally. The theorem of Schramm and Wein is a rigorous lower bound for degree-nΩ⁡(1)n^{\Omega(1)} polynomial estimators; it does not by itself rule out every polynomial-time algorithm. Thus the complexity-theoretic conclusion for the convex-body example is conditional on the standard low-degree conjecture for planted-submatrix estimation.

Remark G.7 (Why the construction is useful).

The point of Kn,kK_{n,k} is that the computational difficulty is not hidden in the representation of the constraint set. Its gauge is the SDP (G.2), while the metric-entropy bound (G.8) shows that the entire convex relaxation remains statistically estimable at a scale well inside the conjectured computationally hard regime for planted-submatrix estimation. Hence the example separates efficient access to the convex body from efficient minimax-rate estimation over that body.
